stories.Headline: Airbnb is building an AI travel agent
stories.Summary:
Airbnb said on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that it is building its own AI travel agent and plans to release it in the first half of 2027. The company shared the plan in its third-quarter shareholder letter and on the earnings call that followed, saying it intends to build an "AI-native Airbnb." The agent is designed to help users research, plan and book trips on the platform. It is separate from Airbnb's AI customer support assistant, which is already running.

The company says the agent will not be a plain chatbot. It will draw on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements, including maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries, and assemble them in real time to fit each request. If a user wants a car rental, for example, the agent would generate a custom display for it, and it will also help invite co-travellers. After a booking is made, the agent is meant to help with changes to a reservation, payment problems, refunds and rebooking, and to offer 24-hour safety support, though Airbnb did not say what that support will involve. Over time, Airbnb wants it to plan a whole trip in one place, across homes, hotels, services and experiences, and CEO Brian Chesky said it will be able to go outside Airbnb's own listings while staying within travel.

Chesky explained the thinking on the earnings call. He said current AI agents such as Muse and Instinct handle simple routine jobs like restaurant reservations and appointments, but that travel is different because discovering where to go and stay is part of the experience. He cited a figure that 80 percent of travelers say they enjoy researching trips, and said people want to look at photos, compare homes and decide together with their companions. In his view, general-purpose agents are not the best tool for that, which is why Airbnb is making its own. He described the interface as "post-chat-based," with less text, though it will keep a chat element.

The announcement came with strong results. Revenue rose 19 percent to about $4.9 billion in the third quarter, with net income of $1.9 billion, and Airbnb raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast to the high teens from the mid-teens. Chesky said it was the company's fastest revenue growth in more than three years. The company also said it shipped more than 50 products and features in the quarter, nearly 70 percent more than a year earlier, and that its existing AI support assistant resolved around 40 percent of customer support issues without human agents, up from roughly 30 percent the previous quarter. Airbnb had previously said only that the agent would arrive within the next year, so the first-half 2027 window is a firmer commitment.

stories.Headline: CloudBolt Adds New AI Agent Governance Capabilities to Its Cloud Management Platform
stories.Summary:
CloudBolt Software, based in Rockville, Maryland, announced on November 5, 2026, new agent governance capabilities in its CloudBolt CMP cloud management platform. The features let AI agents provision and manage infrastructure under the same policies, permissions and limits that already apply to people. Platform teams decide which actions agents may run and which credentials and authentication they can use, and CMP enforces those choices every time an agent acts. The company said the capabilities are available now to all CMP customers, and teams new to the platform can try them through a no-cost plan.

Under the new setup, OAuth support maps each AI agent to a named user in CMP, so the agent inherits that person's groups, environments, rights and limits rather than relying on a shared service account. Agents can see only the blueprints administrators have published in the governed catalog, and policy pre-fills fields such as cluster, network and cost center. A request that would normally need 20 inputs to provision on Amazon EC2 may need only two or three. Administrators can require a maximum lifespan so agent-built resources do not run indefinitely, and approval workflows, budgets and quotas apply to agents just as they do to people. Each CMP action also carries its own AI setting, so routine work like power, snapshot and resize can be opened to agents while deleting a server stays limited to people, and a hidden action does not appear to agents at all.

CMP checks every agent action against the user's permissions and policies when it runs, regardless of how the request was worded or which AI model sent it. Agent requests land in the same order history and job records as portal requests, giving teams one audit trail across people and agents. A new agent dashboard records each session, including the tools called, the orders placed and the user the agent acted for. Yasmin Rajabi, chief operating officer at CloudBolt, said customers keep asking how to allow AI agents to do real infrastructure work without losing control, and that the same catalogs, approvals and cost policies customers built over the years now apply to every agent. Co-founder Alexandre da Rocha said that because every interface is becoming a chat window, the guardrails are what must be unified, and that CMP decides whether a given agent may act whatever the prompt says.

The company pointed to a gap between adoption and oversight, citing Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise survey of 3,235 business and IT leaders. In that survey, 74% expected their companies to use AI agents at least moderately by 2027, but only 21% said they have a mature governance model for agentic AI. The new capabilities build on Model Context Protocol support CloudBolt introduced in May and the natural-language interface that arrived with the CMP redesign in August. The announcement comes as other vendors also add agent controls, with Google Cloud extending governance tools across its agent runtimes and Smartsheet adding oversight features to its work platform.

stories.Headline: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling, and the S&P 500 tumbles 4.4%
stories.Summary:
Wall Street suffered a harsh sell-off driven by artificial intelligence stocks, and the S&P 500 index fell 4.4%. The Associated Press reported the drop on November 5, 2026, describing a market that was left reeling by the heavy selling in AI-linked companies. The decline then spread beyond the United States, as a second AP report said Asian benchmark indexes also moved lower on worries about AI after the American drop. The articles available here carry the headlines but little of the underlying detail, so they do not say which specific companies fell the most or what set off the selling. The one hard figure the articles provide is the 4.4% fall in the S&P 500, which is one of the broadest measures of the American stock market.

The second story, headlined as a decline in Asian benchmarks, ties the regional weakness directly to concern over AI and to the earlier tumble on Wall Street. Neither article, as provided, lists index levels, point losses, dollar values wiped out, or percentage moves for individual stocks. No new rule, law or requirement is attached to the sell-off in the material given, and no deadlines or other dates are mentioned beyond the day of publication. The articles do not name any executive, analyst, regulator or investor who spoke about the sell-off, and they offer no statements that can be attributed to a particular person or company. The Associated Press is the only source in the material, and it presents the move as a market event rather than the result of a single decision by one party.

Because no one is identified as responsible and no explanations are quoted, it would be inaccurate to say what caused investors to sell or who bears blame for the losses. For context, the surrounding AP pages show the sell-off sitting among a busy set of business headlines, including a bid rejected by Wendy's and a new Amazon Prime service. stories.Headline: North Carolina To Receive $7.6 Million in GM Data Privacy Settlement
stories.Summary:
General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle allegations that it collected and sold drivers' personal driving and location data without their permission. A coalition of attorneys general announced the deal in late October, and state outlets reported on it in early November 2026. North Carolina's share is roughly $7.66 million, while Ohio expects about $8 million. The case centered on the Smart Driver program run by GM's OnStar subsidiary, which tracked driving habits from 2016 to 2024, including hard braking, rapid acceleration, speeding above 80 miles per hour and late-night driving.

Investigators said some drivers were enrolled without consent, and that more than 370,000 others were wrongly told through the OnStar app that they were not enrolled. Ohio's attorney general put that figure at 380,000 drivers. The coalition also alleged that GM passed driving and location information to data brokers, which supplied it to insurance companies that used it to help set premiums. Ohio's account notes that the New York Times revealed in 2024 that GM had been sending driver behavior data to LexisNexis, which produced reports for insurers who then adjusted premiums or even denied coverage. GM discontinued the Smart Driver program in 2024, after the Times reporting.

Under the settlement, GM must get express consent before collecting or sharing driving and location data. It must also limit the information it collects, strengthen consumer privacy protections, and add oversight and training at dealerships. The deal also requires third-party data protection assessments. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission imposed its own five-year ban on GM disclosing driver location and behavior data to consumer reporting agencies. That order also requires affirmative express consent before data is collected or used, and makes it easier for consumers to opt out and delete collected data.

The North Carolina outlet described the coalition as bipartisan and made up of 36 states, led in North Carolina by Attorney General Jeff Jackson. Jackson said GM had promised drivers their information would stay private and would not go to insurers without their permission. Ohio's coverage said Ohio joined 34 other states and Washington, D.C., in the suit, and Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said GM broke consumers' trust by selling the data without their knowledge or consent. Wilson added that Ohioans should not have to worry that information gathered by their own vehicles will be used against them, and that companies must be held accountable when they put profits ahead of privacy.

stories.Headline: Stocks plunge as election results fuel AI regulation fears
stories.Summary:
US stocks fell sharply on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, after the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections raised fears that governments could slow or pause the construction of AI data centers. The S&P 500 fell 4.4%, its worst day since President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs shook markets in April 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833 points, or 3.4%, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%, leaving the Nasdaq 11.9% below the all-time high it set last month. The day followed a rally on Wednesday, when investors welcomed the end of election uncertainty and Trump's remarks that he would accept the results.

Voters appear to have driven the concern. Of 45 data center ballot initiatives around the country, voters backed restrictions in most of them, with 39 measures to restrict AI passing and only one, in North Dakota, voting against. Democratic candidates also won in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, regions seen as key for data centers. UBS analysts estimated that possible construction pauses could put roughly 30% of the data center capacity planned for 2028 at risk, and voters across parties say they dislike the higher power bills that data centers cause.

The selloff hit AI-linked companies hardest. In midday trading, Nvidia fell 8.2%, Micron nearly 14%, Intel 6.8% and Dell nearly 13%, while CoreWeave dropped over 12% and Nebius Group nearly 17%. SpaceX shares slid 9.5% and Tesla fell over 11%, after Elon Musk spent heavily against Democratic candidates in Texas who went on to win, including $230 million against Senate candidate James Talarico. Analyst Dan Ives said a SpaceX and Tesla merger now faces a tougher regulatory path in 2027. Michael Monaghan of Founders 100 ETF said markets rallied on certainty the day before, and that investors are now weighing possible political resistance to AI infrastructure, especially at the state and local levels.

The shock spread abroad. South Korea's KOSPI fell more than 4% in early trading, with SK hynix down 7.74% and Samsung Electronics down 5.96%, and the exchange triggered a sell sidecar, a five-minute halt on program sell orders. European shares were also pulled lower, and Swissquote analyst Ipek Ozkardeskaya described a rotation from technology to other sectors and from US to non-US markets. Gold rose just over 1% to $4,115 per ounce. Bobby Blanco of Strategic Wealth said the market is "on sale" for long-term buyers, and a Korean analyst noted that markets after midterms have tended to react more to good news than bad.

stories.Headline: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
stories.Summary:
Democrats swept Texas in the midterm elections, and the result may threaten the state's place as the fastest-growing data center market in the US. James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. Democrats will also take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa both made data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.

The change had already begun before the votes were counted. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits, and developers said his office had stopped answering their emails. Panelists at the DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, said Texas had been the easiest place to build for years until that point. Hinojosa backed tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to create construction jobs, but during her campaign she moved toward calling for a full moratorium.

The projects already underway in Texas are enormous. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts, roughly matching the nation's largest data center, SpaceX's Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than doubling the largest one now operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, meant mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts, which would make it the second-largest data center under construction in the US, behind only Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana. Any delays or moratoriums would add to worries that the AI buildout could stall, and banks and lenders are already becoming pickier about what they fund. Voters elsewhere sent a similar message, backing measures to shield ratepayers from higher electricity bills linked to data centers and, in some cases, favoring wider bans on new ones.

It is not clear that data center opposition drove the Texas results, and following through may prove difficult. Dallas County and nearby counties went blue, but Ellis County, which leads in data center permitting requests, voted for Abbott and Paxton, as did Mitchell and Scurry Counties in west Texas. Cameron County, another hot spot, shifted to the Democrats. Because decisions involve city governments, county officials and state offices, local leaders may resist sweeping state limits, and construction unions that supported some Democratic campaigns could push back against a moratorium.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's 15% Bond Yield Is a Warning for AI Debt. Here Are the Stocks Most Exposed.
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a "neocloud" provider of AI infrastructure services, was the subject of a November 3, 2026 Motley Fool article by Leo Sun, which argued that the company's bond yields are a warning for AI-related debt. The article said the average yield to maturity on CoreWeave's senior unsecured bonds ranges from 14.1% to 15.6%. It also said the company ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities and a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. Most of the senior notes were trading at about 80 cents on the dollar, a discount of roughly 20%.

On the business side, CoreWeave has grown from three data centers at the end of 2022 to 51 today, with more than a quarter-million Nvidia GPUs. Revenue rose from $16 million in 2022 to $5.13 billion in 2025, while its net loss widened from $31 million to $1.17 billion over the same period. The company spent about a quarter of its revenue on interest, paying $1.23 billion in 2025 and $1.18 billion in the first half of 2026. Its share count has risen 19% since its March 2025 IPO, and it holds $10.8 billion in convertible debt with cash coupons of 1.75% to 2.875%, which could dilute existing shareholders if converted into new shares at maturity.

Sun, writing for The Motley Fool, said the 20% discount on the notes suggests investors are not fully confident that CoreWeave will stay solvent through the early 2030s, when its senior bonds begin to mature in 2030. He noted that the company would probably have to issue even higher-yielding bonds if the Federal Reserve keeps raising its benchmark rates. Analysts expect revenue to climb from $5.13 billion in 2025 to $43.55 billion in 2028, but they see the net loss barely improving, from $1.20 billion to $1.09 billion. Sun concluded that this will make it hard for CoreWeave to expand without taking on more debt.

For context, the article compared CoreWeave with two faster-growing peers. Nebius ended its latest quarter with a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7, and IREN with 2.8, while their share counts rose about 15% and 78% respectively over the past two years. Nebius' senior notes carry average coupons of 1.7% to 2.2%, and IREN's convertible notes were issued at 1% to 3.5%. Sun said CoreWeave is much closer to trouble than its competitors, though it has a $104 billion backlog from the second quarter of 2026 to convert into revenue. He warned that if rates keep rising, pressure on CoreWeave could make it harder for smaller players such as Nebius and IREN to secure financing at reasonable rates, and he urged investors in neocloud stocks to recognize those long-term risks.

stories.Headline: Global media discuss mass communication in AI era - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A sub-forum of the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, brought together representatives of media, think tanks, government departments and other institutions from China and abroad. They called on media organizations to use intelligent technologies to deliver reporting that is accurate, fair, authoritative and trustworthy. The breakout session was titled Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Chinese Modernization and centered on the theme of AI Plus and a new consensus on global communication governance. Participants discussed how media can adapt to change, seize opportunities and meet challenges together in the AI era.

The event also included several firsts and launches. The world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchor made its official debut there. The sub-forum held a signing ceremony for the Xinhua News Agency AI Industry Alliance (Beijing Base), along with a launch ceremony for a research project on mobile news image technology and authenticity standards. Participants urged their media colleagues to build consensus and to promote dialogue among civilizations through openness and inclusiveness. The summit itself runs from Nov. 5 to 9 and draws nearly 500 delegates from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government departments and international organizations across 112 countries and regions.

Two speakers were singled out in the reports. Huo Xiaoguang, vice president of Xinhua News Agency, said traditional mainstream media around the world are generally going through major transformations as AI develops. He said China's mainstream media are carrying out systematic reforms to secure new competitive advantages in the emerging communication ecosystem. Xinhua, he added, is willing to work with all parties to safeguard media credibility, promote the inclusive sharing of technological achievements, and strengthen mutual understanding and friendship among different civilizations.

Bayo Onanuga, the Nigerian president's special adviser on information and strategy and his spokesman, said the profound impact of AI can no longer be ignored, and that much of it is positive. He argued that, unless people were willing to return to the Stone Age, they must face the trend and treat it seriously. The summit is co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality. Ahead of the gathering, Khalid Mahmood, chairman of the Board of Governors of the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad and a former Pakistani ambassador to China, told Xinhua that the summit would give news organizations worldwide an important platform to explore how technological progress can serve the public interest. He noted that AI has made it possible to access, process, analyze and distribute information at unprecedented speed, and he planned to attend.

stories.Headline: ICAIR 2026: Africa Risks Economic Dependence Without Home-grown AI Technologies, Experts Warn
stories.Summary:
Academic leaders and technology experts warned at a conference that Africa risks permanent economic dependence on advanced nations unless it shifts from importing artificial intelligence technologies to building its own. They spoke at the 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, known as ICAIR 2026, which ran from November 3 to 5, 2026, at the University of Lagos in Nigeria. The event was organised by the Machine Intelligence Research Group at the University of Lagos and carried the theme Artificial Intelligence for Africa's Sustainable Economic Growth. It brought together academic leaders, researchers and technology experts to examine how the continent could use AI for sustainable development.

The experts said Africa's economic future and technological sovereignty depend on developing home-grown AI models, building indigenous digital infrastructure and equipping its young population with relevant skills. Dr. Oladipupo Sennaike, who heads the local organising committee and chairs the planning committee, said Africa cannot remain a passive spectator in the latest technological revolution. He noted that the agricultural and industrial revolutions created new economic powers and that the digital revolution transformed the global economy, adding that Africa must position itself to benefit from the AI revolution. He urged African countries to move from importing AI solutions to developing technologies that address their own challenges.

In his keynote, Prof. Kanshukan Rajaratnam, director of the School for Data Science and Computational Thinking at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, said the defining challenge of the AI era is who will shape the technology and benefit from its economic opportunities. Sennaike wrote that the conference aimed to go beyond presenting research papers and to create an environment where people exchange ideas and find opportunities to work together. He named other confirmed keynote speakers as Dr. Sunday Oladejo of Stellenbosch University and Mr. Opeyemi Folorunsho, vice president of research and development at Moniepoint. He said the different backgrounds of the speakers would bring valuable perspectives on the link between research, innovation and industry application.

Sennaike said the conference was not only for computer scientists, listing software developers, data scientists, entrepreneurs, investors, lecturers, students, policymakers and journalists among those who should take part. He said physical and virtual participation were both provided because not everyone could travel to Lagos. He stressed that Africa has considerable talent and no shortage of ideas, but must keep building research capacity, institutional support, investment and collaboration to turn those ideas into solutions. He added that the responsibility of shaping Africa's AI future cannot be left to other parts of the world.

The article adds that it raises questions about whether other overseas customers could face similar limits.

The article describes the episode as evidence of regulatory uncertainty facing cloud providers that use offshore facilities to serve Chinese technology companies. The next development to watch, it says, is whether Oracle discloses the financial impact and whether it can replace the lost capacity with commitments from other customers. stories.Headline: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Nov 5 a set of policies meant to win local support for data centers, in the works since August and released just after the US midterm elections. The company said it will stop using non-disclosure agreements with public officials when it negotiates or discusses future sites, though proprietary information will stay confidential. It will also give residents access to construction plans and the likely effects on traffic, noise and lighting. Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, said the centers will provide ongoing work because the hardware inside must be updated every three to five years. He added that one OpenAI facility in southern Ohio is expected to create 2,500 long-term jobs with an average annual salary of US$80,000 (S$102,000).

The announcement followed a rough week for the industry at the ballot box. Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia. Seven municipalities passed permanent bans on new data centers, and ten others voted to cap construction by size or electrical footprint. Defiance, Ohio, approved a ban on new centers needing more than 25 megawatts by 63% to 37%, while 77% of voters in Edgewater, Florida, and 82% in Alhambra, California, backed outright bans. Bloomington, Illinois, and Peru and Wiscasset in Maine approved moratoriums, and in Wilmington, Ohio, eight in ten voters rejected a rural rezoning that would have paved the way for a new center.

Democrats also flipped governorships in Texas, Georgia and Ohio with candidates who promised to pause new data center permits and tighten construction rules. Shares of data center operators and power companies tumbled on Nov 4 as investors bet the results could bring tougher permitting, higher costs and slower building. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said at a separate event on Nov 4 that the industry needs to do a better job explaining to local communities why data centers can help them. Lehane described the new projects as unlike the older idea of a black box in a pasture that gave little to its neighbors, and he noted that partners such as Oracle build and own much of OpenAI's data center infrastructure, with the capacity dedicated to the start-up. Elon Musk, who reportedly gave $224 million to Republican candidates in Texas, wrote on X that data centers in space looked pretty appealing.

The vote reflects public attitudes that were already visible before the election. A June survey by Reuters and Ipsos found that only 14% of Americans would support a data center being built near them. OpenAI's leaders have spent two years building ties with President Donald Trump's administration to shape federal AI policy, and Sam Altman gave US$1 million to Trump's inaugural committee, while Brockman gave US$25 million to a Trump super PAC in 2025. Asked how the company would answer skepticism from Democrats, Lehane pointed to his long experience in the party, including serving as a top lawyer and spokesperson in the Clinton administration and as press secretary to Al Gore during his presidential run. The articles do not say how communities will respond to the new policies.

stories.Headline: Zetrix AI and China Academy of Information and Communications Technology Unveil Know Your Agent (KYA) Service to Bring Trust and Accountability to AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Zetrix AI Berhad, working with the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT), announced a Know Your Agent (KYA) service on November 5, 2026. Zetrix AI's Group Managing Director, TS Wong, made the announcement at the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen, China. The launch was made at the same time at the ICT Development Forum 2026 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The service is meant to bring more trust, transparency and accountability to AI agents, which are increasingly being used to make decisions, deal with businesses and carry out transactions on their own.

Under the framework, each participating AI agent receives a verifiable digital identity tied to an authenticated person or organisation. Owners can set limits on what an agent may do, including which services it can reach, what information it can use, who it can transact with and how much it can spend. A business could, for example, let an agent pay approved suppliers up to a set limit while requiring human approval above it. When an agent hands a task to another agent, the delegated authority cannot go beyond what was originally granted, permissions can be revoked, and signed records of activity create an auditable trail. The service builds on W3C Verifiable Credentials and uses AvatarLabs' Agentic Wallet technology to manage credentials, check delegated permissions and keep evidence of what agents do.

Wong said greater autonomy must come with greater accountability, and that the aim is a future where every agent can be identified, every permission verified and every action traced to an accountable owner. Xiaoyu YOU, Head of International Department, ASTRON network, CAICT, said the need for such services will keep growing as agentic AI takes on more responsibility. She said she expects the joint service to help build a cross-border trusted network enabling interoperable agentic AI worldwide. The companies say the idea is to let agents operate with more independence while staying identifiable, accountable and trusted across borders.

The launch includes a planned cross-border pilot involving organisations from the Middle East, Africa, China and ASEAN, with participation subject to confirmation. It will test how agent identity and authorisation can be recognised across jurisdictions while local control over identity systems and trust decisions is kept, covering areas such as cross-border trade, digital payments and government services. Zetrix AI and CAICT plan to submit the findings to the International Telecommunication Union's study group on standardisation, known as ITU-T SG17, through its Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI, and the results are also to go to IEEE and other standards bodies. Separately, on November 4, CAICT, a research institute under China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, led 20 founding organisations including Huawei, Alibaba, Tencent and Xiaomi in releasing a self-discipline convention on AI agent development at the same Wuzhen summit. It sets out eight measures, among them trust systems, interoperability, security, governance and user protection, and the founding companies pledged to lead on implementing them under oversight from industry associations and the public.

The rest of the article is general advice, so a full account of the correction itself is not possible from this material. The article says tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500.

It cites Goldman Sachs research finding that, as of September, roughly half of the index's earnings per share growth in 2026 has come from corporate investment tied to AI, such as building data centers. Some prominent analysts and economists, it adds, have warned that the hundreds of billions of dollars AI companies are spending on chips, memory and data centers are too costly and may not pay off. Gran says no one knows what comes next, and that a correction of 10% would not necessarily turn into a bear market of 20%. Gran's advice is to hold a broadly diversified portfolio, such as an S&P 500 ETF, for five years or more and ride out the volatility. He points to the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, which has returned about 12% annualized over the past five years despite an 18.2% decline in 2022.

He notes that the S&P 500 has delivered annualized returns of 9.98% over 98 years. Investors holding a few volatile tech stocks who want to reduce risk, he says, should do so before any big sell-off, and those losing sleep might diversify beyond tech or beyond funds tracking the Nasdaq-100. A related headline in the article's reading list says Goldman Sachs expects S&P 500 earnings growth to slow to 18% in 2027. The article does not say when or whether a correction will be confirmed, and it gives no further detail on what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kids Hooked on AI Chatbots Are Showing Dramatically Worse Mental Health
stories.Summary:
A new survey from the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation has found that heavy use of AI chatbots among children is tied to worse mental health. Futurism reported on the findings on November 5, 2026, and NaturalNews.com summarized the report the following day. According to the survey, 90 percent of children aged nine to 17 have used an AI chatbot. The majority, 58 percent, use one for schoolwork, and 57 percent said they also turn to AI when feeling sad, stressed, lonely or overwhelmed.

The survey found that the use goes beyond coping. Twelve percent of students said they use AI for friendship or companionship, and a separate survey from last year found that nearly one in five high schoolers said they or a friend had used AI for a romantic relationship. Young people who turn to AI while in emotional distress were more likely to report poor mental health and well-being, along with a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. A 15-year-old in Texas, Arjun Sharda, told Oregon Public Broadcasting he kept asking ChatGPT whether he would be okay after fearing he would fail an early chemistry test.

Kayla Anderson, a psychologist and the JED Foundation's vice president of research and evaluation, said the data allowed researchers to compare how young people use AI with indicators of well-being and suicidal history. She cautioned that the evidence does not establish causation. In her words, it is unclear whether AI use contributes to poor mental health or whether students already in distress are more likely to turn to it. Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who was not involved in the work, pointed to other research suggesting both may be true. She said kids with worse mental health seek out AI for help, but that the use may make those struggles worse.

The findings come amid a wave of government action. NaturalNews.com reported that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed 13 bills on September 15, 2026, to regulate minors' access to social media and AI chatbots, including limits on addictive features for users under 16. New York's law, signed by Governor Kathy Hochul, bans unsafe AI companion features for minors and takes effect January 1, 2027. New York City also moved in early September to bar student AI use in public schools through eighth grade. Florida has sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging the company hid serious risks of ChatGPT, particularly for children, and NaturalNews.com says ChatGPT faces at least eight lawsuits alleging it worsened users' mental health.

stories.Headline: AI & Tech Brief: Exclusive | AI safety groups target committee gavels
stories.Summary:
A conservative AI policy group has warned Republicans that they need a major rethink of their approach to artificial intelligence before the next presidential election. The Alliance for a Better Future shared a post-midterms memo first with Semafor, reported on November 4, 2026 by senior tech correspondent Ashley Gold. The memo argues that AI policy helped deliver Democratic majorities in the midterms, and that its effect was closely tied to economic concerns. It says Republicans who adjust correctly can turn AI into an asset in 2028, both for the country and for the party.

The memo describes liberal efforts to link economic worries with anti-elite populist feeling about AI as a "deadly one-two punch." It says those worries pushed AI up the list of voter concerns so quickly that Republicans did not notice. Republican candidates and their allies also failed to answer Democratic attacks that tied their candidates to a pro-AI and data center message, the memo says. It warns that fully embracing President Trump's light-touch approach to AI regulation would be a mistake for future Republican candidates.

The group recommends several steps. These include passing bills on chatbots and children, writing Trump's voluntary AI accord into law, and adopting economic policies that help workers. It also urges Republicans to push companies toward uses such as curing disease and away from "experiments that only benefit the developers themselves." The memo says it would be political malpractice for Republicans not to correct their course on superintelligence policy, since they risk permanently handing the issue to Democrats.

The memo comes from a group led by Janet Kelly, a former Virginia Republican official. The Alliance for a Better Future focuses on pro-family, pro-worker AI policy, and groups such as the Heritage Foundation sit on its advisory council. The group is pressing for stronger AI guardrails than the Trump administration currently supports. The articles do not say how Republican leaders or the White House have responded to the memo.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Stations Face New AI Ad Disclosure Requirements.
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania has become the latest state to regulate artificial intelligence in advertising. Gov. Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act on October 22, 2026, after the legislature passed Senate Bill 806 earlier that month. The measure moved through the Senate by a vote of 48-2 and the House by 163-40, after winning unanimous approval in committees in both chambers. It takes effect on December 21, 2026, and it may reach ads that are seen by Pennsylvania consumers no matter where the advertiser is based.

The law requires advertisers to disclose AI use only when synthetic content gives consumers a false impression about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised. Synthetic content covers images, video, audio and text that were generated or significantly modified with AI, though text-only content is excluded, as are parody, satire, commentary, criticism and material that is evidently fictional. A disclosure must be clear and conspicuous, appear when the synthetic content is first presented, and use the same medium as the ad. For radio, podcast and streaming audio, it must be delivered at a volume and cadence that a listener can hear and understand, and where technically feasible it should be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. The attorney general and district attorneys can seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $3,000, along with attorney fees and court costs, and prosecutors do not have to prove an advertiser acted intentionally.

State Sen. Nick Pisciottano, a Democrat from Allegheny County who sponsored the bill, called it a major step for consumer protection. He said consumers deserve to know when AI is used to create a false impression of a product or service, and that the bill sets a commonsense transparency standard while still letting businesses use the technology. The tech industry group NetChoice opposed the measure in an October 4 letter to lawmakers. It argued that federal and state laws already ban deceptive advertising, so an AI-specific regime adds no protection, and it warned that the formatting rules could overwhelm short videos, small display ads and audio spots.

Many questions remain open, especially for broadcasters. Unlike New York and California, Pennsylvania does not expressly exempt stations that carry commercials made by third parties, and the law does not say whether stations could be held liable for ads produced by outside advertisers. It also does not define a false consumer perception, explain how much an ad must be modified before disclosure applies, or say whether penalties are counted per ad, per airing or some other way. Legal analysts suggest companies review their AI-generated ad assets and ask agencies and production vendors how those assets were made, and they note that a disclosure does not protect an ad that otherwise violates false advertising laws. Other states are also moving, including California, where a law signed last month requires ads with synthetic performers to disclose that, and New Jersey, where a pending proposal would limit generative AI in advertisements for dwellings.

stories.Headline: MeitY unveils indigenous AI Models EKA-1, Dhr 2B and 5B under IndiaAI mission20261103210340
stories.Summary:
On 3 November 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology unveiled three indigenous artificial intelligence foundation models, EKA-1, Dhr 2B and Dhr 5B. The models were developed by two Bengaluru-based companies, Socket AI and ZenteiQ, under the Foundation Model initiative of the IndiaAI Mission. EKA-1, made by Socket AI, is a 26-billion-parameter model for mathematics, coding and reasoning, trained on 7.5 trillion tokens. It supports more than 100 Indian and international languages as well as programming languages, and can handle multi-step tasks and execute code. Dhr 2B and Dhr 5B, made by ZenteiQ, are mixture-of-experts models trained from scratch on Google Cloud Tensor Processing Units.

The Dhr models support English and 10 Indian languages and can run on tested mobile hardware without an internet connection. ZenteiQ said it is releasing the model weights under the Apache 2.0 licence, with technical documentation and evaluation tools, through AIKosh. The models are accessible through AIKosh for researchers, students, innovators, enterprises and the general public. MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan said the models have specific uses beyond general-purpose work, including mathematics, coding, scientific research and cybersecurity. He highlighted their ability to run in air-gapped environments, which he said could support wider adoption of enterprise artificial intelligence.

Krishnan said the initiative would strengthen India's strategic autonomy in artificial intelligence and widen the availability of models suited to domestic needs. He said smaller models could improve productivity and efficiency across applications, and that the government would keep supporting their refinement and development. He described the models as a wider national resource because they are open to the public through AIKosh. A day earlier, on 2 November 2026, MeitY had launched a handbook on Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI training. Krishnan unveiled that handbook, developed with support from the iSPIRT Foundation, at a roundtable in Bengaluru.

The DEPA handbook sets out a techno-legal framework that lets institutions collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data. It combines contractual permissions, controlled computing environments and privacy safeguards, and it tracks data provenance so the origin, permissions and use of data can be traced through training. Krishnan said India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to use data responsibly and securely, and that MeitY is committed to taking the framework forward. Principal Scientific Adviser Ajay Kumar Sood said that under DEPA the model travels to the data rather than the reverse, which he said enables multi-party and cross-border collaboration. The roundtable drew representatives from government, industry, academia and research.

stories.Headline: Embodied AI's Next Frontier: Integrating Intelligence with Real-World Systems
stories.Summary:
New research published on November 4, 2026, highlights the challenge of integrating intelligence, sensing, movement, computing, energy management and connectivity into embodied AI systems that can perform reliably in demanding environments. The findings come from a white paper titled From Specialized to General-Purpose: 2026 White Paper on Embodied AI Technology Evolution and Industrial Deployment. It was jointly published by Avnet, the National and Local Co-Built Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center and GYH.AI. Embodied AI combines artificial intelligence with physical systems such as robots and autonomous machines, enabling them to perceive their surroundings, make decisions and act in the physical world.

The research identifies four factors that will influence the shift from specialized embodied AI applications toward broader industrial deployment. System integration is fundamental to performance, because AI models, computing platforms, sensors, motion control, energy management and communications must function as a coordinated system. Technology selection must reflect application requirements, balancing performance, energy efficiency, reliability, scalability and cost. The path to general-purpose embodied AI will be gradual, building on specialized systems designed for defined tasks, and industrial deployment requires lifecycle planning covering testing, software compatibility, component availability, safety, maintenance and long-term support.

Edward Tsaur, VP of Avnet Design Services, Marketing & Communications for Asia Pacific, said much of the discussion around embodied AI focuses on individual technologies, but the next stage will depend on how well they work together. He said the challenge is not just making systems smarter but ensuring they perform reliably, adapt to changing conditions and deliver consistent results over time. He added that across Asia Pacific there is growing interest in intelligent systems for manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and other operational environments. He said collaboration across the technology ecosystem will be critical to translating advances into practical solutions, looking beyond individual components to how hardware, software and engineering expertise can work together.

Separately, Envision announced on November 2, 2026, the world's first commercial deployment of an integrated 800-volt direct current power system in a large-scale AI data center. The system is powering live computing workloads at Envision's Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, delivering power end to end from grid input to computing loads. The 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, bringing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. The system combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware, coordinated in real time by Envision's Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model.

Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems, said AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage and the grid to meet computing demand. He said the integrated 800V DC system is now powering live computing workloads, demonstrating an end-to-end architecture that connects renewable energy supply with computing demand. The Galaxy campus began operations in August 2026 and has a planned capacity of 3GW, designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision aims to scale the approach through its Mission Gobi initiative, which targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Launches GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst: Adds GIFs, SVG Export and 6-Second API Generation
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released Images 2.6 on November 4, 2026, rolling it out across ChatGPT, Codex and the API. The core of the release is GPT-Image-2.6, which ships to developers as two models called Flare and Sunburst. OpenAI says the update generates images 50% faster than before. It also adds GIF output, SVG export, edits guided by markup, and a new complexity setting.

The two models are aimed at different jobs. Flare is built for quick iteration and can return an image in as little as 6 seconds when quality is set to low. Sunburst targets detailed compositions and more consistent results across repeated edits, at medium or high quality. The complexity parameter has three levels, low, medium and high, and defaults to high if left out; OpenAI warns that higher settings can add delay and cause unwanted changes, and there is no separate fee for adjusting it. Pricing is token-based and the same for both models, listed at $8 per million image tokens in and $30 per million out.

In ChatGPT, users can turn a prompt or a photo into an animated GIF, change the animation speed, edit individual frames and share the result. They can also save and tag reference images of people, pets and characters and reuse them without uploading again. Markup-guided edits are listed as supported for both models in the API guide, and OpenAI says markup is coming to the API. The reviewer of the release noted that OpenAI has not published benchmark scores or a per-image cost table for 2.6.

On usage, OpenAI says people now generate more than 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and the API, up from more than 3 billion eight weeks earlier at the Images 2.5 launch. That works out to over 500 million images a day. The Japanese service AIVideoFree, based in Singapore, announced support for both models on November 5, charging 23 credits per image and giving new users 100 free credits, enough for about four images. The company said Sunburst took first place on the Image Arena comparison site as of November 4, according to DesignArena.

stories.Headline: Democrats win, vow data center halt, rattle AI stocks in US and Korea
stories.Summary:
Democrats won the U.S. midterm elections, and the result immediately shook markets tied to artificial intelligence. On the 5th, the Nasdaq fell 5.52% in one day, and Reuters reported that about $2.5 trillion in market value of Nasdaq companies disappeared, the largest single-day drop on record. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix also fell for two straight days on the 5th and 6th. Other stocks took hits too, with CoreWeave down about 7 percent, Iren about 6 percent, Oracle 4.3 percent and Cipher Mining 17 percent.

The central worry is that Democratic governors-elect will act on pledges to pause new data centers. The Information reported that 34 of 36 gubernatorial candidates who were elected or likely to win backed at least one kind of data center regulation. Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, where the industry is concentrated. Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to lead Texas in more than 30 years, defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and wants approvals halted until lawmakers pass rules, local residents given a say, households shielded from grid costs, and industry tax breaks ended. Texas accounts for about a quarter of U.S. data center capacity due online by 2030, and Wells Fargo puts its share of planned capacity at 27 percent.

Hinojosa said voters had delivered a mandate for change, and told CNN her team would prepare legislation to protect residents from the harms of data centers, with a pause until safeguards exist. She takes office in January. Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms said new construction should be temporarily halted while stakeholders discuss future policy, and Ohio's Amy Acton pledged to stop projects that do not fully cover power and water costs, disclose information and meet environmental standards. In Congress, Annie Andrews of South Carolina has proposed a two-year moratorium on new data centers, while Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan called for pausing or halting advanced AI development. Aidan Yao of Amundi told Reuters the election was less a vote on President Trump than a vote on AI.

Data centers that already hold permits should be less affected, but new projects in states with Democratic governors could become hard to build. Governors influence permits, regulations and tax incentives, though lasting rules and the end of tax breaks in Texas would need the Legislature. Goldman Sachs estimated that about 45% of planned U.S. data center capacity could be affected if restrictions spread, and Morgan Stanley analysts saw a high risk of delay for Ohio projects, including a 10-gigawatt project involving Nvidia. Residents had already protested over higher electricity bills and water shortages before the vote. The Texas House was still undecided the morning after the election, and Democrats needed a net gain of 14 seats there.

stories.Headline: Expedia Says Travelers Plan With AI Agents but Book Direct
stories.Summary:
Travelers are increasingly using AI assistants to plan trips, but they still tend to complete their bookings with brands they trust, according to Expedia Group. CEO Ariane Gorin made the point on the company's third-quarter earnings call, held around November 4, 2026. She said the real strength of agentic AI is in discovery, and that people want to book with a brand that will take care of them if something goes wrong. Traffic from agents is high intent, she said, and third-party data shows Expedia leading in citation share in the U.S. She told CNBC the company has not yet seen AI agents change customers' booking habits, and that travel's complexities would make it hard for AI to fully replace travel services.

On the numbers, Expedia grew gross bookings 11% and revenue 12% in the quarter, while B2B bookings rose 19%. Advertising growth slowed to 7% from 13% the prior quarter, and CFO Derek Andersen said product changes are coming to give advertisers better campaign tools. Expedia has partnered with Google in AI Mode, announced a Meta Muse integration expected to go live in the U.S., and is testing OpenAI's new ad products. Qantas is the first partner on Expedia's new agentic template, and Reserve Now, Pay Later has been rolled out across all its brands. Inside the company, an agentic voice experience on Vrbo resolved more than 15% of inbound contacts in its first two months, and travelers who used the new activity agent were twice as likely to book an activity within seven days.

Gorin said agent traffic does not appear to cut into direct traffic, and is either incremental or taken from other paid channels. She added that the volume is too small to draw conclusions, and the company said the economics of its agent partnerships are still being worked out. She also said a small team built an autonomous hotel onboarding agent in less than a quarter, work that once took multiple quarters and many more people. In the booking flow, a compare agent and a property expert agent help travelers weigh hotels, which she said pushes people deeper into the funnel and leads to larger purchases. CNBC reported that Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance came in below analysts' expectations.

Rival Booking Holdings reported a similar picture on its own earnings call on November 3, 2026. CFO Ewout Steenbergen said users of its AI assistants at Priceline and Agoda converted at about twice the rate of non-users, and Agoda assistant users had average booking values about 20% higher. Referrals from large language models still account for significantly less than 1% of Booking.com's room nights, he said, though they have accelerated in recent weeks. Booking Holdings expects a slowdown in the fourth quarter, forecasting a 1% to 3% increase in room nights and a 2% to 4% rise in gross bookings. CEO Glenn Fogel suggested regulation could slow adoption of horizontal personal AI agents in parts of the world, particularly Europe.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s FlashProve Aims to Prove Which AI Model Wrote an Answer
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has released FlashProve, an open-source prototype for what it calls provable inference, which lets anyone confirm which model produced a given AI answer without seeing the model's weights. Technology Org reported the news on November 5, 2026, saying a single Nvidia H100 GPU can now generate cryptographic proofs for a 400-billion-parameter model at about 110 tokens per second, and that an ordinary computer can check each proof in seconds. The provider first publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint that pins down one exact set of weights while keeping them hidden. It then produces proof files showing that the committed model generated the exact tokens in a reply, and anyone holding the commitment, the prompt and the reply can run the check. The system relies on a zkSNARK, a proof that a computation ran correctly and reveals nothing else about it.

Anthropic tested the system on Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that uses about 17 billion parameters per token, with publicly available 4-bit weights. The offline commitment takes about 39 minutes on a server with one H100 and 24 CPU cores, and it stays valid for about 16 million requests. Proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 223 seconds, and each proof is 18.78 MB, or about 19 MB for a 1,024-token request. A client downloads a commitment of about 6.5 MB, and a proof is checked in 17 seconds on 24 threads or 21 seconds on a single thread. Proving still costs far more than serving, taking roughly 70 to 95 times as long per GPU as running the same requests through vLLM, while one earlier open-source effort needed 14.3 hours and produced a 93.6 GB proof for 1,000 tokens of the same model.

The work comes from Anthropic's researchers, who say Claude produced much of the improvement. To make the result auditable, the team stated its top-level security guarantees in Lean, a formal verification language, and released a slow but provably correct Lean verifier alongside a fast C++ one. The release, which includes a technical report, a protocol specification, prover and verifier code and the Lean proofs, is under the Apache 2.0 license on GitHub. The researchers described it as intermediate progress rather than a completed research agenda, and said they want others to take what has been done and improve it. Anthropic notes that no lab has deployed the system.

The researchers say the aim is to let users, evaluators and regulators check that the model being served is the one claimed, guarding against cheaper substitutes, tampering with the token stream, or a more advanced model posing as an authorized weaker one to dodge monitoring. The prototype has clear limits: it proves an exact integer version of the model under greedy decoding, so floating-point or sampled replies may drift from the proven computation. It supports only mixture-of-experts models, handles contexts of up to 1,024 tokens, and leaves side-channel attacks such as timing measurements out of scope. Anthropic had set a public goal of building a provable inference prototype by September 30, 2026, and says it met that goal through a separate project that signs its inference traffic and recomputes it on a trusted server, while FlashProve pursues the same aim through cryptography alone. Model routing is now routine across the industry, and the EU has opened its first AI Act enforcement case against OpenAI and Anthropic, which is the backdrop for the interest in provenance.

stories.Headline: KPI Partners Inaugurates Expanded Hyderabad Office to Scale Agentic and Enterprise AI Delivery
stories.Summary:
The articles provided do not actually report on KPI Partners opening an expanded Hyderabad office, so that event cannot be described from them. What they do cover is two separate pieces of enterprise AI news from early November 2026. On November 3, TechGig reported that Neuraluna, a Seattle-based enterprise AI company, announced a larger presence in India. On November 4, The Register published a sponsored feature describing a full-stack enterprise AI offering that ASUS unveiled at NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on October 21 and 22.

Neuraluna was founded in December 2024 and already serves enterprise customers across the US, Europe and the Middle East. Its platform lets experts build teams of AI agents around their own knowledge and methods without writing code, and firms can use those teams on complex projects or to turn specialist expertise into digital services. Each client engagement runs in its own isolated workspace so that data and agents never cross between organisations, and the platform draws on models from several AI providers to avoid vendor lock-in. Customers keep control of their information, permissions and AI usage. The company also runs an Access Program offering free and discounted access to nonprofits, researchers, educators and civic teams, and it says it works with business schools, consulting firms and medical consultancies.

Neuraluna was co-founded by Dinesh Chahlia, an IIT Delhi alumnus who serves as chief executive, and Phani Solomou, a London Business School alumna. Chahlia said the India expansion is meant to give the country's deep pools of expertise more reach, and that the company is there to empower experts rather than automate them. Solomou said AI is changing what clients can do for themselves and what they will pay experts for, and that Neuraluna helps firms apply their expertise at a scale and cost that makes new services and markets commercially viable. The company says the move reflects India's growing role in its global enterprise AI strategy.

The ASUS feature, written as sponsored content, places such moves in a wider shift toward companies running AI in-house. It cites IDC figures showing the worldwide server market grew 30 percent in a single year to $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, with inference expected to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year. ASUS calls its Berlin announcement the Enterprise Agentic AI Solution, built from AI servers, a software stack and a services operation called ASUS AI HUB. Paul Ju, senior vice president at ASUS, argued that agentic AI workloads lean heavily on CPUs, which creates bottlenecks in conventional GPU-focused servers. The hardware includes the 3U hybrid-cooled XA NR11-E12L and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12, both built on NVIDIA's HGX Rubin NVL8 board, and ASUS claims up to 50 percent less maintenance time on them.

stories.Headline: “AI will generate nearly half of network traffic by 2035”
stories.Summary:
Nokia published its Global Network Traffic Report on 4 November 2026 from its base in Espoo, Finland, forecasting that artificial intelligence will drive nearly half of global network traffic by 2035. The company says networks will increasingly have to serve connected machines as well as people, with AI pushing up demand for uplink capacity, faster response times and processing closer to users and devices. It expects total traffic to nearly quadruple from 2026 levels to almost 3,789 exabytes per month, with 44% of that driven by AI. DCD, republishing a piece from SDxCentral two days later, put overall growth at 28 percent a year and the AI-native share at roughly 1,681 exabytes per month.

The report breaks the AI figures down further. Traffic generated directly by AI applications and workflows is forecast to rise 60-fold from this year's level, at a 58 percent compound annual growth rate, reaching 987 exabytes per month or 26 percent of global traffic. Another 694 exabytes per month, or 18 percent, is expected to come from AI-influenced traffic such as extra video consumption or online shopping. Agentic AI traffic is projected to grow about 160-fold to 585 exabytes per month, a 76 percent rate, while physical AI traffic from robots and robotaxis is set to grow 105-fold to around 67 exabytes per month, a 68 percent rate. Physical AI is expected to send more than 90% of its traffic over the uplink by 2035.

Most AI traffic is expected to stay in the central cloud, but edge and metro core infrastructure is projected to carry 36% of AI-native traffic by 2035, with the edge handling nine percent and the metro core 27 percent. Nokia links this shift to more efficient models, low-latency needs and data sovereignty requirements, which it says will support a more distributed setup it calls the AI grid. Enterprise AI traffic is forecast to grow at a 59 percent rate, faster than consumer AI, with industrial IoT devices such as cameras, drones and sensors producing about 70 percent of it. Beyond AI, the report says fixed wireless access will account for more than one-third of consumer cellular traffic by 2035.

Pallavi Mahajan, Nokia's Chief Technology and AI Officer, said AI is changing what networks must provide, not only how much traffic they carry. She argued that networks built for traditional internet applications will have to support machines that need real-time responses and strain the uplink, and that network readiness should be central to AI planning rather than an afterthought. Nokia also warned that rising uplink demand will stress cellular networks, noting that latency and jitter begin to climb once a cell's uplink utilization passes 70 percent during busy hours. The report rests on a bottom-up model of consumer, enterprise and AI traffic, combining application usage, device activity and agentic workflows with third-party research, expert review and Nokia lab testing.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Tries to Ease Backlash Against AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a National Community Compact on Thursday, November 6, 2026, promising to pay for the power its data centers use and to give communities more say over construction. The announcement came two days after midterm elections that went against the data center buildout supporting the AI industry. Reuters reported on November 4 that 41 data-center-related ballot measures went before voters, and according to Ballotpedia, all but one moved in an anti-data-center direction. Democrats also won the governorships of Texas, Georgia and Ohio, and those winners had promised to pause new data-center permits and tighten construction rules.

Under the compact, OpenAI says it will cover the electricity it consumes and the incremental infrastructure costs needed to serve its sites. It will provide financial assurances before major spending begins, so other utility customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled. The company will disclose site-level water and electricity use, publish construction plans, and commission independent noise studies before operations start and then every year afterward. It will also stop requiring nondisclosure agreements from public officials as a condition of negotiations, though it keeps narrow protections for security and commercially sensitive information. The compact outlines locally tailored agreements for future campuses, community input into development plans, and annual public progress reports.

OpenAI also released proposals for government action. These call for utility rules that assign large customers the grid costs they create, easier connections for facilities that can safely reduce demand, faster transmission upgrades and expanded clean-electricity tax incentives. The company also wants public tax-incentive terms, measurable commitments, and ways to recover benefits when developers fall short. OpenAI said the proposals build on its Stargate Community commitments from January, followed by specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability, and called this announcement the next step in that effort.

JP Perez-Etchegoyen, chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm Onapsis, noted that the commitments apply only to campuses OpenAI owns and operates, not to capacity built by its partners. He said OpenAI's own blueprint concedes that voluntary measures do not provide durable confidence, and that what would reduce uncertainty is those proposals becoming law for everyone building AI capacity, plus independent verification. Until then, he said, enterprises should treat the compact as a signal, not a planning assumption. Bloomberg reported that about 40% of pending U.S. data center capacity is planned for states where new governors have promised to stop or pause construction. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh estimated that spending cuts and slower approvals could keep up to 10 gigawatts from coming online in 2027 as scheduled, and Data Center Watch found that 94% of elected governors support regulating or restricting data center development.

stories.Headline: Want Google Search In The Classroom? You'll Need AI As Well, What It Means For NYS
stories.Summary:
Google has announced a change to its K-12 education software under which schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose student access to Google Search entirely. Under the new framework, AI tools will be switched off by default for student accounts, and school administrators will have to opt in manually to turn them on. Because Google has built generative AI deeply into the backend of its search, it will no longer offer a standard version of Search without AI. If a district toggles the AI features off, student accounts will simply show a message saying Search is unavailable. WIBX reported on the policy on November 6, 2026, and a Yakima Herald-Republic headline from November 3 describes it the same way, saying students using Google search in classroom accounts will need access to AI tools.

The practical effect is an all-or-nothing choice for districts. In New York State, which the WIBX report says has strict rules on student privacy and technology, New York City Public Schools already enforce an outright ban on generative AI for students from Pre-K through 8th grade. Proposed state legislation would further restrict unmonitored AI tools in the lower grades. If those bans stay in place, the report says, districts statewide must legally block Google's AI features, which would cut off Google Search on all district-issued Chromebooks and managed Google accounts.

New York school boards therefore face a hard decision as the policy rolls out. They can relax their local AI restrictions to keep student access to Google Search, or they can move student devices to alternative search engines that do not use AI. Google points to a new feature called Guided Learning, which is designed to tutor students step by step instead of writing answers for them. Critics, according to the report, argue that the policy leaves schools with little real choice. The articles provided do not include a direct statement from Google or from any New York education official about how districts will respond.

The change comes as Google itself is reshaping search around AI. A separate report from Analytics India Magazine on November 4 says AI Overviews and AI Mode now give users summaries and conversational answers, and that Google's search advertising growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter of 2026, with Search making up less than half of its revenue for the first time. Google has said AI Mode queries run about three times longer than normal searches. The articles do not say when the school policy takes effect or how many districts will be affected, so what New York districts decide to do remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Wall Street Sees Risks to AI Boom After the Democratic Sweep
stories.Summary:
Stock futures slid sharply early on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats won commanding victories in key races across the country in Tuesday's midterm elections. S&P 500 futures fell by more than 0.5 percent, Dow Jones futures dropped by more than 100 points, and Nasdaq 100 futures lost more than 1 percent, at one point sinking as much as 2.5 percent. Futures then recovered, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 back in positive territory and Dow futures up more than 1.4 percent by 5:45 a.m. ET. Markets in Asia closed mixed as investors there weighed the fallout.

A follow-up report from Investor's Business Daily said the Nasdaq tumbled sharply on Thursday before bouncing back on Friday, and that top AI stocks were set to close the week lower. The main worry is the trillion-dollar AI data center boom, which analysts expect to face greater scrutiny now that Democrats control Congress and several key governorships. Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, and in Texas Gina Hinojosa beat Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Amy Acton in Ohio have called for pausing data center construction in their states.

Democrats were also projected to win Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, where data centers were a major campaign issue. Tech stocks have driven much of the rise in U.S. markets over the last two years, with the Nasdaq 100 up 40 percent since Election Day 2024, and Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft and Alphabet have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into AI models, data centers and equipment. Analysts at several firms laid out what the results could mean. Sarah Bianchi of Evercore called the outcome a "blue tsunami" and described it as a rebuke of President Trump's shift away from economic issues, adding that Democratic wins in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which hold a large share of the U.S. project pipeline, mean new pauses and restrictions on data center development.

She said 2027 is shaping up to be turbulent as developers adapt to a changing policy landscape. JPMorgan Chase analysts warned of a possible AI sell-off on assumed higher regulation, citing potential data center restrictions and higher taxes on corporations and top earners, and said healthcare and clean energy could be relative beneficiaries. They also flagged investigation risk for CEOs close to Trump, noting that companies including Nvidia, Apple and Comcast have donated millions to his projects, most notably his ballroom. Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research had earlier said an Abbott loss in Texas was the one surprise that could plausibly spook markets, and Elon Musk joked on X that data centers in space looked appealing.

Markets were already nervous before the vote about whether the AI investments would deliver returns. The Nasdaq 100 entered a correction on Monday, a 10 percent drop from its recent high, and on Friday the S&P 500 and Nasdaq had their worst days since mid-June after mixed earnings from Intel and Amazon. Treasury yields dipped slightly on Tuesday night as traders guessed that an AI slowdown could mean fewer companies tapping bond markets. Top Democrats have signaled interest in investigating some of Trump's projects in January, when their new majority gives them subpoena power.

stories.Headline: US midterm blue tsunami jolts Asian markets as tighter AI, fiscal scrutiny looms
stories.Summary:
Voters in the US midterm elections on Tuesday delivered a strong rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry, according to The New York Times. They backed governors and legislators who have promised to protect individuals from threats posed by AI, and they pushed back hard on data center construction. Tech executives had given record donations to candidates friendly to the industry, but those efforts did not carry the day. Democratic leaders who won are now eager to investigate the close ties between AI companies and the administration.

The clearest numbers came from local ballot measures on data centers. Of 41 local initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development in 40, and more than half of those 41 were in Ohio. Governors and congressional candidates who ran on anti-tech platforms also prevailed in Texas, Ohio, Georgia and other states. Senior Democrats promised to move quickly against the industry once they take up their new authority. The article's full details were cut off before it could list specific rules or legislation.

Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a think tank, said to expect a tsunami of new rules and oversight. Democrats' stated aim is to scrutinize the relationship between AI firms and the administration, though the available text does not name which senior Democrats made the promises. President Trump has taken the position that the industry should be mostly free of regulations that could slow the country's race against China for AI leadership. The Republican-led Congress and White House have done little to regulate the industry over the past two years.

That hands-off approach stirred broad anger, the article said. Communities across the country protested the building of giant, energy-hungry data centers near their homes, and many objected to Republican leaders' reluctance to impose AI safety rules. Fears have grown about the safety of advanced models, the threat to jobs and even the possibility that AI could end humanity. What comes next appears to be a period of closer scrutiny of the industry, though the articles provided do not lay out a timeline or specific measures.
