stories.Headline: Silicon Valley lawmaker to focus on affordability, AI after election win - San José Spotlight
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley Congressman Sam Liccardo, whose district includes parts of Santa Clara and San Mateo counties, said after the November 2026 midterm elections that he was hesitant to treat the Democratic win as a mandate for his party. He said voters were less concerned with ideology and more concerned with their finances. Democrats flipped the U.S. House and Senate in those elections, and Liccardo began his second term with two priorities: affordability and artificial intelligence safety. Liccardo's district contains the headquarters of several large tech companies, including Meta and Google.

On affordability, Liccardo said he will back congressional Democratic efforts to eliminate tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump, raise the minimum wage, extend Affordable Care Act tax credits to lower healthcare costs, and end the war in Iran. On AI safety, no comprehensive federal law exists, although some states have passed their own rules. In September, Liccardo announced an AI safety framework that he planned to introduce when Congress returned on a Monday after an extended recess. The proposal responds to a July letter signed by 1,300 employees of major tech companies urging policymakers to support tools for pacing the frontier of automated AI development. The framework calls for a binding U.S.-China safety agreement covering testing, evaluation, independent auditing, and transparency, along with a government hotline for urgent communications about AI risks.

Liccardo said that an AI safety bill should be moved quickly and that a bipartisan bill is already in play, adding that colleagues can adjust it but it needs a floor vote. Some people who see AI development as a race argue that a U.S. safety framework would let developers abroad, particularly in China, gain ground, which is why Liccardo puts international cooperation at the center of his plan. He also said he is focused on the backlash against data centers, whose construction totaled $720 billion from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in 2026 alone. Communities from Wisconsin to Florida have objected to environmental impacts, higher electricity bills, and a lack of transparency from AI companies. Liccardo said he is working with policymakers, industry players, and environmental groups on an approach that would protect communities while allowing data center growth, and he argued that the grid expansion data centers require could help move an energy sector that still relies mainly on fossil fuels toward greener sources.

Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management have begun approaching investors to sell portions of a roughly $40 billion financing deal tied to SpaceX's artificial intelligence chips, Bloomberg News reported on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. The two firms are reportedly asking some potential buyers to take stakes of up to $500 million before the formal syndication process begins. The multi-tranche financing is said to keep debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and is described as the largest arrangement of its kind for graphics processing units on record. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Goldman Sachs declined to comment, while Apollo Global and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests.

SpaceX said in October that an affiliate of Apollo Global Management would buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them back to the company in a transaction involving about $40 billion in principal payments. The leases are set to run for a little over five years from the date the equipment is delivered. That delivery is expected in the first half of 2027. The arrangement is meant to fund the growing computing needs of SpaceX's AI business. Its structure lets the company expand its computing capacity without taking the full cost onto its own books at once.

Responsibility for structuring and marketing the financing rests with Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management, according to the Bloomberg account. SpaceX confirmed the lease arrangement in October but did not respond to questions about the investor solicitation. Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the report, and Apollo Global did not immediately reply. The reporting relies on people familiar with the matter, and the figures have not been independently verified by Reuters.

The deal reflects the heavy spending that major technology companies are making on computing power to build artificial intelligence products. Financing it through leases and outside investors is one way to spread that cost across several parties. The articles do not say when the formal syndication will open or how many investors will take part. The first hardware deliveries are expected in the first half of 2027, which will be the next concrete milestone.

stories.Headline: European Parliament President Metsola warns against using AI to draft laws
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the European Commission said in its annual simplification report that it has begun using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and to simplify existing ones. The report, presented that Wednesday, described new digital tools that help staff spot overlaps, inconsistencies and duplicates across legal acts. The Commission is also strengthening legal training and staffing so that new rules are not overly complicated. The changes form part of a wider plan to cut red tape and administrative costs for businesses across areas such as tech, agriculture, migration, environmental protection and taxation.

The Commission reports that it has produced 12 so-called omnibus packages to revise and simplify existing legislation, which it estimates will save the EU economy €22.3 billion in costs. It also launched 874 infringement procedures between August 2025 and July 2026, which the report describes as the highest number in the last 10 years. The Commission is pressing member states to stop "gold-plating," the practice of adding extra requirements when turning EU law into national law, and it expects to sign a pact against gold-plating with governments by the end of the year. Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who oversees simplification, called for a joint effort with member countries. He warned that some omnibus proposals may end the legislative process with much less simplification than the Commission proposed, because governments keep weakening them during negotiations.

Responsibility for the simplification drive rests with the Commission, which is led by Ursula von der Leyen, who has made simplification a central part of her second term. Dombrovskis said the agenda is already changing daily life for small business owners, who now spend less time on forms. Separately, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has urged lawmakers to be careful about adopting AI in decision-making. Speaking to MEPs, she said AI can help draft amendments but cannot replace debate or the critical thinking that complex legal decisions require, and that elected representatives must remain personally responsible for their decisions. She wants Parliament to be open about its AI use so citizens can hold their representatives to account.

The articles show that the institutions are moving in parallel, with the Commission leaning into AI for drafting and review while Parliament works on guidelines. Parliament's administration is preparing rules based on transparency, keeping confidential documents off public platforms and checking all AI output carefully. Staff have been required to disclose AI use since 2024, but MEPs are not yet bound by that rule for speeches or amendments, and binding it would likely require a change to Parliament's Rules of Procedure considered by the Committee on Constitutional Affairs. Parliament is also building an internal platform called EPGenAI Hub for sensitive data. The articles do not say when the rules for MEPs will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Where US Courts Stand on AI Training
stories.Summary:
Courts in the United States have not yet settled whether AI developers may train their systems on copyrighted works without permission, and the rulings so far point in different directions. On 29 September 2026 the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held that training an AI legal research tool on case summaries was not fair use, the copying exception in US copyright law. Two California judges had ruled for AI developers on training in June 2025, but on different grounds, so neither decision binds other courts. The judges weigh four factors when deciding fair use, including the purpose of the copying and its effect on the market for the original work. In AI cases the dispute centres on whether training is transformative, meaning it serves a new purpose, and whether it harms the market for the source material.

A summary judgment ruling, issued before trial when the key facts are not disputed, can settle the question for the parties in one case. The US Copyright Office's report of 9 May 2025 said some AI training may qualify as fair use and some may not, leaving the matter to courts and possibly to Congress. The question is also being argued across the Atlantic. Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave a non-binding opinion on 3 November 2026 in case C-250/25, a Hungarian news publisher's claim against Google's Gemini chatbot. He told the EU's top court it should find the training questions inadmissible, but offered provisional views anyway.

In those views, training on copyrighted material is generally lawful in the EU if the developer avoids pirate sources, respects paywalls, bot blocks and machine-readable opt-outs, and shows it took steps to stop the model reproducing specific works. OpenAI asked a New York court on 4 September 2026 to rule that training its models is fair use, and that request remains pending. Meanwhile the Rio Times reports that Brazilian and Norwegian media groups won court orders suspending new terms from Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. Because no court has settled the core question, developers and rights holders on both sides of the Atlantic are still waiting for a binding answer.

stories.Headline: The EU AI Act explained: what it bans, what it requires and the new 2027 deadlines
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act, Europe's first broad law regulating artificial intelligence by how systems are used, entered into force on August 1, 2024 and is being phased in over several years. The law sorts AI systems into four risk tiers: unacceptable, high, limited and minimal. Its heaviest obligations fall on a comparatively small set of uses where errors can cost someone a job, a loan, their liberty or their safety, while most everyday AI faces no new duties. Because the rules reach providers whose system outputs are used in the EU, the law also matters to companies outside Europe.

Some practices have been banned since February 2, 2025. These include manipulative or deceptive techniques that cause significant harm, exploiting people's vulnerabilities because of age, disability or economic situation, and social scoring that leads to disproportionate bad treatment. Predicting crime from profiling alone, building facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping, and emotion recognition in workplaces and schools are also prohibited, as is most live facial recognition in public spaces by law enforcement. The July 2026 amendments, known as the Digital Omnibus on AI, added a further ban on systems that generate non-consensual intimate images of real people or child sexual abuse material, which applies from December 2, 2026. High-risk systems, such as those used in hiring, credit scoring, education, medical devices and critical infrastructure, must meet strict requirements before and after they reach the market.

The 2026 package pushed back the largest compliance deadlines, giving companies more time to meet the high-risk requirements. Providers of such systems must document their intended purpose, assess and manage risks, and keep records, while deployers must follow provider instructions and monitor how systems operate. Limited-risk systems, including some chatbots and AI-generated images, must be disclosed to users as AI. Responsibility depends on role: importers and distributors have their own duties, and a deployer that substantially modifies a system or changes its intended purpose can take on provider obligations.

Supporters argue that clear, use-based rules protect people from the most serious harms, while critics say the law's definitions and timetable leave businesses uncertain about compliance. Enforcement is carried out by national authorities and EU-level bodies, and the articles describe penalties for violations without giving every detail. The Digital Omnibus delays show that the timetable itself has been contested and revised, so the final shape of obligations for many companies may still change. The articles do not say how the law will be applied in practice in the years ahead.

stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania lawmakers have a proposed bill that would give residents the right to access, correct, or delete the personal data that data brokers hold about them. Data brokers collect, analyze, and sell personal information from many sources, and the industry, valued at an estimated $200 billion, is largely unregulated. A researcher at the Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington called the field the Wild West and warned of privacy invasions and real-life harms. Sensitive details such as medical history are among the most valuable items sold, and scammers can use them to target people.

Prices for personal data vary widely. Basic details like name, address, phone number, email, and gender can sell for as little as 5 cents to 50 cents, while richer data such as income level, shopping history, and date of birth can fetch between $1 and $5. Much of the material comes from public records like property deeds, voter registrations, court filings, and marriage licenses, and people also hand over information through loyalty programs, warranty registrations, and contest entries. Removal services charge between $20 and $250 a year, and with more than 750 data brokers in the U.S., asking each one directly is slow. Only four states, California, Texas, Vermont, and Oregon, currently require data broker registration and consumer opt-out, while sixteen others let consumers request deletion.

The proposed Pennsylvania measure must pass before the legislative session ends next month or it will expire. The articles do not name the bill's sponsors or report any official statement on its prospects. Experts quoted in the coverage advise people to take control of what they share, such as setting social media profiles to private, limiting app permissions, and checking with their county about protecting property records. The articles do not say what will happen if the bill passes or fails beyond the expiration deadline.

stories.Headline: EU court adviser: AI chatbots that replace reading the news may breach publisher rights
stories.Summary:
On 3 November 2026, Advocate General Szpunar of the EU Court of Justice delivered an Opinion on whether AI chatbots that use online news may infringe press publishers' rights. The Opinion concerns Like Company v. Google Ireland Limited (C-250/25), a case about Google's Gemini chatbot and articles published by a Hungarian news business. It addresses press publishers' related rights rather than authors' copyright, and the judges have yet to rule. The Opinion separates two activities that are often lumped together.

Training a model on material is treated differently from retrieving an article to answer a user's question, and the Advocate General sees no need for the Court to decide the training question in this case. He also distinguishes a factual summary of a source from a recognisable reproduction of its protected expression. Lost website traffic alone is not enough to show infringement, and paraphrasing does not escape liability if the original expression survives. Facts themselves are not protected, and very short extracts and individual words fall outside the right. Responsibility is treated as turning on system design, safeguards and evidence rather than on the user's prompt alone.

The Advocate General does not propose automatic liability for providers whenever a user prompts an infringing answer, but says pointing to the user is not enough where the business model facilitates reproduction or reasonable safeguards are missing. Publishers are advised to record what a chatbot accessed and returned, while a claim that a service makes content available to the public would require systematic reproduction across related queries, not one unusual answer. On the facts of the Hungarian dispute, the Advocate General doubts infringement, noting that effective access restrictions and recognisable expression appear absent and that Google seems to have adopted appropriate safeguards, subject to the national court's findings. The Court typically follows an Advocate General's Opinion, but it is not bound to, and the wider legal framework for AI, copyright and related rights remains unsettled. Even so, the Opinion signals how access controls, output design, evidence and licensing may matter in future disputes.

stories.Headline: Democratic Party's Congressional Sweep Sparks AI Regulation Storm; Nasdaq Plunges Nearly 4% Intraday, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Craters Over 8%
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell sharply on Thursday, November 5, wiping out the rally that followed the midterm elections, after Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate and took several key governorships. Investors worried that artificial intelligence and data center construction would now face tougher regulation, and selling hit chip, memory and AI infrastructure companies hardest. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.52% to finish at 24,315.00. The S&P 500 slid 4.36% to 7,353.73, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.25% to 9,011.14, its worst day since March 16, 2020. The Nasdaq and the Russell 2000, which fell 4.45%, both ended more than 10% below their recent highs, which put them in correction territory.

Individual stock losses were steep. SanDisk fell 22.26% to $806.43 a share, Micron dropped 17.46% to $656.39, and Western Digital, AMD and Seagate each lost more than 16%. Nvidia sank 9.26% to $181.60, shedding $447 billion in market value in one day, and Intel fell 10.33% to $52.25. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's ADR slid 10.78%, and ASE Technology's ADR crashed 20.77%. The VIX volatility gauge jumped more than 60%, and money moved into safe havens, with the 10-year Treasury yield falling about 6 basis points to 4.83% and spot gold rising to about $4,082 an ounce.

A major trigger was Senator Bernie Sanders, who called for a national moratorium on data center construction, though that remains a political proposal and not an enacted ban. Meta's president and vice chairman, Dina Powell McCormick, said building data centers would become more difficult after the election, but she noted that some winning governors want to keep local jobs and investment. Texas is a focus, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and campaigned on pausing new data center approvals until stronger protections for communities are in place. Analysts offered mixed views: Daniel Ives said the AI buildout now looks slower and more time-consuming than it did 48 hours earlier, while Chris Zaccarelli argued that commercially viable projects can still go forward. Rosenblatt's Kevin Cassidy said it is unclear what politicians will actually do, and that investors dislike uncertainty.

The shock follows a strong rally the day before, when the Dow rose more than 1,500 points after President Donald Trump quickly acknowledged the results and political uncertainty eased. Texas holds nearly three times as much proposed data center capacity as Virginia, the next closest state, and UBS estimated that roughly 30% of the new U.S. data center capacity projected for 2028 could be at risk from construction pauses. Hinojosa can make appointments to state commissions and call special legislative sessions, but tax changes or new statutory protections would need lawmakers' support, and Republicans are expected to keep their state Senate majority. Analyst Yagiz Sullu said Democrats could revisit the more than $1 billion in annual tax breaks Texas gives data centers, while Josephine Liu said a six-month delay would be especially costly for highly leveraged developers. Investors will next watch the October nonfarm payrolls report due Friday, and the broader question of whether AI investment can keep growing remains central to confidence in tech stocks.

stories.Headline: ‘Blade Runner 2049’ Producer Settles Lawsuit Against Warner Bros. Discovery Over AI Images
stories.Summary:
Alcon Entertainment, the producer of Blade Runner 2049, has settled its copyright claim against Warner Bros. Discovery over AI-generated images. The case was disclosed in court filings on November 5, 2026, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Alcon and the studio told the court they had reached a deal, but the terms were not made public. The filing stated simply that the two sides had reached a settlement.

The dispute began with a 2024 unveiling of Tesla's robotaxi, which was staged from a studio lot in partnership with Warner Bros. Discovery. During the presentation, Elon Musk showed an image of a man in a trench coat surveying a ruined city in misty orange light. Alcon argued that the picture was meant to look like a still from the film, which follows Ryan Gosling's character exploring a ruined Las Vegas. The company also said it did not want its film linked to Musk because of his political and social views.

Alcon brought claims against the studio for direct and contributory copyright infringement, with the latter covering knowingly helping another party infringe. The direct infringement claim was dismissed after the court found that the studio was not responsible for overseeing Tesla's work on the presentation. Lawyers for both sides had moved to dismiss the remaining claims against the studio in September. Alcon continues to pursue its lawsuit against Tesla and Musk. Tesla and Musk have argued that using the image was fair use, a legal doctrine that permits some use of copyrighted material without a license.

The case raises an open legal question about whether an AI image generator that copies part of a copyrighted work without a license amounts to infringement. Musk said at the event that he wanted the duster the character wears but not the bleak apocalypse depicted in the film, and Tesla argued he used the image to contrast with a dystopian future. Warner Bros. Discovery and Alcon did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The articles do not say how the case against Tesla and Musk will proceed.

Articles.Title: ‘Blade Runner 2049’ Producer Settles Lawsuit Against Warner Bros. Discovery Over AI Images

stories.Headline: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an annual gathering on artificial intelligence, was held in Rome on November 5 and 6, 2026, at the Pontifical Gregorian University. The forum, founded in 2024, aimed to build an interdisciplinary community that supports the development of AI products serving the Church's mission. It was centered on Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas and drew companies working in Catholic AI, venture capital and angel investors, and prominent AI researchers. Organizers said the event would cover four areas: evangelization, healthcare, education, and responsible AI development with safeguards online.

In his opening remarks, Cardinal Michael Czerny, a founder of the Vatican's inter-dicastery commission on artificial intelligence, argued that learning should be a shared dialogue rather than an isolated transaction. He warned that everyone is affected by AI yet few are truly listening to one another. Vincent Higgins, CEO of the Builders AI Forum, described the goals of the event. Montse Alvarado, prefect of the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication, urged participants to ask who they should be while shaping this technology, and to draw on the network in the room rather than lose their interdependence.

Over the two days, speakers addressed accountability and the needs of families and schools. Megan Garcia, whose son Sewell died by suicide after forming a romantic attachment to a chatbot, told EWTN News that the central question is who is responsible when AI harms a child. She said companies should submit to third-party testing before release and must not keep, share, or sell children's data. Many participants argued that AI used in Catholic schools should align with Church teaching and philosophy, and that families should discuss together what should be available or filtered. Matthew Sanders, CEO of Longbeard, which organizes the forum, said AI designed to suit a billion people is an impossible task.

Participants also discussed how AI can serve faith formation, with Longbeard's Magisterium AI product a focus of several sessions. Bishop Stephen Wang of the Diocese of Arundel and Brighton said many people explore faith through AI and that seminarians already use it, so formation should prepare them to use it discerningly. Erich Kerekes, CEO of the Hallow app, said prayer is a relationship that AI cannot provide, and Alvarado stated that AI is a tool through which messages are communicated, not a person. Czerny said the Church must first show AI builders that it is listening. Coverage of the forum reports these views but does not describe further policy steps or outcomes.

Articles.Title: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference

stories.Headline: AI adoption surges among ‘Best Law Firms’
stories.Summary:
Best Lawyers released its 2027 Best Law Firms rankings on November 5, 2026, covering 15,671 U.S. law firms across 127 practice areas and 188 geographic markets. The rankings are in their 17th edition and represent the top 3.41% of U.S. firms. The research drew on 30,024 lawyers who cast more than 3.8 million votes, 109,963 client references, and 1,053 interviews with firm and practice group leaders. Valerie Smith, senior research manager at Best Law Firms, said the results show how excellence takes shape across specialized local firms and national ones. Alongside the rankings, the third annual Best Law Firms U.S. Legal Market Report, based on survey responses from 5,753 firms in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, tracks how the profession is adopting AI.

Among firms with 20 or more lawyers, 28% reported fully implementing generative AI across multiple practice areas, up from 11% the year before. Full adoption among firms with 150 or more lawyers rose from 23% to 56%. Firms are also adding safeguards, as the share providing training on AI risks climbed from 22% to 63%, and those with clear policies for AI in client matters rose from 14% to 47%. A gap remains, since 95% of the largest firms have such policies while only 26% of solo practitioners do. Traditional billing is still widespread, with 70% of firms offering alternative fee arrangements, down slightly from 72%.

Flat fees, retainers, and contingency fees were the most common options. AI is starting to affect billing, however, as 25% of GenAI-using firms reported reduced billable hours for certain tasks, up from 19%, and another 27% reported higher efficiency without changing their hours. Smith said that makes AI a question of pricing and client value as well as technology. The report also found that smaller firms grew revenue quickly, while firms with 150 or more lawyers produced 83% of reported revenue. Average pro bono hours per lawyer fell to 25.6, a second straight year of decline and about half the American Bar Association's 50-hour benchmark.

A separate JD Supra article by Deborah Farone, a law firm business development advisor, describes a joint IBA and LMA webinar on AI and legal marketing that drew more than 1,200 registrants from 939 firms in 104 countries, with roughly 700 attending live. Panelists from Bowmans, Bass, Berry & Sims, Gibson Dunn, and Pierson Ferdinand described their experiences and emphasized treating AI as an ongoing learning process rather than a finished project. They advised starting with the problem a tool is meant to solve, using AI to speed up pitches and proposals, and keeping lawyers responsible for verifying all output. Farone wrote that the question has moved from whether firms should use AI to how they should use it well.

Articles.Title: AI adoption surges among ‘Best Law Firms’

stories.Headline: OpenAI Promises to Foot AI’s Power Bill After Voter Revolt. Who Enforces It?
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Thursday that people living near its future AI campuses should not have to pay for the electricity those sites use. The pledge came two days after voters in several states backed restrictions on data center expansion. The company published its commitments in a document it calls the National Community Compact, which covers campuses it both owns and operates. Under the compact, OpenAI says it will pay the full cost of powering its compute campuses and will cover the grid costs that those projects create.

It also promises financial assurances before expensive grid upgrades, so that other customers are not left paying if a project shrinks or fails. Each facility would receive a water plan, annual progress reports and independent noise studies, along with public energy and water figures. The company also said it would limit nondisclosure agreements with officials. A separate policy blueprint asks lawmakers and regulators to apply similar requirements across the industry.

The compact itself does not describe penalties for noncompliance, a dispute process, or independent checks on the electricity and water numbers, so residents would have no clear way to force corrections or recover losses. The compact also does not say whether it covers facilities that partners such as Oracle build and own, which Reuters reported make up much of the infrastructure reserved for OpenAI. The blueprint goes further on costs, urging state utility regulators to create large-load tariffs that make major electricity users pay the added costs they cause. It also calls for mandatory reporting, narrow limits on officials' nondisclosure agreements, and rules letting governments reclaim tax breaks when developers miss agreed commitments.

The announcement follows an election in which voters backed restrictions on data centers in multiple states and candidates pushing for tighter oversight won key races. Those results signal that communities want a larger voice in where these facilities are built and how they affect nearby residents. OpenAI says every future campus it owns and operates will get its own local compact and an annual public progress report. The articles do not say whether those commitments will be enforced by any outside authority.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Promises to Foot AI’s Power Bill After Voter Revolt. Who Enforces It?

stories.Headline: BILL Slashes Underwriting Times From 3 Hours to 12 Minutes With AI
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence agents are saving BILL's teams more than 1,400 hours per month, which is equivalent to about eight full-time employees. BILL CEO and founder René Lacerte said this on Thursday, November 5, 2026, during the company's first quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings call. The savings come from more than 100 AI agents that his risk team built over the past year to perform work around the clock across several functions. Lacerte said these agents complete defined tasks on their own, such as pulling case files, drafting credit assessments and writing model documentation.

Lacerte highlighted three agents that work together as a suite called Robin to handle underwriting cases. Robin routes each case to the right underwriter, pulls the customer's data into a summary and offers a one-click link to make a decision. Previously, an underwriter had to assemble each case through chat messages, email and separate dashboards. Lacerte said each case now takes about 12 minutes instead of three hours, which he described as faster, better and more personalized service for small and medium-sized businesses. He also said the company launched five products during the quarter and built a Visa pilot in four weeks.

Lacerte said the company's AI-powered Chat with BILL now handles 45% of customer support conversations. He also said the company's restructuring during its fiscal year 2026 was designed to accelerate its transformation into an AI-native company. Earlier, PYMNTS reported that in May Lacerte had said BILL planned to cut its workforce by 30% by the end of that quarter as it sharpened its focus on AI. Weeks later, he said the company had overhauled its leadership team as part of that transformation. Lacerte presented the first quarter progress as an early indication that the strategy is working.

Articles.Title: BILL Slashes Underwriting Times From 3 Hours to 12 Minutes With AI

stories.Headline: Dollar-yen slips to lower 157 range as AI regulation fears slam U.S. stocks; Tokyo seen bidding yen first
stories.Summary:
On the morning of November 6, 2026, the yen strengthened in Tokyo trading, rising to 157.29-31 per dollar, up 89 sen from the previous day's close. The move followed a sharp sell-off in U.S. stocks on November 5, after the Democratic Party won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held on November 3. Investors feared tighter rules on data center construction, which has supported AI investment, and the Dow fell more than 1,800 dollars, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%. Nikkei 225 Futures also fell 3,520 yen in Osaka night trading, prompting risk-off yen buying and the unwinding of currency hedges. The yen gained against the euro as well, reaching 176.63-66 yen per euro.

Expectations for a rate hike at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting fell to about 70 percent, down roughly 13 percentage points from the previous day, while the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield dropped to the 4.81 percent range before closing at 4.84 percent. The Dow closed at 51,523.06 and the Nasdaq Composite at 24,315.00. In Osaka, the December Nikkei 225 Futures contract closed at 57,400. Analysts expected the Nikkei Stock Average to extend its decline on November 6, which was adding to demand for the yen. Overseas investors who had hedged yen exposure on unrealized gains in Japanese stocks also unwound positions, amplifying yen buying in the short term.

The article attributes these moves to market reaction rather than to any single official action, and it notes that no U.S. regulation has yet been enacted in the reporting. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Barkin said on November 5 that, given firm demand, low unemployment, and inflation above the Fed's 2 percent target, gradual rate hikes are appropriate, though the stock turmoil was pushing down expectations for future hikes. The article also says the yen remains under some downward pressure, since newly issued 10-year Japanese government bonds yield below 3 percent and the interest rate gap with the United States keeps yen selling persistent. Dollar-yen has traded within the daily Ichimoku cloud since mid-October, with 157.18 as the lower bound and 158.44 as the upside target. The article concludes that risk-off yen buying is likely to continue in Tokyo for now, and that the direction of the yen will likely depend on whether the decline in semiconductor and AI-related shares subsides.

Articles.Title: Dollar-yen slips to lower 157 range as AI regulation fears slam U.S. stocks; Tokyo seen bidding yen first

stories.Headline: In-depth view on how EU copyright law applies to gen-AI offered by CJEU adviser
stories.Summary:
The Court of Justice of the EU's advocate general, Maciej Szpunar, has issued a non-binding opinion on how EU copyright law applies to generative AI, in a case brought by a Hungarian publishers' claim over press publisher rights. He said training large language models on copyright-protected works would generally amount to copyright infringement, but that such training can fall within the text and data mining exception in EU copyright law. The opinion was published on 5 November 2026 and was framed as a view on matters the court has not been asked to decide in the underlying case. Szpunar's analysis covered a wide range of AI and copyright issues.

Szpunar said whether the text and data mining exception can be relied upon for LLM training should be assessed case by case. He also said AI developers would definitely need a licence to use copyright works for training where rights holders have explicitly opted out of text and data mining in a machine-readable format. In other words, the exception does not give developers a free pass when rights holders have reserved their rights in that way. The opinion therefore points to a licensing requirement that depends on how rights holders have expressed their objections to such use.

The underlying dispute concerns claims by a Hungarian publisher that Google infringed press publisher rights through output produced by its AI chatbot, Gemini. Press publisher rights are rights that EU-based publishers of press publications hold in addition to their copyright, including exclusive rights to authorise or prohibit reproduction and online communication of their publications to the public. Szpunar's views on AI training go beyond the specific questions the court must answer in that case. Because the opinion is non-binding, the court is not required to follow it when it rules.

Articles.Title: In-depth view on how EU copyright law applies to gen-AI offered by CJEU adviser

stories.Headline: K-Semiconductors Shaken by AI Regulation Concerns... Expectations Rise for EVs
stories.Summary:
The Democratic Party's win in the U.S. midterm elections is raising concerns in South Korea that new limits on data centers could hit the semiconductor sector, according to a report by SBS reporter Choi Seung-hun from Seoul, published on November 6, 2026. The stock market already appears to be reflecting these worries. The report notes that Texas is projected to account for 30 percent of all electricity consumed by U.S. data centers by the year after next. The newly elected Democratic governor of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, has pledged to suspend all data center approvals until laws are in place to protect residents.

The concern stems from the large amount of electricity each data center uses, which is comparable to that of a small town. Residents have complained that they could end up paying, through their electricity bills, for expanded power plants and transmission grids. Similar movements are under way across the country, and among 36 candidates who have been elected governor or are leading vote counts, 34 backed regulating data centers and 12 pledged to halt construction altogether. Analysts cited in the report suggest that around 1,000 data centers could be suspended or delayed nationwide. Such a slowdown could affect Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which supply chips to these facilities, as well as domestic suppliers of electrical equipment and infrastructure.

Lee Joon, director of the Strategic Industries Research Center at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade, said that supply and demand could loosen, prices would likely fall, and profitability would suffer, which he described as the scenario of greatest concern. The report also covers the other side of the picture. Domestic automakers such as Hyundai Motor and Kia are hoping for a revival of electric vehicle purchase subsidies, a push led by Democratic lawmakers. KOTRA has forecast that South Korea's power and shipbuilding sectors could gain opportunities, given the bipartisan support in Washington for those industries.

Articles.Title: K-Semiconductors Shaken by AI Regulation Concerns... Expectations Rise for EVs

stories.Headline: AI Regulation Fears Spark Black Storm as Taiwan Index Futures Night Session Plunges Nearly 3,000 Points, Breaks Below 40,000 Mark
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's stock index futures fell sharply in their night session, and the selloff carried into the spot market the following morning. The drop followed a steep decline in U.S. stocks on November 5, 2026, after the Democratic Party won a strong victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Investors feared that artificial intelligence and data center construction would face tougher scrutiny over water, power, and land use. Taiwan Index Futures closed the night session at 38,936, down 2,946 points or 7.03%, breaking below the 40,000 level. TSMC Futures fell 9.84% to 2,026, close to the limit-down threshold.

When the spot market opened on November 6, the weighted index began at 38,916, down 2,659 points, and quickly broke below both the 40,000 mark and the 38,784.53 annual moving average. By 9:03 a.m. it had dropped to 37,902.46, a decline of 8.83%. TSMC opened down NT$220 and was trading at NT$2,025 by that time, off 9.6%, while Hon Hai, Delta Electronics, Quanta Computer, and Largan Precision each fell about 9% to 10%.

Japan's Nikkei 225 also lost more than 3,000 points in early trading, and South Korea's KOSPI triggered a circuit breaker after falling more than 8% intraday. Across the AI supply chain, from chipmakers and server makers to power and optical component suppliers, selling pressure was broad. The sell-off in the United States was severe. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25% on November 5 to close at 9,011.14, its biggest single-day drop since the March 2020 pandemic crash.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, entering a technical correction, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.44% and the S&P 500 fell 4.36%. Analysts cited in the reporting attributed the move to expectations of stricter review of data centers, particularly over water, power, and land permits rather than chips themselves. Senator Bernie Sanders has publicly called for a nationwide moratorium on data center construction, and UBS estimates that about 30% of the U.S. data center capacity planned for addition by 2028 could be affected by such measures. A CNBC survey found that 56% of voters listed AI and data centers as a key voting issue.

The episode followed a sharp rise in Taiwan stocks earlier in the year, and the weighted index had already fallen about 16.9% from its October 6 high of 49,968.92 before the latest slide. E.Sun Asset Management said the decline reflects a repricing of the AI industry's long-term growth and valuations rather than a deterioration in corporate earnings, with Taiwan's price-to-earnings ratio falling from a peak of 22 times last month to below 15 times. The VIX index rose to an eight-month high. Investors are now watching short-term capital flows and how regulatory policy on data centers develops in the coming months.

Articles.Title: AI Regulation Fears Spark Black Storm as Taiwan Index Futures Night Session Plunges Nearly 3,000 Points, Breaks Below 40,000 Mark

stories.Headline: AI Regulation Fears Intensify After Midterms; Dow Reverses to a More Than 1,200-Point Rout, SanDisk Plunges 20%
stories.Summary:
On the evening of Nov. 5 Beijing time, U.S. stocks opened mixed, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average up as much as 0.63%, before the market reversed sharply under the political shock of the midterm elections. The Dow turned negative and fell more than 1,200 points, about 2.2%, intraday, while the S&P 500 dropped about 3.3%, the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged about 11%. Memory chip stocks took the steepest losses, with SanDisk down 20% intraday and Western Digital, Seagate, Micron and AMD each falling more than 15%. Even post-election gainers such as Apple slipped into negative territory by midday.

The selloff followed a Democratic sweep of the Nov. 3 midterms, which put both the Senate and the House under Democratic control. According to a tally by CNBC on Nov. 4, 41 data-center-related ballot measures across 10 states went before voters, and nearly all backed restrictions or rejected development-friendly proposals. On Nov. 4, Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona called on Democrats to pause advanced AI development, regulate the industry and ban artificial superintelligence, and she and nine other lawmakers have introduced the Artificial Superintelligence Ban Act of 2026. Qualcomm's earnings added pressure, as its fiscal fourth-quarter handset chip revenue fell 26% year over year and its adjusted EPS guidance midpoint of $2.25 for fiscal 2027's first quarter came in below analyst expectations. The articles note that none of these measures has become law, and data center timelines still depend on permits, power supply and customer commitments.

Market analysts and the articles' own reporting frame the decline as a repricing of AI investment rather than a fall in memory prices. A TrendForce forecast from Sept. 30 expected DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% and NAND Flash prices 15% to 20% quarter over quarter in the fourth quarter of 2026. Qualcomm management also linked its handset weakness to rising memory costs, which push up device prices and dampen demand. Oil and gold moved higher as investors sought physical assets, and separately, Houthi health authorities reported 12 deaths from Saudi-led coalition airstrikes in Yemen, a development Saudi Arabia had not yet answered. The articles say investors should watch whether AI data center approvals and federal legislation take effect, whether memory price increases extend into 2027, and whether other chip suppliers follow Qualcomm with conservative guidance.

Articles.Title: AI Regulation Fears Intensify After Midterms; Dow Reverses to a More Than 1,200-Point Rout, SanDisk Plunges 20%

stories.Headline: Nasdaq plunges 5.5% on AI regulation fears... 3,400 trillion won wiped from market value in a single day
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, local time in New York, the three major U.S. stock indexes fell sharply, led by artificial intelligence and technology shares. The sell-off followed the U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress and gained control of several state and local governments. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1,421.52 points, or 5.52%, to 24,315.00, and the S&P 500 lost 334.89 points, or 4.36%, to 7,353.73.

The Nasdaq and S&P 500 posted their steepest percentage declines since April of last year, when President Donald Trump announced reciprocal tariffs. According to The Wall Street Journal, companies in the Nasdaq index lost about $2.5 trillion in market value that day, roughly 3,400 trillion won and the largest one-day drop on record. Companies in the S&P 500 lost about $2.9 trillion, also a record. The Nasdaq had already fallen more than 10% from its record high set last month, which placed it in a technical correction.

Investors feared that the Democratic victories would bring tighter rules on new data center construction, particularly in Texas and Georgia, where the industry is concentrated. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street's so-called fear gauge, rose to 28.09, its highest level in eight months. Market strategist Michael O'Rourke of JonesTrading said that a political slowdown in data center investment could make current earnings estimates invalid, and that investors did not know where expectations would reset. Chip leaders Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD fell 9.3%, 10.6% and 17.3%, while Tesla and SpaceX, whose chief executive Elon Musk had backed Republican candidates, dropped 10.8% and 9.3%.

The selling spread beyond technology, and all 11 sectors of the S&P 500 declined as investors moved toward safe-haven assets. The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note fell to 4.84% from 4.90% the previous day. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped more than 12%, its steepest fall since 2020, and at one point the Magnificent Seven lost more than $1 trillion, about 1,356 trillion won, in combined market value. Jonathan Kofina of Meridian Equity Partners said the market remained highly vulnerable amid the uncertainty ahead.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq plunges 5.5% on AI regulation fears... 3,400 trillion won wiped from market value in a single day

stories.Headline: Broadcom Sinks 9% as AI Regulation Fears Deepen Chip Rout
stories.Summary:
Broadcom fell 9% on November 5, 2026, in a broad chip selloff, even though the company had released no news of its own. Traders were reacting to the Democratic wins in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, with fears of tighter AI rules and slower data center construction. A large phone chipmaker's guidance issued after the close on Wednesday added to the pressure. The selling spread across the AI supply chain, with ASE Technology Holding down 19%, Everpure down 16%, Ciena down 15% and Applied Digital down 17%.

Those suppliers fell harder than Broadcom despite recent strong results. ASE Technology said on October 29 that its third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier, and Everpure reported 38% revenue growth in its fiscal second quarter ended August 2. Applied Digital's leased campuses, worth about $36 billion of revenue over their base terms, are located in North Dakota, Louisiana and Alabama, which the article describes as guilt by association. Analysts still expect Broadcom's normalized EPS to rise from $6.82 in fiscal 2025 to $30.37 in fiscal 2028.

The article notes that Broadcom had $179.2 billion of committed contract value at August 2, up from $33.3 billion nine months earlier. The article says Broadcom went into the drop trading below 19 times forward earnings, well under its five-year average of 24 times. It also flags financing exposure, since Broadcom backstops up to about $29 billion of leases for Anthropic's chips, plus up to about $43 billion more under a second package. CEO Hock Tan had earlier called land, power and the building shell "more than a big concern" on the third-quarter call.

The writer argues the selloff prices in a policy risk that has not yet touched Broadcom's results. The next test is Broadcom's December 9 report and its fiscal 2027 AI outlook, where management's view of about $115 billion of AI revenue for fiscal 2027 will be closely watched. The article concludes that if that outlook holds, today's drop could look like a gift, and if not, the market had read the situation correctly. The piece is published by TIKR and includes a disclaimer that it is not investment advice.

Articles.Title: Broadcom Sinks 9% as AI Regulation Fears Deepen Chip Rout

stories.Headline: New Bill provides more bite against AI cybercrime
stories.Summary:
Courts in Malaysia will soon be able to freeze property linked to cybercrime even before suspects are formally charged, according to Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi. He made the statement in a written parliamentary reply, describing the power as part of the Cybercrime Bill 2026, which Parliament passed in July. The measure is aimed at online fraud syndicates, particularly those that exploit artificial intelligence. The Bill is intended to tackle the misuse of AI for online fraud and other forms of cybercrime.

It also seeks to repeal the Computer Crimes Act 1997 (Act 563), which the government says has legal gaps. Under Clause 54, courts may issue preventive orders on applications by the Public Prosecutor or authorised officers, whether or not a suspect has been charged. These orders include cessation orders, restitution orders for victims, compliance orders, and property restriction orders that stop assets such as fraud proceeds from being disbursed. Clause 23 widens the offence of impersonation committed through computer systems, which Zahid said was needed because existing laws no longer cover deepfakes.

Clause 2 extends Malaysia's jurisdiction to cybercriminals abroad, provided the offence involves computer systems in Malaysia or Malaysian victims. Zahid said legal action can be taken against such offenders even when the offences were committed overseas. Bukit Aman Commercial Crime Investigation Department director Comm Datuk Rusdi Mohd Isa welcomed the Bill in a statement. He said cybercrime and online fraud are no longer limited by geography, since syndicates can operate from overseas using digital infrastructure, AI and identity impersonation.

Rusdi said the cross-border provisions give police a clearer legal basis to act against perpetrators located abroad. He also said the police welcomed stronger investigative powers over the preservation and disclosure of data, the collection of traffic data and the interception of communications. The Cybercrime Act is to be enforced in early 2027, according to a separate Home Ministry report cited in the related stories. The article does not say how the new orders will be used in practice or how courts will assess applications for them.

Articles.Title: New Bill provides more bite against AI cybercrime

stories.Headline: Govt won't oppose Labour bill to tackle AI abuse imagery
stories.Summary:
The Irish Government has said it will not oppose a Labour Party bill aimed at tackling AI-generated sexual abuse imagery, according to a report by RTÉ political reporter Sandra Hurley published on 5 November 2026. Labour TD Alan Kelly introduced the legislation, which would amend the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act. Kelly said the bill would close gaps in Irish law and strengthen legal accountability for online platforms. The move follows an investigation launched earlier in 2026 by the European Commission into Grok, the AI tool that is part of the social media platform X, over its use of sexually explicit images, including potential child sexual abuse material.

The bill would explicitly cover sexual abuse images that a person generates or alters using AI. It would criminalise generating such images without consent for publication or distribution, and make it an offence to encourage or knowingly facilitate their generation for that purpose. Kelly said the responsibility should also extend to companies that provide these tools, and that major publishers including X, Meta, TikTok and Google must answer for their conduct under the law. He also said that if enacted, the bill would hold social media executives criminally liable for harmful content, since fines have had no impact on companies that build them into their baseline costs. The bill was updated to address the nudification of images that Grok allowed, the reporting says.

Minister of State at the Department of Justice Colm Brophy told the Dáil that the Government would not oppose the bill because its aims match the Government's commitment to a zero-tolerance approach to domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. He said the coalition shared the widespread revulsion expressed in the House at the non-consensual manipulation of images, mainly of women and children. Brophy confirmed that Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan had secured Cabinet approval that week not to oppose the bill. He also noted that several other bills before the House aim to tackle the same problem, while Kelly said any of them, or a combination, could be used as long as something is enacted quickly.

The debate comes more than nine months after the Grok and X controversy, which Kelly said has left the Government still failing to deliver the changes needed to protect people from AI-generated sexual abuse. Fellow Labour TD Ciarán Ahern said online material was encouraging young people toward harmful behaviour and that online culture had been allowed to fester. Brophy commended Kelly for his work on the bill and outlined existing statutory measures that govern this area. The articles do not say when the bill will be debated further or voted on.

Articles.Title: Govt won't oppose Labour bill to tackle AI abuse imagery

stories.Headline: Infineon's Order Book Is Filling Up, but Washington's AI Rules Are the Wildcard - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Infineon's shares fell sharply on Wednesday, 5 November 2026, as a wave of political anxiety hit the semiconductor sector. The reports put the daily decline at 11 percent in one reading and 7.3 percent in another, figures that describe the same trading session. The sell-off was attributed to the Democratic victory in the US elections and to fears that tougher regulation of artificial intelligence could slow the construction of AI data centers. Other chipmakers, including ON Semiconductor, Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and STMicroelectronics, also traded lower, and no company-specific trigger was initially identified.

The market appears to have repriced the outlook for future regulatory conditions rather than any drop in Infineon's reported business. The articles note that if tighter rules do delay AI data center expansion, the timing of related opportunities could slip, but that outcome is a risk rather than a certainty. Infineon has recently pushed the AI theme on several fronts: on Tuesday, 4 November, it announced the OptiMOS-7 family for AI servers, data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, and on Wednesday it signed a memorandum of understanding with SOLUM on high-voltage direct current solutions for AI data centers. The articles describe the SOLUM arrangement as a shared plan rather than secured revenue. A strategic agreement with Vertiv, closed the previous day, covers the supply of silicon and silicon-carbide power semiconductors over three years, including 800-VDC power supply systems.

The articles say the next major test is the annual results, due on Tuesday, 10 November, covering the fourth quarter and fiscal 2026. Before that release, JPMorgan kept its "Overweight" rating on Infineon with a price target of 96 euros, and analyst Sandeep Deshpande expected the 2027 targets to come in slightly above market consensus. The company also had other news in the same period, including a technology cooperation with Qualcomm Technologies on a microcontroller-based subsystem for Snapdragon Ride reference platforms, and an investment of roughly EUR 1.1 billion at its Villach site for gallium-nitride power semiconductor production through 2034, with about EUR 319 million in funding earmarked under the European Chips Act. Infineon will also present at electronica in Munich from 10 to 13 November.

Articles.Title: Infineon's Order Book Is Filling Up, but Washington's AI Rules Are the Wildcard - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Three Broward Schools Earn First Microsoft AI/Copilot Innovation Awards - Broward County Public Schools
stories.Summary:
Three Broward County schools, Pompano Beach High School, Peters Elementary and Indian Trace Elementary School, have become the first monthly winners of the Microsoft AI/Copilot Innovation Recognition Program. Broward County Public Schools created the program to honor schools that use Microsoft Copilot to address real teaching and operational challenges. Each winning school receives $4,000 and a chance to compete in the School of the Year competition. Fourteen schools applied in September, and the winners were recognized at the November 4 School Board Workshop meeting. The district announced the results in a post dated November 5, 2026.

At Pompano Beach High School, staff in English Language Arts, science, social studies, math, electives, administration and counseling use Copilot to draft lessons, differentiate assignments, write family communications and summarize meetings. The article says staff have logged more than 5,300 Copilot interactions since April. AI liaison Colleen Crisan helped build that momentum through a staff session called "The AI of the Tiger: Taming the Grading Beast." Peters Elementary used Copilot to merge teacher schedules, multi-tiered system of supports data and progress monitoring lists into one response to intervention meeting schedule. The literacy coach used it to build small-group reading plans for grades 2 through 5, and the math coach used it to create lesson plans aligned to B.E.S.T. standards.

Indian Trace Elementary School began the year with schoolwide Copilot training for every Pre-K through 5 classroom. Staff learned a shared prompting method called Goal, Context, Source and Expectations, along with a privacy-first approach to small-group planning. The article quotes Katherine Shamoun, an ESE Support Facilitator, who said that starting from scratch takes less of her time, leaving more time to review and adapt materials for students. The district presents the common training as already saving teachers time. The article does not give a specific figure for time saved.

All three schools now advance to the School of the Year competition. The district says applications for the program are accepted every month, and it invites other schools to share how they use AI. The article is an official district post, so Broward County Public Schools is the party responsible for the announcement and its framing. The post credits the winning educators with pairing creativity with new tools. It does not describe any criteria beyond the stated purpose or give details about the School of the Year competition's timeline.

Articles.Title: Three Broward Schools Earn First Microsoft AI/Copilot Innovation Awards - Broward County Public Schools

stories.Headline: Interactive Web Applications Combine Artificial Intelligence with Modular Scientific Simulation Engines
stories.Summary:
Researchers Richard Salter and Wayne M. Getz have introduced an open, browser-based simulation platform called NuWebKit, described in a paper published in Frontiers in Systems Biology. The system runs simulations inside standard web browsers or on remote servers, so users do not need to install client software. It includes artificial intelligence features that turn plain language prompts into working simulation code, along with an editable runtime framework that lets users change mathematical formulas directly on a running interface. The authors say the goal is to make advanced mathematical modeling easier to access across biological, epidemiological, and ecological fields. The platform builds on the authors' earlier work on Numerus Designer and Numerus Studio and relies on a feature called Runtime Alterable Module, or RAM, which is a software mechanism rather than computer hardware memory.

A single code base serves all modeling domains, and each project is customized through a JSON configuration file called project DNA. Simple educational models run in native JavaScript on the client side, while demanding calculations can be hosted on servers using Java and WebSockets. The engine handles continuous systems with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method and discrete systems with Euler integration, and it supports spatial and agent-based models using hexagonal grids and configurable boundaries. Users can save up to twenty-six custom configurations as browser presets, and the platform also offers parameter fitting, sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo tools. Models are written in NuML, a domain-specific language with two custom operators, and the AI features can generate both NuML code and accompanying technical documentation from a prompt.

The authors tested the AI features on classic problems. Given short prompts, Gemini produced working code for the Hodgkin-Huxley squid giant axon model, and the simulated dashboard showed a steady firing rate of sixty-eight hertz with a spike amplitude of one hundred five millivolts, which the authors say matched theoretical predictions exactly. In an ecological test, the software generated a four-class age-structured Leslie matrix model with sensitivity graphs, and DeepSeek produced a stochastic population viability model whose extinction-time histograms came from runs of five hundred to one thousand iterations. The platform also offers three export tiers for data and an R connection called RConnect that lets statistical analysts run batch simulations from R scripts. The articles provided do not say whether the platform has been adopted by outside users, nor do they describe any planned releases, updates, or next steps beyond the publication itself.

Articles.Title: Interactive Web Applications Combine Artificial Intelligence with Modular Scientific Simulation Engines

stories.Headline: Stacey Abrams on DEI, artificial intelligence and regulation ahead of Democrat midterm wins
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Stacey Abrams spoke by phone with the UWM Post ahead of the Wisconsin gubernatorial election, while she was in Wisconsin campaigning with David Crowley and attending canvass events in Milwaukee and Oak Creek. Abrams, a voting rights activist and former Democratic minority leader in the Georgia House of Representatives, was asked about diversity, equity and inclusion, artificial intelligence and regulation. The interview was published on November 5, 2026. The article does not describe a single event or action beyond the interview itself.

On the Wisconsin ballot question concerning DEI, Abrams said the measure is written to sound benign but would remove protections against discrimination. She argued that DEI covers laws that have expanded access to rights, and that a yes vote could bar the state legislature from correcting systemic discrimination. As an example, she described a disabled student who might lose the ability to seek enforcement of an Individualized Education Program through the federal Office for Civil Rights. On artificial intelligence, she said the technology is a tool whose use depends on the people controlling it, and she pointed to its potential to improve healthcare access. She also discussed the Milwaukee Common Council's one-year pause on data center construction, saying moratoriums give communities time to address costs and environmental effects and that data center decisions should include community input.

Abrams also addressed AI regulation at the state level, citing the call by AI executive Dario Amodei to slow AI development and arguing that regulation signals caution rather than opposition to innovation. She said Wisconsin candidates including Crowley and Attorney General Josh Kaul would want public input into how AI is governed. She contrasted this approach with a federal stance she described as opposing any AI regulation, and said Democrats frame regulation as a question of how the technology should be used. The article does not report the election result, any legislative action, or any next steps beyond the campaign context.

Articles.Title: Stacey Abrams on DEI, artificial intelligence and regulation ahead of Democrat midterm wins

stories.Headline: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Samantha Piteri-Molina, vice president of business and strategy at Forge Biologics, spoke with BioSpace about the contract manufacturer's direction and the wider gene therapy field. She is a BioSpace 40 Under 40 honoree who helped guide Forge through its acquisition by Ajinomoto, a Japanese food and biotechnology company, for $620 million in late 2023. Since then, Forge has grown to more than 425 employees, up from 327 as of July 2023, while keeping its retention rate above 92 percent. Piteri-Molina said the goal is getting gene therapies to patients who are waiting for them. The company supports adeno-associated virus gene therapy development and commercial manufacturing.

Piteri-Molina sees near-term value in using artificial intelligence to analyze the large amounts of data that gene therapy manufacturers already generate. She said better collection, analysis and interpretation of that data could create efficiencies as manufacturers make more of the vectors used to deliver these therapies. She also sees potential for AI in drug development, including construct optimization and building assays for specific programs. She was more skeptical of general-purpose chatbots, arguing that tools addressing technical problems are a better use of resources. The interview also points to a growing pipeline, with more programs moving through clinical trials and more approvals than before.

Forge is based in Columbus, Ohio, which the article describes as a hub for cell and gene therapy. Piteri-Molina credited research at Nationwide Children's Hospital, and companies spun out of that work, with contributing to four FDA-approved gene therapies. She said the area has drawn specialized talent and that Columbus's location gives Forge a supply chain advantage, since most of the U.S. population is about a day's drive away. This matters because gene therapy materials need temperature-controlled shipping and tight timelines. Piteri-Molina also said investment in domestic manufacturing makes sense, but she cautioned against letting that focus narrow the industry's view, because rare disease patients are spread across many countries.

She closed by emphasizing that the patient communities the industry serves are global and that stakeholders aligning more closely would help those patients. She said patient groups are waiting to see how quickly treatments reach them. In her words, it is a privilege to do this work and it carries a responsibility. The article does not give further details on upcoming plans for Forge.

Articles.Title: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing

stories.Headline: Billionaire Musk’s Tesla, SpaceX tumble in post-US midterm AI meltdown
stories.Summary:
Shares in Elon Musk's companies Tesla and SpaceX fell sharply on November 5, 2026, after Democrats performed better than expected in the US midterm elections. Tesla dropped 11 per cent that day following a 3.3 per cent fall the day before, while SpaceX tumbled 9 per cent after a 3.8 per cent decline on November 4. Together the two companies lost roughly US$460 billion in combined market value since the results became clear. The sell-off was part of a wider slump in technology stocks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 falling 6.4 per cent, its worst single-day performance since March 2020.

Investors worried that Musk's plans to expand his business empire could face more resistance under a less friendly Congress. Democrats won a majority of seats in both chambers and took key positions in Texas, the state where Tesla and SpaceX have their headquarters. Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who had held the state's top office since 2015. Analysts also flagged the possibility that a proposed merger between Tesla and SpaceX could become harder to complete, though the articles say it would not automatically be blocked.

Democratic candidates in Texas directed much of their criticism at Musk himself. Hinojosa called for a moratorium on data centres and questioned his political donations to Abbott as well as state tax breaks his companies received. James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in a generation to win a US Senate seat in Texas, accused Musk of trying to buy the seat and said Musk had spent close to half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates. Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers said that moving businesses to a state seen as friendly, then spending heavily on candidates who lost, would carry consequences.

Musk's net worth fell by US$71 billion to US$793 billion on November 5, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, after a drop of US$33.5 billion the day before. He remains the richest person in the world, but his fortune is well below its peak of US$1.3 trillion following SpaceX's initial public offering in June. Special committees at both companies are reviewing the potential merger, and Bloomberg reported a push to complete it before the Trump administration's term ends. Analysts quoted in the articles said the market is reacting to a possible slowdown across AI-related businesses, including SpaceX's artificial intelligence segment and Tesla's autonomous vehicles.

Articles.Title: Billionaire Musk’s Tesla, SpaceX tumble in post-US midterm AI meltdown
