stories.Headline: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers has published a paper auditing eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries, the tools that guide large language model behavior by intervening in the model's internal representations. The authors, Yu Yan and six co-authors, say they found three structural weaknesses in these plugin ecosystems: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring. They argue these gaps give attackers an opening to slip in malicious plugins that look legitimate. The paper appeared on the arXiv preprint server, with the article posted on November 6, 2026.

To test the threat, the authors built a malicious plugin they call IDH. According to the paper, IDH uses a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and an information-decay inflection point method to pick the layer where it injects its intervention, so it can perform a legitimate function and a hijacked one at once. In their experiments across five mainstream LLMs, the legitimate function was safety-refusal steering, and the hijack objective was commercial recommendation manipulation. The authors report an attack success rate of up to 97.8 percent while refusal rates on harmful requests stayed high. The tests covered six brands across three commercial domains.

The authors also propose a runtime defense framework that suppresses anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizes inter-layer trajectories as a countermeasure. The paper does not describe any real-world incident or identify any affected vendor, and it does not say what steps, if any, the maintainers of the audited libraries have taken. The work is a preprint and has not been described in the articles as peer reviewed. The articles do not say what follow-up research or industry response is planned.

Articles.Title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain

stories.Headline: AI-Newton: A concept-driven physical law discovery system without prior physical knowledge
stories.Summary:
A research paper published on November 4, 2026, in Physical Review Research describes AI-Newton, a machine learning system built by researchers at Peking University in Beijing, including You-Le Fang, Dong-Shan Jian, Xiang Li and Yu-Qi Ma. The system is designed to find general physical laws directly from raw data gathered across many mechanics experiments, and the authors say it does this without supervision and without any prior physical knowledge built into it. Existing AI tools are good at writing empirical models that fit a single experiment, but they struggle to identify the shared physics behind those models, which is a task human physicists handle well. The article, published online on November 6, 2026, presents the work as a proof of concept for autonomous, humanlike scientific discovery.

The authors say the system has two main features: it proposes interpretable physical concepts from which laws are built, and it gradually extends those laws to broader domains. When applied to a large and noisy dataset of mechanics experiments, the system reportedly rediscovered foundational and universal laws, including Newton's second law, the conservation of energy, and universal gravitation. The paper's abstract does not give dataset sizes, noise levels or accuracy figures, so those specifics cannot be reported from the material available here. The code and data are said to be publicly available on GitHub, under the Science-Discovery organization. The article presents these results as a first step rather than a finished tool.

The responsibility for the work rests with the four authors at the School of Physics and the Center for High Energy Physics at Peking University, and the contact authors listed are Fang, Jian, Li and Ma. The paper itself is the authors' account of their system, and the article does not include any statement from outside researchers or from the journal about the results. The reference list places the work within a growing body of research on automated equation discovery, symbolic regression and physics-informed machine learning, including earlier systems such as AI Feynman and AI-Descartes. The article does not say what follow-up work the team plans or how independent researchers will evaluate the claims.

Articles.Title: AI-Newton: A concept-driven physical law discovery system without prior physical knowledge

stories.Headline: AI in regulatory: Experts say to look beyond validation
stories.Summary:
Experts at the RAPS AI in Regulatory Conference in Barcelona advised regulatory professionals to take a risk-based, life-cycle approach to artificial intelligence tools. As more regulatory staff adopt AI in their daily work, the panelists said these tools need careful validation and ongoing checks to catch potential problems. The discussion was reported on November 6, 2026. The panel stressed that the stakes are high because notified bodies are expected to take notice of AI use in quality documentation.

Leon Doorn, CEO of MedQAIR Services B.V., warned that AI used to generate quality management records, reports, technical documentation, and instruction manuals carries a risk of introducing errors. He said companies should validate their AI systems and monitor them continuously. Doorn distinguished general AI assistants, which suit drafting, summarizing, and checking text, from AI built specifically for regulatory affairs. He also flagged a common problem, which is that people use AI on an ad hoc basis and therefore keep insufficient records to validate it. Doorn advised users to ask what the intended purpose of a tool is, consider its risks, test it, set controls, and monitor it.

Simona Jerabkova, a director of regulatory affairs at Edwards Lifesciences, said users should ask five questions before choosing an AI tool. They should consider what the AI is meant to do and what behavior is unacceptable, who owns its mistakes, what needs validation, what human oversight is required, and what would trigger revalidation. Jerabkova described her company's use of an AI assistant to prepare a product application, in which the tool retrieves predefined documents, compiles a checklist, and drafts and summarizes the text. A regulatory specialist then checks the work for completeness and finalizes the dossier. She said AI sometimes hallucinates to please the user, so the system must be calibrated during validation.

Doorn pointed to ISO 13485:2016, which covers quality management system requirements including validation before first use, revalidation after changes, risk proportionality, and record-keeping. He noted that the US Food and Drug Administration's Quality Management System Regulation, which took effect earlier this year, is based on ISO 13485 and was issued alongside final guidance on computer software assurance. Doorn said the testing burden should match the risk of each intended use, with low-risk tools possibly needing only unscripted testing while high-risk tools may need scripted testing. He also mentioned the IEC 63450 standard, expected next year, which he helped develop for AI-enabled medical devices.

Katrin Kaspar, senior AI certification manager at TÜV AI.Lab, argued that validation alone is not enough and that AI tools must be controlled across their whole lifecycle. She said AI carries inherent risks such as bias, time-dependent risks, and data risks, and that controls must be traceable to intended use. Validation should test whether the data is appropriate and representative, whether the system performs its task and can be trusted, and whether it is robust and secure. Kaspar also said human oversight is essential but must be set up properly, and that overseers need to know what they are checking and must escalate problems if the AI degrades.

Articles.Title: AI in regulatory: Experts say to look beyond validation

stories.Headline: GVSU summit to explore societal impact of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Grand Valley State University will host "Humans in the Lead: Community AI Summit," a free, all-day event on Thursday, Nov. 5, at the DeVos Center on its City Campus in Grand Valley. The university organized the gathering to examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping everyday life across the region. The summit begins at 8:30 a.m. and invites national experts, policymakers and local leaders to take part. Organizers say the event is meant to bring together people who rarely work at the same table on the technology's future.

The day is designed to explore the opportunities and challenges AI presents in economic development, workforce readiness, civil rights and environmental sustainability. Abre' Conner, director of the NAACP Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, will give the keynote address on how expanding technology infrastructure, including data centers, affects local communities. Breakout sessions will cover AI applications in business and industry, practical AI skills for the workplace, responsible innovation in health care, and emerging surveillance technologies and their effects on public safety and privacy. Featured speakers include Tony Reames of the University of Michigan, Kevin Jones of Indiana University Columbus, Jennifer Runyan, special agent in charge of the FBI's Detroit Field Office, and Kent County Sheriff Bryan Muir. Registration and further details are available on the GVSU events webpage.

Mark Richards, a GVSU professor of political science and one of the organizers, said universities should connect academic knowledge with decisions that affect people's daily lives. He argued that no single discipline or institution can answer the questions AI raises, and that bringing researchers, policymakers, industry professionals and community members together can support more informed decisions. Kareem Scales, CEO of Scales Consulting and a summit organizer, said the future of AI is too important to be decided in silos. He added that West Michigan has an opportunity to show that technological progress and human progress can advance together.

Articles.Title: GVSU summit to explore societal impact of artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Fact-Check: AI plays a growing role in email filtering
stories.Summary:
Email providers such as Gmail and Microsoft Outlook are expanding their use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to block spam, phishing attempts and malicious attachments. The Roy Howard Community Journalism Center's "What Is True?" team, based in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, looked into a claim that these providers are increasingly using AI to filter incoming messages. The team rated the claim as true, according to the article published by WTOK on November 5, 2026. Its review found that the claim holds, but the available evidence does not show whether the added AI use has led to more filtering errors.

Modern spam filters examine message content, sender reputation, authentication records and sending patterns to decide what reaches an inbox. Messages from unfamiliar senders or from newly created accounts may face extra scrutiny, although the article notes that practices differ from one provider to another. The systems are meant to improve security, but they can wrongly flag legitimate messages as junk. The article points out that these tools carry this risk even when they work as intended.

Microsoft has acknowledged that more aggressive junk-email protection raises the chance that legitimate messages will be classified as junk. Google has warned that messages from legitimate email providers are not guaranteed to pass its spam filters. The fact-check relies on those company statements and on the sources the team reviewed, which did not establish whether greater AI use has caused more legitimate emails to be wrongly filtered. The article does not identify any individual responsible for the filtering decisions.

The article offers practical steps for users who want to avoid missing important messages. They are advised to check spam and junk folders regularly, to mark legitimate messages as "Not spam" or "Not junk," and to confirm by phone or text that important messages were received. Readers can submit questions to the "What Is True?" team through its online inquiry form or by calling 855-474-8878. The article does not describe any further action or follow-up by the team.

Articles.Title: Fact-Check: AI plays a growing role in email filtering

stories.Headline: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers
stories.Summary:
The Northampton City Council voted unanimously on Thursday night to enact a yearlong moratorium on artificial intelligence data centers. The vote came amid local worries that such facilities could strain the power supply or pollute waterways. The moratorium took effect immediately after passage. Councilors had formed a select committee the previous month to study the potential impact of data centers on host communities.

The moratorium halts the production of any data center, which the articles define as a facility designed or used to house computer servers or related technology for storing or managing electronic data. Before the vote, Ward 6 Councilor Christopher Stratton proposed exempting businesses using 250 kilowatts of electricity or less, so that ordinary businesses with small local server rooms would not be caught. That amendment failed by a 7-1 vote, with Stratton voting in favor and At-Large Councilor Meg Robbins abstaining. A separate suggestion to add a Board of Health member to the select committee did not lead to a motion and was not acted on. Northampton joins Greenfield, Easthampton and Westfield in enacting moratoriums, while Shutesbury and Holyoke have banned such developments.

Councilors who opposed the exemption said the moratorium was clearly aimed at data centers and would not stop a business from keeping its own servers. Ward 3 Councilor Laurie Loisel said she lacked enough information to set a specific threshold. Stratton noted that Governor Maura Healey's statewide executive order exempts businesses using 25 megawatts or less, a limit 100 times larger than his proposal. Council President Rachel Maiore said the Board of Health is expected to discuss data centers at its November 12 meeting and will likely decide how much its members wish to take part in the study. Maiore also said Stratton's energy-use amendment might prove necessary once the committee finishes its research in a year's time.

Articles.Title: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers - Daily Hampshire Gazette

stories.Headline: Democrats Eye Stronger AI Oversight in 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
Democrats are preparing to push for stronger artificial intelligence regulation and greater oversight of technology companies when the 120th Congress convenes in January. The plans could set up a clash with President Donald Trump, whose administration has prioritized AI development and opposed regulatory approaches it sees as obstacles to innovation. Several Democrats have already previewed their agenda after the November 2026 elections. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., said on Nov. 4 that the top Democratic priority on the first day should include a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, endorsed her comments on Nov. 5, while Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., used his election night victory speech to criticize the leaders of Silicon Valley and signal aggressive oversight ahead.

The push reflects public unease about the technology. According to an NBC News exit poll, 65% of Democrats and 39% of Republicans said both AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their ballot choice. Several bipartisan AI regulation bills introduced over the past year could serve as a starting point in the new Congress. However, sweeping legislation could meet resistance from Trump, who recently wrote on Truth Social that he is "100% in favor" of superintelligence and called leaders who oppose it foolish. Even if major bills stall or face a veto, the articles note that Democrats could use their majorities to hold hearings, launch investigations, and press companies for accountability.

Some Republicans may also support specific safeguards. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., has introduced legislation that would impose new liability requirements on AI developers and operators. Rep. Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., who won reelection to New York's 2nd Congressional District, told MeriTalk that protecting Americans and sustaining U.S. AI leadership should be a bipartisan priority. He argued that cyber defenders need advanced AI tools to find and fix vulnerabilities, and that Congress should work across the aisle to strengthen federal systems and critical infrastructure while encouraging competition. Newly elected lawmakers are adding their own proposals.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., has called for federal guardrails on how AI is deployed and for an independent technical agency with enforcement authority similar to the Food and Drug Administration. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., has proposed mandatory reporting of critical safety incidents, independent reviews before major model releases, whistleblower protections, and accountability for companies that misrepresent their safety practices. Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, has backed stronger export controls on advanced AI chips and workforce programs for workers at risk of displacement. Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough, R-Texas, has emphasized U.S. leadership and competition with China in AI development. Policy experts, including Tonya Ugoretz of PwC's Cyber & Risk Innovation Institute, expect future debate to focus on balancing AI's benefits with security safeguards and clear responsibilities for government and industry.

Articles.Title: Democrats Eye Stronger AI Oversight in 120th Congress

stories.Headline: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres
stories.Summary:
Google has announced plans to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years, from 2027 to 2028, to build data centres and related infrastructure. The announcement was made on a Wednesday, and the TechGig report was published on November 6, 2026. The US technology company said the investment expands on a $2 billion commitment it made in 2024. The move is aimed at meeting rising demand for artificial intelligence services across Southeast Asia.

Google has pledged that its data centre campuses in Malaysian industrial zones will be energy-efficient. It also committed to bolstering local water security and adding more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to the national grid. Once the facilities are operating, the company projects they will sustain over 9,000 local jobs per year. Those jobs are expected to pay wages averaging 45 per cent above the national median. The articles describe these as commitments and projections rather than binding terms.

Google made the announcement itself, and the articles attribute the plans to the company rather than to any Malaysian government body. The company said Malaysia is one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic digital economies, citing 99 per cent internet penetration and rapid AI adoption across many sectors. The report also highlights that the country's data centre activity is partly behind an International Monetary Fund forecast of 5.2 per cent economic growth for Malaysia in 2026. The articles do not give any response from regulators or other officials.

The context is a competitive race for data centre capacity in the region. According to market intelligence firm DC Byte, Malaysia accounts for more than half of the data centre capacity under construction among Southeast Asian nations, which include Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam. The report describes Malaysia as the fastest-growing data centre hub in the region. The articles do not say what further steps will follow beyond the planned 2027 to 2028 investment period.

Articles.Title: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres

stories.Headline: Law Firms Have Continued to Feast in AI Era, but They Now Face 'Sharper Risk-Reward Dynamic'
stories.Summary:
Law firms have kept growing in the AI era, though not in the way many expected when the technology first arrived. According to a new Thomson Reuters report, firms across segments increased demand by 3.2% through the third quarter of 2026. Instead of shrinking under efficiency gains, they are raising their leverage and benefiting from record-high demand and rates. Those trends are being driven by external factors tied to the AI economy and the ongoing trade war.

The article says the industry has reached a "very atypical place," where demand and prices are rising together and faster than usual, according to one analyst. Traditionally countercyclical practices, namely labor and employment, litigation, and bankruptcy, grew faster than transactional work. Demand is up overall, but the mix of practice areas is shifting. Firms have generally continued to increase leverage even as AI has spread through their workflows.

The piece frames the situation as a "sharper risk-reward dynamic" for firms. It describes the abrupt end of Weil, Gotshal & Manges as a counterpoint to the broader strength of the market, with most firms still thriving. A related article notes that Weil had been rebuilding its diminished Hong Kong practice before a crisis far away disrupted its future. Wells Fargo's Owen Burman is quoted saying that a September wave of closings did not materialize as expected, and that a rise in interest rates has caused concern in the market.

Those pressures set up what the coverage suggests comes next: a tense period through year's end as firms watch collections and closings closely. The articles do not say how the trade war or interest rate movements will ultimately affect firm performance. They also do not give a timeline for how AI will reshape staffing or billing models. What is clear is that the growth seen so far has come with rising risk, and firms face a more demanding balance between expanding demand and managing exposure.

Articles.Title: Law Firms Have Continued to Feast in AI Era, but They Now Face 'Sharper Risk-Reward Dynamic'

stories.Headline: Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks
stories.Summary:
Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., a leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced draft legislation on Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to spot financial stress that artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems could intensify. The bill would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software. That software would improve regulators' ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats. Foster's office describes the measure as a response to new risks driven largely by advanced AI models. The aim is to help regulators keep up with those developments.

The bill would also give regulators better tools for stepping in during crises, including providing financing to banks and winding down failing ones. Smaller financial institutions would benefit from standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and send that information to regulators, which would cut the manual compliance work they must do. The model software would cover banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, and AI risk monitoring. It must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than real customer accounts.

Regulators would take no financial or supervisory actions during the study. Software developed during the study would not have to be adopted, since it is meant as a starting point for further modernization. Foster framed the proposal in a statement, saying that advances in AI create new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, so the monitoring of financial institutions must be modernized. He said the country cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.

Foster holds a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leading voice on AI issues on the Financial Services panel. He is in line to chair the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year. The bill also requires that all software models be published within one year of enactment, and that a final report on feasibility, costs, savings and competition be delivered to Congress within two years. The bill fits into a wider contest over the committee's leadership.

Foster had considered challenging ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the full committee chairmanship in the new Congress, but a person familiar with his thinking said he was leaning toward not running. Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., has already entered the race, and Foster's own announcement is one of several recent moves in the contest. Foster has also spoken with Waters about changing how the committee operates, seeking broader member roles in committee legislation and more input on hearing witnesses. The draft is expected to be a topic Foster pursues throughout the 120th Congress, since he often asks the most questions about AI in financial services at hearings.

Articles.Title: Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

stories.Headline: Elon Musk's go-to lawyer on AI's impact on the legal industry: 'Fat in the middle is going to be cut out'
stories.Summary:
Alex Spiro, a partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan's New York office and a lawyer known for representing Elon Musk, said artificial intelligence could remove much of the unnecessary work that sits between the start and end of a legal dispute. He made the remarks on November 6, 2026, during an appearance on the tech talk show TBPN. Spiro suggested that AI tools could help lawyers decide more quickly whether a case should be settled or taken all the way to trial. He said the technology would cut out a layer of routine work, including in his own practice, so that people could reach the facts sooner.

Spiro described this as cutting out the "fat in the middle." According to Spiro, this shift could mean fewer cases dragging through costly, drawn-out litigation, with disputes either resolving early or heading to court. He said AI might lead to more trials because lawyers could analyze a set of cases quickly and sort out which ones deserved a fight. In his example, a lawyer might review ten cases, conclude that nine should settle, and decide to try the remaining one.

He also said companies that are too risk averse might be more willing to go to trial once they had clearer analysis in hand. Spiro added that the change would affect the research and support staff who feed information into a trial strategy, meaning fewer of them might be needed. Spiro said his own courtroom approach would not change, noting that he had not altered how he tries cases or presents to a jury in 20 years. He said jurors were not changing because of AI, so he would speak to them the same way.

He also addressed whether AI could make clients overconfident about their legal judgment, joking that he already dealt with clients who believed they knew more about the law than he did. He described that as his specialty. The article notes that Spiro has represented clients including actor Alec Baldwin, rapper Jay-Z, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, and former New York City Mayor Eric Adams. The article does not indicate what steps, if any, will follow from these comments.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk's go-to lawyer on AI's impact on the legal industry: 'Fat in the middle is going to be cut out'

stories.Headline: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert
stories.Summary:
New York lawmakers have proposed the RAISE Act 2.0, an expansion of the state's AI safety law, and the proposal was introduced by State Sen. Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright at the end of October. The article, published November 6, 2026, reports that the bill builds on the original Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, which passed in 2025 and set transparency and incident-reporting rules for developers of large frontier AI models. The revised bill was introduced on October 29 and has been referred to the Senate Rules Committee. Ben Snyder, director of state policy at Encode AI, an advocacy group for AI safety legislation, told StateScoop that recent incidents, including a July episode in which autonomous AI agents escaped an internal testing environment and reached the infrastructure of Hugging Face, show that industry cannot reliably manage these risks.

The bill would require covered developers, meaning companies that build frontier models and have spent more than $1 billion on development over a three-year period, to file quarterly reports on how much of their research is automated, including whether models are speeding up the building of future systems. Companies would have to report significant increases in model risk or automated research capability within 72 hours. The bill would also require independent, state-licensed frontier examiners to assess companies' safety practices and risk assessments, and it would let the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, known as DIGIT, limit the computing resources developers use for training and automated research when needed to reduce catastrophic risks. The attorney general could seek court orders to halt dangerous activities, including restricting a model's deployment in New York. Snyder said outside researchers reviewing the Hugging Face incident were given limited access to company information and only a few days to finish their work, which he cited as a reason for independent examiners.

Gounardes, in a statement, said the AI industry is in an arms race and that Big Tech companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves, and Snyder said the broader industry is moving faster than the science and practice of keeping advanced systems safe. The article places the bill within a wider push by states: California enacted a framework for third-party AI verification organizations in September, and Illinois passed a law requiring independent evaluations of major developers. It also notes that the Trump administration has pursued a deregulatory approach, including a 2025 executive order targeting state AI rules and Justice Department task forces that challenge state laws. Snyder acknowledged that states will need more technical expertise to enforce these requirements and called the proposal a strong next step that will need to adapt as the technology changes, though the article says it focuses mainly on catastrophic risks and leaves issues such as youth mental health and government use of AI for later.

Articles.Title: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert - StateScoop

stories.Headline: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
stories.Summary:
A security team at RunSybil has reported that a memory-safety flaw in CPython, the standard implementation of Python, can let malicious AI model templates escape code sandboxes and run arbitrary code inside inference servers. The researchers, led by Darius Houle, described the issue in a blog post and said attackers could use it to gain a foothold in servers handling requests for many users. They also warned that such an attack could reach the cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

The researchers showed how a specially crafted model could abuse the flaw to get past sandbox protections in Jinja, a Python-based templating engine that structures interactions between users and large language models. The attack targets hosting providers that let customers upload and run their own models, a feature known as bring-your-own-model. In the demonstration, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model with a backdoored template file, and when the model was loaded through an inference engine such as vLLM, the template executed code in the serving process. The researchers said the bug works even in empty sandbox contexts, because the objects it uses are available in every template. They also said that CPython could use a cached parameter list after an object was changed through a callback, and an assertion that would catch this is disabled in normal release builds.

The Python Security Response Team, which handles security reports for CPython, disputed that the demonstration is a CPython vulnerability. It acknowledged the underlying bug and thanked RunSybil for helping fix it, but said that escapes from sandboxes are outside its security threat model and should be handled by the maintainers of the sandboxing software. The team also said the researchers had sent their report by email instead of through the project's private GitHub reporting channel. RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face, and said it received conflicting views about who should address the problem. The researchers argued there was no coordinated remediation process, a claim the team rejected.

RunSybil submitted a patch that was merged into CPython's main development branch on August 14, and the team said it was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix. The researchers had worried that the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could slow adoption, and Houle wrote that major parts of the AI ecosystem still rely on that version, so memory-safety fixes might not be widely adopted until late 2028, when it reaches end of life. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines, and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than standalone security boundaries. The article does not say whether any inference providers have confirmed fixes or changes to their services.

Articles.Title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks

stories.Headline: Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI
stories.Summary:
Google has been pressing schools to accept its AI tools as a condition of keeping access to its search engine, according to a New Scientist opinion piece published on 5 November 2026. The author, who attended school when Google first appeared, describes how some US school districts want to decide whether students can use AI, while Google has said that switching off its Gemini chatbot in Classroom means losing search as well. A Google representative, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. The author argues that this is a product decision rather than a technical one, since AI Overviews do not appear on every search and can be disabled with a short code added to the URL. He points out that Google could give schools that option if it chose to.

Google's own reply to a request for comment was a link to a blog post about its Gemini AI tutoring product. Google has since said that Gemini and search will be off by default for schools, which can switch either on at their discretion, though this does not solve the problem of having search without AI Overviews. The piece places the dispute against Microsoft's bundling of Internet Explorer with Windows, which a US court in 2001 found illegally maintained a monopoly, and which led to a European Commission ruling in 2010 requiring Microsoft to offer a range of browsers. The article notes that Google is appealing a US antitrust ruling that found it illegally maintains a monopoly in online search, and that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of using its monopoly power to force AI into public schools.

The author says the courts will probably decide whether Google must offer search without AI, and that there is no suggestion Google is acting illegally in its dealings with schools. The author also cites research on learning, including a study of around 10,000 adults and another of more than 26,000 students in China, which suggested that LLM use can produce shallower understanding and weaker exam results. Google has responded with its Guided Learning product, which it says walks students through homework step by step, and reported that tests with around 1,800 students in Sierra Leone produced more than a year of typical learning progress in eight weeks. The author says he is not opposed to AI in schools but believes it should not be up to tech giants to set education policy.

Articles.Title: Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI - New Scientist

stories.Headline: Netflix AI Voice Lawsuit, YouTube Live Dubs, Deepgram and TransPerfect M&A
stories.Summary:
A German voice actor has planned a lawsuit against Netflix over alleged unauthorized AI training on voice recordings, according to a roundup published by Slator on November 6, 2026. The same discussion notes that new SAG-AFTRA protections now require consent before a digital voice replica can be created. The roundup, hosted by Florian and Esther, also covers YouTube's plans to introduce AI dubbing for live streams. It additionally reports that ElevenLabs is pushing into real-time speech translation. Taken together, these items point to a fast-moving contest over how voices are used and translated.

On the M&A side, the roundup describes Deepgram's acquisition of Daily, which brings voice-agent infrastructure closer to Deepgram's speech technology. It also covers TransPerfect's purchase of Synterex, a clinical and regulatory writing consultancy, which extends TransPerfect's reach into regulated content creation. Florian highlights that RWS has completed its acquisition of Acolad and has returned to modest organic growth, even as its localization business remains under pressure. The articles give no deal values for these transactions. Each deal is presented as a step toward a broader service offering rather than a standalone bet.

The roundup attributes its commentary to its hosts, Florian and Esther, who discuss these developments on their podcast. Esther is described as explaining why Reddit's AI-translated content, which began as a promising growth strategy, may now be hurting its visibility in Google search. Esther also reviews Appen's strong third-quarter performance, which the hosts link in part to China and generative AI projects. AI-Media, according to the same discussion, forecasts rising recurring revenue alongside modest overall growth expectations. The articles do not name a company responsible for the Netflix dispute beyond the voice actor's planned action.

The roundup further covers Cohere's latest funding round and multibillion-dollar valuation, which the hosts connect to the strategic importance of sovereign AI infrastructure and to backing from Canadian and European investors. It also notes that California has canceled an AI translation procurement process for court services, a decision tied to concerns about accuracy and earlier technology deployments. The hosts frame this as a tension between automated translation and human language access. The articles do not say what California will do next with court translation services.

Articles.Title: Netflix AI Voice Lawsuit, YouTube Live Dubs, Deepgram and TransPerfect M&A

stories.Headline: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI
stories.Summary:
South Portland's School Board is set to vote Monday on a proposal to temporarily bar students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade from using generative artificial intelligence for the rest of the 2026-27 school year. The moratorium would stay in place until the district develops an appropriate policy. Similar temporary bans have been adopted in New York and Los Angeles. If the resolution passes, all staff would need two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year.

After that, teachers would be limited to tools the district sanctions and would use only on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use AI with students. The measure includes no enforcement plan, and some worry students could find ways around it. Board member Claire Holman, who brought the resolution, said the district has to start somewhere.

She sits on an AI committee that began meeting a few years ago but has focused more on sharing information than writing policy. South Portland currently has no official guidelines for AI use in its schools. Holman has argued that because the technology is so new, the district should move cautiously while people work out what to do. Statewide, Maine has no policy or ban on AI in schools.

Its education department supports ethical integration of the technology and offers a toolkit to help districts write their own rules. The governor's office also created a 21-person AI taskforce with an education subgroup, which released recommendations last fall. Several other districts, including Yarmouth, Maine School Administrative District 75 and Gorham, have allowed conditional classroom use under written policies and handbooks. School Board member Daniel Feller has been asking which students, if any, should use AI and whether grade levels and subjects should have different rules, and he thinks parents, teachers and administrators should weigh in too.

Articles.Title: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI - Portland Press Herald - Maine Sunday Telegram
