stories.Headline: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has announced that it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc., the company behind Code Storage and a family of open-source developer tools. The announcement was made on November 4, 2026, and the coverage carried by TechGig followed on November 6. The deal is intended to expand what OpenAI's Codex platform can do for building, understanding, and reviewing software. OpenAI says the acquisition will help AI agents play a larger role throughout the software development process.

The acquisition would bring Pierre's tools into OpenAI's developer ecosystem and build on Git workflows that developers already use. Pierre's Trees tool helps developers navigate project files, while its Diffs tool lets them review code changes, and both are already used in the Codex application. Diffs also includes an Edit mode that lets reviewers fix code where they spot a problem. Pierre additionally developed Highlights, a fast syntax highlighter that updates as code is typed or generated by an agent, and it designed the API for Code Storage. Pierre's open-source projects will remain open source, and customers can keep using Code Storage after the deal closes.

OpenAI's leadership stated the purpose of the acquisition in its announcement, saying its own engineering work showed that the systems around Git need to change as more work happens in parallel. The company noted that earlier that week it had described how it was scaling Git with Pando, its in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. OpenAI said it wanted to set a standard for modern software development, from the first branch an agent creates to the moment code is deployed. The company also said it wants Codex to link the code a company releases with the decisions its people make. The deal is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals, and until it closes the two companies will remain separate and independent.

stories.Headline: AI stock rout: Should Singapore investors buy the dip or cut exposure?
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off in US technology stocks has spread to Asia and Singapore, leaving investors to weigh whether to buy the dip, cut their exposure or wait. The Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4% on Nov 5, two days after the US midterm elections, wiping out about US$2.5 trillion in market value. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 12.2%. Chip-heavy markets in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan were hit on Nov 6, and Singapore-listed technology stocks also took a beating.

The fall followed a Democratic sweep of Congress, which raised the prospect of tighter scrutiny of artificial intelligence. Investors were already questioning how quickly spending on chips and data centres would turn into profits, and experts said crowded AI bets and borrowed money may have amplified the drop as funds rushed for the exits. Investors are watching whether greater scrutiny of electricity and water use, grid costs and permits leads to rules that delay data centre construction. They are also looking at whether major cloud providers trim their spending plans and whether chipmakers cut their earnings forecasts.

Saxo chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said in a note to investors on Nov 6 that AI demand and existing infrastructure had not disappeared overnight, and that many leading technology companies still have substantial cash flows and competitive advantages. She described the change as one in market sentiment and in how investors judge future growth, regulatory risk and acceptable valuations. Brian Levitt, chief global market strategist at Invesco, called the sell-off a reset in one of the market's most crowded trades, warning the correction could continue. He also said lower prices are making some AI stocks more attractive to long-term investors.

Chanana advised that long-term investors who can ride out further losses may keep investing regularly if their holdings still suit them. She suggested those with spare cash focus on firms with strong balance sheets, steady cash flow and reasonable valuations, and spread purchases over time. Heavily exposed investors could shift money towards established cash-generating businesses or other sectors, while those trading on margin should work out how far prices could fall before they must add cash or sell. Afdhal Rahman, executive director of wealth advisory at OCBC, said in a Nov 6 note that cloud giants such as Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are relatively well placed in the near term, while he favours graphics processors, custom chips and networking equipment. He was more cautious about smaller AI cloud providers that rely heavily on debt.

stories.Headline: What AI Leaders Can Learn from the Midterms
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held on November 3, 2026, while Republicans kept the White House. Markets reacted on Wednesday, with U.S. stock futures falling overnight as investors weighed the chance of tighter rules on AI, cryptocurrency and data centers. Futures later recovered after President Donald Trump said he would accept the results, according to Reuters. Elon Musk, who put more than $400 million behind Republican candidates, joked on X that data centers in space looked appealing after several of his chosen candidates lost.

The biggest worry for the technology sector is possible limits on AI infrastructure, especially power-hungry data centers. In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on new data center construction until the state deals with their electricity and water demands. Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, said fears of a broad halt to AI buildout were overblown, though new regulations could slow some projects. He estimated that 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI capacity could be affected, according to MarketWatch.

Other voices were more upbeat. Deborah Cunningham of Federated Hermes said a split government could act as a blockade against new legislation, and divided government has historically been viewed favorably by markets because it can limit big policy shifts. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said Trump's acceptance of the results eased some fears of prolonged confrontation and gridlock, though she expected major policy disagreements to continue. Continental CFO Roland Welzbacher said companies in the U.S. need stability and a reliable economic framework, and Fraport CEO Stefan Schulte suggested the outcome might ease worries about customs problems for travelers, while warning against reading too much into it. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic donor Reid Hoffman called the results a wave against Trump and urged Democrats to build an economy that serves every American.

Away from Washington, the legal industry is also working out how to use AI, as described in a JD Supra piece by Deborah Farone about a joint webinar of the International Bar Association and the Legal Marketing Association. More than 1,200 people from 939 firms in 104 countries registered, far above her expectation of 100 to 200, and about 700 joined live. Panelists from Bowmans, Bass, Berry & Sims, Gibson Dunn and Pierson Ferdinand said firms should start from a real problem, take small steps, verify everything AI produces, and stay accountable for the final work. They also advised preparing for client conversations about who benefits from the speed AI creates, and hiring for judgment and curiosity over prompting skills.

stories.Headline: Whitehurst Backs Data Center Pause But Calls Anti-AI Memes ‘Hypocrisy’ - St. Johns Citizen
stories.Summary:
Three moves from St. Johns County, Florida, and Ohio, Georgia, and Texas, now show how the data center debate is spilling into the 2026 elections. On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, the St. Johns County Commission voted 5–0 to suspend applications for medium and large data centers for one year, starting November 15. The pause gives county staff time to study where such facilities could go, how they would fit with nearby development, and whether local infrastructure could support them. Commissioner Christian Whitehurst backed the pause but criticized critics who use AI-generated memes against data centers, calling it hypocrisy. In Ohio, Amy Acton's campaign announced her victory in the governor's race on November 4, 2026, after she spoke to supporters the day before.

Her platform sets conditions that projects must meet before proceeding, covering costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and siting. Those conditions would require project backers, not taxpayers or surrounding communities, to bear the full cost of gas, water, and electricity. Developers would also need to invest in their own generation and show that projects would not raise electricity prices or weaken regional reliability. Acton's platform would end data center nondisclosure agreements, add clawbacks to tax incentives, and require siting on brownfields or previously developed industrial land rather than farms. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms's August 31, 2026 proposal called for a pause on new data center construction while the state reassessed its position.

Her approach would use the pause to study the issue and design a response afterward, while Acton has already set entry conditions in advance. Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who declared victory, proposed an immediate moratorium until the legislature enacts protections, and Governor Greg Abbott had already ordered a permit halt on September 21, 2026. Whitehurst said he doubted that any applicant would seek a data center in St. Johns County at the scale covered by the moratorium, and he cited a Florida Power & Light staffer who said the county was unlikely to be a candidate over the next 20 years. He argued that people who want less demand for data centers should start by using less data themselves. Deputy County Attorney Kealey West said staff would consult utility providers, the St. Johns River Water Management District, and other stakeholders during the review.

Acton's campaign and Ohio's Secretary of State have said that election-night results remain unofficial until certification, which is expected about three weeks after the election. Georgia's returns, last updated at 4:19 a.m. on November 4, 2026, showed Bottoms leading Rick Jackson with 54.31 percent of the vote. Hinojosa said Abbott called to congratulate her and offer transition assistance.

Across these races, the policy approaches differ in sequence and detail, though all three use the language of a pause or moratorium. The St. Johns County county commissioners will rely on the state study that West said should be ready in July 2027, and the county expects to consider it then. Ohio's conditions and Georgia's review will determine how restrictions take shape, and Texas's durability depends on legislative action. Reporting from Unite.AI notes that the substantive differences remain open, depending on how each proposal is implemented.

stories.Headline: EXL acquires data and AI consulting market leader Aimpoint Digital to expand forward-deployed AI capabilities and accelerate enterprise transformation
stories.Summary:
EXL, a global data and AI company listed on Nasdaq under the symbol EXLS, announced on November 5, 2026, that it has acquired Aimpoint Digital, a data and AI consulting and platform engineering firm. Aimpoint Digital is known for building enterprise data and AI platforms and has deep expertise with partners such as Anthropic, Databricks and Snowflake. The announcement was made from New York. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The acquisition adds approximately 250 experienced AI engineers, platform architects, analytics consultants, decision scientists and AI strategists to EXL's data and AI capabilities. EXL says this expands its forward-deployed talent base, puts senior AI expertise closer to client teams, and adds capacity for complex, multi-year transformations. The two companies plan to give clients more continuity from the first strategy conversation through architecture, engineering, production deployment and managed operations. That connected approach is meant to reduce handoffs, establish clearer accountability and speed the path to measurable results. The deal also deepens EXL's relationships with key technology partners and widens its partner ecosystem.

Rohit Kapoor, EXL's chairman and chief executive officer, said clients need a partner who can take them from AI ambition to impact at enterprise scale. He said Aimpoint Digital's strategists and engineers bring the hands-on skill to turn AI strategy into production reality on the platforms clients trust most. Combined with EXL's data foundations, industry expertise, agentic AI solutions and operational scale, he said, the company can offer clients a single, accountable partner for the whole journey. Ben Yopp, chief executive officer and cofounder of Aimpoint Digital, said joining EXL will allow the firm to do more breakthrough work on a much larger scale. He said Aimpoint Digital supplies AI strategy and engineering talent, while EXL adds industry expertise, global reach and the ability to run AI in operations.

The company framed the move against a backdrop in which enterprises are investing heavily in AI, yet many struggle to move projects from pilot to production-scale value. It also noted that demand for strategic data and AI work outpaces the available talent. The purchase follows EXL's recent acquisition of iMerit, a provider of AI model training, evaluation and reinforcement learning. Together, the two deals are meant to extend EXL's ability to support clients from strategy and architecture through engineering, deployment and managed AI operations. EXL, founded in 1999 and headquartered in New York, has more than 74,000 employees across six continents.

stories.Headline: AI stocks tied to Texas data center boom slide after Hinojosa win
stories.Summary:
Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and AI-related stocks with ties to the state's data center boom fell in the hours that followed. Overnight trading on Robinhood, as cited by CNBC, showed Nasdaq-100 futures down 2%, the XLK technology ETF down 2%, CoreWeave down 7%, and Nebius and Oracle each down 4%. On Wednesday, SpaceX and Tesla shares dropped about 4% before trimming losses, even as the broader market surged, and CoreWeave, IREN and Vertiv also traded lower. By Thursday the selling had widened, with the Nasdaq Composite closing down 5.5%, the S&P 500 down 4.4% and the Dow down 1,833 points, or 3.4%, according to the Associated Press as relayed by the Dallas Express. Nvidia sank 9.3%, Advanced Micro Devices fell 17.3% and CoreWeave lost 9.8%.

Hinojosa, who is expected to take office in January 2027, has called for a moratorium on new data center projects until protections are in place for electricity supplies, water resources and local communities. Texas is a major hub for cloud providers and AI developers, and tighter permitting rules or changes to tax incentives could affect project approvals and expansion. Many listed companies have direct exposure, including CoreWeave, which has contracted capacity at Galaxy Digital's Helios campus in West Texas, and Cipher Digital, which is building its Black Pearl facility near Wink for Amazon Web Services under a 15-year lease. Riot Platforms has a lease with AMD at Rockdale with potential expansion to 200 MW, Hut 8 has commercialized 704 MW at its Beacon Point campus in Nueces County, and Alphabet has committed $40 billion to Texas through 2027. Oracle is involved in the Stargate campus in Abilene.

Dan Ives, a managing director at Yorkville, said the Democratic wins, especially control of the Senate, will create major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in Washington over the next two years. He said those hurdles will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US, and that Texas is the biggest worry, since around 25% to 30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from the state. Ives described Hinojosa as a known anti-data center politician and said SpaceX and Musk are caught in the middle of the political fight. Elon Musk wrote on X that data centers in space were looking pretty appealing. Fundstrat's Tom Lee, writing before the results, argued that President Trump's veto power could block any anti-AI bills and that Democrats would likely embrace data centers for the money and jobs they bring.

Under Abbott, Texas had already paused certain data center permits pending reviews of grid capacity and water resources, and the prevailing view was that the pause would have ended had he been reelected. Data center concerns were a key issue in the 2026 midterms, with growing public opposition to facility locations, power infrastructure expansion and fears that rising electricity demand could push up consumer costs. Financing worries and valuation questions had already pressured the sector before the election. Ives noted that one silver lining could be a slowdown in AI spending, and he remains bullish long term. He said negotiations and politics in Texas will be significant and that Big Tech will need to adjust to the new political landscape.

stories.Headline: Pediatric Brain Tumors: Prognostic AI Model Guides Precision Therapy Choices
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence model called MANTIS, built from DNA methylation profiling, was reported in Nature Genetics to give a look at outcomes for children with medulloblastoma and ependymoma. The study was published in the journal, and the article is dated November 5, 2026. The researchers say the tool may help guide personalized treatment decisions, including how intense a child's treatment should be, in order to balance effects on thinking and learning against survival goals. The model was developed by a team of researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

The tool was trained on genome-wide DNA methylation array data, covering methylation patterns and copy number changes, from 2,786 patients. It produces individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period. Its concordance indices reached up to 0.80, plus or minus 0.07, which the article says was above the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. The researchers also adapted MANTIS to test radiation dose levels, and it found that about 60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma would not have a significant survival disadvantage when treated with less-intensive, lower-dose craniospinal irradiation, a result that could mean better neurocognitive outcomes.

Senior author Volker Hovestadt, a computational biologist at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said the goal is to move past broad risk categories toward a more individual understanding of each child's tumor. He said this could help match treatment intensity to the biology of the disease and reduce long-term side effects for some patients. First author Sabina Stefan, a postdoctoral researcher at the same institute, said the work shows how AI can learn from molecular tests already used in care. She added that with further clinical study, similar approaches could support personalized decisions for other cancers as well.

The study authors described MANTIS as a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in pediatric brain tumors, and as a blueprint that could be applied to other cancer types. The study was supported by the St. Jude Research Collaboratives program, with further support from the Charles H. Hood Foundation, the Children's Cancer Research Fund and the V Foundation. The article notes that the content has not been reviewed by the American Society of Clinical Oncology and does not necessarily reflect its views. The article does not say when the model might be used in routine clinical care.

stories.Headline: Fridge hacks and finance attacks flag AI insecurity - Academia
stories.Summary:
On November 2, 2026, dozens of Belgian grocery stores and an Ikea superstore saw their refrigerator temperatures rise sharply, with several of the firms involved confirming they had been hit by a cyberattack. One Delhaize supermarket in Boortmeerbeek, about 30 kilometers from Brussels, displayed a sign apologizing that no products were available in its refrigerators and freezers due to cyberattacks. The article, a column by Reuters columnist Mike Dolan published on November 5, 2026, uses these incidents as a starting point. It cites them alongside other recent events, including what it calls the biggest cyber theft in history, the hacking of Ukraine's air defense alert systems, and attacks on encrypted financial accounts. The column does not name the groups behind the supermarket hacks.

The column argues that the pace and scale of such activity could make the economic damage from artificial intelligence far larger than many assume. It says some industry estimates put the global cost of cyber activity at trillions of dollars, and that this cost is likely to rise as financial sector targets increase. Dolan writes that investment safety may need rethinking and market volatility could be stoked, and that the speed with which AI can already cause economic and financial harm deserves assessment. He notes that fears about encryption in banking have usually been tied to future quantum computing, which many experts consider years away. The column also observes that financial markets have focused mainly on whether AI infrastructure spending can continue, rather than on rising cyber risk.

The column attributes the threat to unknown criminal groups, state actors and, in some scenarios, rogue AI models. It cites a Council on Foreign Relations monitor showing that about 77 percent of operations over the past 20 years were suspected to have been sponsored by China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. It also says military leaders assume they are in an arms race over cyber and AI capabilities, with the ongoing Iran war and Ukraine's drone warfare cited as examples. Dolan points to the World Economic Forum's report, in which cyber insecurity, misinformation and adverse outcomes of AI all ranked among the top global risks. He also cites a survey by the UK's Association of Investment Companies, where nearly three-quarters of respondents were worried about misinformation, and its research director Nick Britton's view that AI firms may have to work harder to persuade investors if a market correction occurs.

The articles present this as a broader trend rather than a single dated event, and they do not describe any formal regulation or policy response tied to the supermarket incidents. Dolan's column suggests that rising defense budgets in the United States, Europe and Asia will increasingly go toward cyber and AI capabilities. The column ends by arguing that hacking refrigerators, even without a ransom, reflects a more dangerous and unpredictable global environment that may carry a heavy price. Iren's shares jumped as much as 19% in early trading on Friday, November 6, 2026, after the data center operator reported strong growth in its artificial intelligence cloud business for its fiscal first quarter. The stock had fallen roughly 17% the previous session during a broader sell-off in AI-related shares, so the gain partly reversed that drop. The company, which has moved from bitcoin mining into AI cloud and data center infrastructure, has been hit hard by the recent pullback in neocloud stocks.

Iren, whose customers include Microsoft, reported $200 million in AI revenue for the three months ending September 30, up from $71 million in the prior quarter and $7 million a year earlier. The company posted a quarterly loss of $263 million, which was wider than the average analyst estimate compiled by Bloomberg. Its AI Cloud gross margin of 86% was in line with the previous quarter. Iren also expanded an existing agreement with a leading frontier AI lab and signed a new five-year contract under which the customer prepaid about 90% of the associated GPU costs, reducing the need for additional debt financing.

Iren said it now expects to reach its $4 billion annualized revenue target in January or February, later than the December timeline it had previously forecast. stories.Headline: Enterprises struggle to link AI spending to business value
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are getting better at tracking what they spend on artificial intelligence, yet many still cannot prove the return on that money. According to a recent survey, only 9 per cent of respondents felt confident showing value from their AI spending, even though they understood their costs. J.R. Storment of the Tokenomics Foundation described a "whiplash" this year, as early enthusiasm gave way to spending caps. Companies could see their total AI bills but struggled to tie that spending to results.

Attribution remains the core problem, because firms often cannot assign AI costs to specific activities or cost centres. Enterprises typically draw AI from four to six separate sources, each reporting data differently. Shawn Alpay of the Linux Foundation is working through the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification to unify billing data across providers. The effort plans to work with OpenTelemetry during its 1.6 development cycle to link telemetry data with cost data. Storment also warned that simply moving work to cheaper models can break cached tokens and raise uncached costs.

Jerod Johnson of CData Software argued that AI spend is now driven by agent behaviour in production, making it largely a data and architecture problem. In CData's tests of 27 models, only one in 400 runs succeeded without business context, while 12 models achieved 15 out of 15 successful runs with context. Runs without context averaged 29 turns compared with seven with context, and 37 per cent hit a 40-turn cap versus 2 per cent. Johnson urged firms to measure cost per correct answer rather than raw spending.

Separately, ISG, a global AI-focused research and advisory firm, reports that European enterprises face similar pressure, with AI adoption exceeding expectations but financial returns lagging. ISG will hold its AI Impact Summit Paris on November 9 and 10 at the Pullman Paris Tour Eiffel, bringing together leaders from companies including Pfizer, Thales and WPP. The summit will focus on moving AI beyond isolated experiments, with sessions on measuring business value, sovereign AI, and governance. Its organisers say the goal is to help firms capture returns while keeping control of their data and managing risk.

stories.Headline: Google’s AI success is putting its search dominance at risk
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported earnings last week showing search revenue that came in weaker than expected, and the company said its AI Mode for search, which it monetizes at a lower rate than traditional search, was a contributing factor. The report prompted a sharp selloff in the company's shares, and the stock lost almost 19 percent in October alone, its worst month ever. That decline wiped out $758 billion in market value. Analysts described the result as a major red flag for investors already worried about Alphabet's heavy spending on AI infrastructure.

Search accounted for more than half of Alphabet's 2025 revenue, which is why the weakness matters so much to shareholders. Investors had already been unsettled by soaring capital expenditures, concerns that the company was falling behind in cutting-edge AI models, and negative free cash flow in the previous quarter. The shares had climbed 65 percent in 2025 but have struggled since, sliding into negative territory this year. The stock now trades at about 18 times estimated earnings over the next 12 months, down from 29 times in February and below its 10-year average of roughly 21.

Analysts are divided on how serious the threat is. Citizens analyst Andrew Boone downgraded Alphabet to market perform from outperform in an October 29 report, arguing that the company faces significant execution risk as it moves search monetization toward AI agents. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote on October 30 that this was the first quarter in which the thesis that AI would crush search appeared to have merit. Other investors are more optimistic, pointing to accelerating growth in Alphabet's cloud business and the lower valuation as reasons the selloff may be overdone. The articles note that the company's revenue model for AI-driven search remains unclear and that the outcome is still in its early stages.

stories.Headline: Learning a Prior-Data Fitted Network for Graph Foundation Models via Structural Causal Model Priors
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Ziwei Zhang and nine co-authors has posted a paper on arXiv describing GSCM-PFN, a graph prior-data fitted network for graph foundation models. The article was indexed on doi.org on November 6, 2026, at 06:00 UTC. The authors built on the idea that prior-data fitted networks, which learn from large synthetic datasets, could support prediction across many domains. Their work proposes a model that is pre-trained on synthetic graphs rather than on real-world graph data.

The authors say existing graph foundation models face limits, including small pre-training scale and reliance on aligning with text used by large language models. Existing graph prior-data fitted networks, they add, struggle to model causal relationships among nodes and edges, to generate diverse graph structures, and to design architectures that can learn from complex synthetic data. To address this, the paper introduces a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model that guides synthetic graph generation. It also describes prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling, which the authors use to produce varied graph generation strategies. A third component is a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network, which the authors say comes with theoretical guarantees.

The paper's authors, Ziwei Zhang, Tianyin Liao, Chunyu Hu, Ge Lan, Nuo Xu, Yi Huang, Qingyun Sun, Xingxuan Zhang, Peng Cui and Jianxin Li, report that GSCM-PFN outperformed both conventional graph foundation models and prior-data fitted network-based models across 23 real-world benchmarks. They state that this result was achieved without using real-world graph data for pre-training. The authors also say they prove their structural causal model-based generation prior is more expressive than existing priors. The article includes a link to the code, but the indexed text does not describe any further steps, release plans or independent review.

stories.Headline: Google Faces Criticism in Canada Over AI Requirements for School Search Access
stories.Summary:
Google has announced that students at schools using its services will not be able to access its full search engine unless their school systems also opt in to the company's artificial intelligence features. The announcement, published on Tuesday, November 4, 2026, has drawn criticism from Canadian educators who say schools should decide for themselves which digital tools suit their students. Google Search is widely used for classroom research and assignments, so the link between the two services has raised concern. Canadian school boards are now weighing whether they can keep using a familiar resource without accepting additional AI functions.

Under the new policy, Google's AI products, including its Gemini assistant and Google Search, will be turned off by default for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators explicitly turn them on. The change reverses an August policy that had enabled Gemini by default in Google Classroom. Google has said schools will be able to toggle Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search on or off individually, but it has not explained how Search would work without its AI features. The company has also said it will share more specifics with schools in the coming months, before the changes roll out. Google has said AI Mode and AI Overviews will guide students step by step through problems instead of giving quick answers.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, is responsible for the announcement and has said the company will provide further details ahead of the rollout. In response to questions from CNN, Google said the policy gives schools more choice, not less. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the change, saying that no corporation should have the power to dictate how children are taught. Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said in a statement on X that Google was seeking to exploit its dominance in internet search. Josh Golin, executive director of the children's advocacy group Fairplay, argued that pressing schools into using Google's AI products is likely to backfire.

The move comes amid growing scrutiny of AI use among young students. In September, the Los Angeles Unified School District restricted students from accessing generative AI platforms for the 2026-27 school year, shortly after New York City announced a one-year ban on AI use among elementary and middle school students. The debate reflects broader questions about how technology companies introduce AI into services that schools already depend on. Canadian educators have not yet reported a decision on how they will respond, and the articles do not say what Google's rollout timeline will be.

stories.Headline: Axon Sued for Allegedly Collecting Data on Millions of California Drivers Through Its AI License Plate Readers
stories.Summary:
A proposed class-action lawsuit filed on November 3 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California accuses Axon Enterprise of collecting vehicle and location data on millions of California drivers through its AI-powered license plate recognition cameras. The plaintiffs, Ryan Scott Mun and Felix Phan, say the company runs more than 1,000 cameras across the state and failed to disclose how it collects, stores, uses, and shares the information. The suit seeks more than $5 million in damages and a court order to stop the practices it describes as unlawful. The complaint says the fixed and mobile cameras scan passing vehicles and record plate numbers, locations, travel directions, and details such as color, make, and body type.

Mobile units operate from police patrol cars, and the complaint says Axon introduced them in 2021 and began installing fixed cameras in 2025. The filing also alleges that Axon's Fusus and Axon Evidence platforms combine this data with other sources, letting users reconstruct people's movements. The dispute centers on California's Automated License Plate Recognition Privacy Act, enacted in 2015, which requires operators of these systems to publish a clear usage and privacy policy. The lawsuit claims Axon has not published a policy that meets those requirements, leaving drivers unable to learn who can access their information, how long records are kept, or how to correct errors.

Axon has pointed to safeguards such as encrypted storage, recorded access logs, and human verification of hotlist alerts. The plaintiffs argue those measures do not replace the separate obligation to publish a compliant policy. They also warn that inaccurate records could place a vehicle on a law enforcement hotlist and lead to a wrongful stop or detention. Mun, who lives in Daly City, says he cannot complete his regular trips without passing Axon cameras and that the data could let someone with system access track his daily routines.

Phan, who lives in Palm Desert, alleges that the cameras capture his vehicle and location information as he moves around the area. The proposed class covers California drivers whose vehicle data was captured by a license plate reader and processed or stored through Axon's systems since 2023. The complaint names cameras in locations including Beverly Hills, Burbank, Palm Desert, Daly City, UCLA, and California State University, Long Beach. The allegations are contained in the complaint and have not been tested in court.

stories.Headline: What Shaped Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s Thinking on A.I.
stories.Summary:
Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was shaped early by an interest in artificial intelligence that began during his years as a doctoral student in physics. In 2007, while visiting Princeton University, he discussed Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book on the Singularity with a friend, Colin Heckman, and argued that the milestone could arrive within their lifetimes. According to Heckman, Amodei became fixated on the idea that artificial intelligence had to be built correctly. Amodei was then 24 and had been reading blogs and online forums that debated the technology's potential to threaten humanity. Those influences, according to more than two dozen people who know him, still shape his thinking today.

The same sources describe two linked philosophies that share a firm belief that mathematical reasoning can alter the future of humanity. Amodei came to these ideas through online communities focused on charitable giving and on the risks of advanced technology. His worldview is presented as the foundation for how he approaches the work of Anthropic, which is preparing to carry out one of the largest public listings in the world this month. The reporting says this background helps explain how he regards the technology he is helping to build. The article is an in-depth profile, and the reporters drew on interviews with classmates, teachers, friends and colleagues to reconstruct that history.

Separately, a legal development involving Amodei was reported on Tuesday. A federal judge, Eumi K. Lee of the U.S. District Court, dismissed a direct copyright infringement claim against him by music publishers, though she allowed them to amend their allegations. Lee also expressed doubt that the publishers had offered enough evidence that Anthropic's model, Claude, generated infringing lyrics drawn from more than 20,000 copyrighted compositions. She deferred ruling on those claims and on allegations that Anthropic unlawfully removed copyright management information. Both sides have until the following Wednesday to propose how the case should proceed.

The articles do not describe the outcome of the proposals due next week. They also do not say how the Anthropic listing will affect the company's legal exposure in the copyright matter. stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice
stories.Summary:
Incoming Democratic majorities in Washington have signaled that the hands-off approach to artificial intelligence under Republican control is ending. Midterm voters elected Democratic candidates who campaigned on AI guardrails and passed dozens of state and local ballot measures limiting new data center construction. Exit polling by SSRS found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. At a post-election press conference on Wednesday, Democratic House leadership previewed their plans for the new term.

Representative Ted Lieu of California, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said the party would hold public hearings on AI and pass reasonable guardrails for the industry. He said the Trump administration and House Republicans had made a poor political and policy choice last year by letting the AI industry operate largely unchecked. Lieu co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI, formed last year by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and he said he and his colleagues will release a document outlining policy priorities for the new Congress. Several Democratic candidates who defeated incumbent Republicans ran on broad AI regulation. Annie Andrews of South Carolina advocated a two-year moratorium on data centers, Roy Cooper of North Carolina called for data centers to cover the full costs of their energy use, and James Talarico of Texas wants to prioritize youth safety.

OpenAI responded less than 48 hours after Election Day by announcing new data center commitments, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs. The company said voluntary commitments are a starting point and called for federal, state, and local policymakers to set clear rules for how the industry builds. Democrats are expected to push for rules that would require OpenAI and other AI companies to go well beyond their voluntary safety and accountability standards. Although Democrats won sizeable House and Senate majorities, those majorities are not large enough to override a presidential veto. President Donald Trump has strongly opposed AI regulation and supports data centers, though the article suggests voters' rejection of Republican policies could push him toward compromise.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's models improving nearly twice as fast with help from AI, study finds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's AI models are improving nearly twice as fast as before, according to an independent study by the AI safety nonprofit METR, published on Thursday, November 5, 2026. The researchers found that the technology is playing a bigger role in developing more powerful successors, which suggests AI is accelerating its own development. METR's 11-week assessment, conducted between August and October, drew on confidential research, interviews and performance data from unreleased models. It found that Anthropic's benchmark capabilities had been improving 1.9 times faster since October 2025 than previously. The outside reviewer said the estimate carries high uncertainty.

The findings matter because they point toward recursive self-improvement, a scenario in which AI systems build more powerful versions of themselves without human intervention. METR estimated that AI accounted for perhaps 80% of the current acceleration, though it called that figure uncertain. The researchers said they found no convincing evidence of major bottlenecks that could slow progress over the next year. They also said the acceleration was not driven by faster growth in training compute. Even so, METR cautioned that AI could not yet make highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important stages of model training.

METR said that as of October 2026, Anthropic was likely improving its models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025. It said it would not be surprised if the true rate was closer to 1.5 or 2.5 times the historical rate. Anthropic researchers have reported sharp productivity gains from using AI to write code and run experiments, and informal employee polls suggested improvements of about 12 times, though METR said those figures were unreliable. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Its CEO had called for slowing advanced AI development in September.

The prospect of recursive self-improvement has prompted AI researchers in recent months to warn that such systems could become difficult to align with human goals, monitor and control, which could pose an existential threat to humanity. The shift could also affect an industry that has spent hundreds of billions of dollars on computing infrastructure for advanced models. The timing is notable because Anthropic is preparing to go public, potentially as soon as this month, in what could be one of the largest IPOs ever. The offering will also test investor appetite for AI companies spending heavily on the technology.

stories.Headline: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho revisits AI themes in latest thriller 'Paradise Lost'
stories.Summary:
South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho has built several of his films around artificial intelligence, and his latest, "Paradise Lost," returns to that theme in a psychological thriller. The story follows a mother, Ryu So-young, played by Kim Hyun-joo, who spends nine years relying on an AI recreation of her son after he was abducted on a school camping trip. She sees the boy, forever 10 years old, through augmented reality glasses until the real Sun-woo, played by Bae Hyeon-seong, returns as a grown stranger. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and opens in North American theaters on Friday. The film grew out of an unexpected source, a short story of about three pages written by Yeon's mother, a homemaker who once worked as a cleaner.

Yeon's earlier AI-themed works include the 2023 Netflix film "JUNG_E" and "Colony," a zombie thriller that premiered at the Cannes Film Festival this year. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said the central question of the film is what makes a relationship real. He argued that the AI character has filled a role of continuity for nine years but does not truly contemplate, and that AI mainly gives users the reactions they want. He said that if an AI system refuses a task by saying it does not want to do it, that would suggest it has begun to contemplate, and that he has not seen this happen. He also drew a link between the film's title, taken from John Milton's poem about humanity's expulsion from paradise, and the idea that a life without pain would soon lose its meaning.

Yeon also addressed the broader industry, noting that AI film festivals have appeared in South Korea and Japan and that Hollywood unions and filmmakers have been wary of the technology. He suggested that Asian filmmakers may be more receptive to AI because English-language films have long had larger markets and bigger budgets, pressures that smaller Asian markets did not face to the same degree. He said that as AI and other technologies develop, those pressures are weakening, and that Asian cinema can now take on more science fiction subjects. He added that he finds debates lumping every use of technology under the single label "AI" unproductive. Yeon said the film industry already uses a form of collective intelligence, since before release his team surveys 100 people at blind previews.

stories.Headline: Democratic victories cloud outlook for AI data center rollout
stories.Summary:
Strong wins for Democratic candidates in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, threaten the prospects for energy-hungry data centers in key states and could slow the AI rollout that has carried Wall Street forward over the past four years. Republicans lost strongholds such as Texas, where both the Senate and the governorship went to Democrats who back greater data center regulation. President Donald Trump, who has supported hands-off regulation for what he calls "super intelligence," suffered a stinging rebuke of his Republican party after a campaign marked by growing concerns about the environmental effects of data centers. The prospect of stricter regulation weighed on stocks in AI heavyweights such as Elon Musk's SpaceX ahead of the US markets open, after drops for key chipmakers in Asia including Samsung in South Korea.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, a lawyer who defeated outgoing governor Greg Abbott, called during the campaign for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the legislature can meet to put real protections in place. She has also urged an end to tax exemptions granted to the sector, as has fellow Democrat James Talarico, who was elected on Tuesday as a Texas senator. Abbott had wanted to make the state the "nerve center" of artificial intelligence and data center development, but he noticeably shifted his stance amid a public backlash over energy and water provision. Texas is expected to account for nearly 30 percent of national demand for electricity dedicated to AI operations by 2028, according to calculations by Bloom Energy. Alphabet, the parent of Google, has announced plans to build several data centers in Texas, and Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to the state.

Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the Republican camp, joked after the vote that "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," referring to his goal of a satellite computing network. Patrick Munnelly, market strategist at the brokerage Tickmill Group, said Democratic opposition to rapid data-center expansion could focus on power use, environmental constraints, local infrastructure strain, competition policy and the social consequences of AI deployment. He said none of this necessarily breaks the long-term AI theme, but it can raise the hurdle rate for investment. Veteran financial analyst Jim Bianco posted on X that given the size of the Democrats' victory, including the Texas governorship and a 29 to 1 lead to restrict data centers, politicians who want to remain employed are going to heed these messages.

The regulatory impact will be greatest at state level, highlighting the role of governors in responding to voter concerns. In Georgia, another state with a heavy slate of data center projects, the new Democratic governor Keisha Lance Bottoms has advocated a temporary statewide pause on new data centers, alongside requirements intended to ensure that large customers bear the costs of their infrastructure, according to Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management. Amy Acton, elected Democratic governor of Ohio, is also committing to a tougher regulatory framework on the data center buildout. stories.Headline: NPCI sets up wholly owned tech subsidiary NTSL and appoints Vishal Kanvaty as MD and CEO
stories.Summary:
The National Payments Corporation of India, known as NPCI, said on Wednesday that it had set up a wholly owned technology subsidiary called NPCI Tech Solutions Limited, or NTSL. The new unit is meant to serve as the group's technology and innovation arm. NPCI named its chief technology officer, Vishal Kanvaty, as managing director and CEO of the subsidiary. Kanvaty has been associated with NPCI for nearly a decade.

NTSL will concentrate on AI, blockchain, digital financial infrastructure and global capability centre services. It is also expected to build capabilities beyond NPCI's core payments mandate. In addition, the unit will provide technology services for eKYC Setu, the Unified Ticketing Platform and other digital public infrastructure programmes. NTSL becomes the fourth wholly owned subsidiary of the group, after NPCI International Payments, NPCI Bharat BillPay and NPCI BHIM Services.

NPCI CEO Dilip Asbe said advances in AI and other emerging technologies are opening up new possibilities across digital infrastructure and financial services. According to the report in Inc42, he added that the subsidiary was created to pursue those opportunities and strengthen the group's technology capabilities. NPCI also said Kanvaty has led the development and commercialisation of several platforms that now fall within NTSL's focus areas. NPCI did not disclose the subsidiary's investment outlay, revenue targets, customer pipeline or timelines for rolling out new services.

NPCI is the umbrella body that runs India's retail payments and settlement systems, including the Unified Payments Interface, or UPI. The move comes as India looks to advance AI research and development, especially in banking and financial services. At the Global Fintech Fest in September, NPCI launched AiNxt and AtOM, platforms meant to help enterprises build AI agents and automate workflows across the payments ecosystem. UPI handled a record 25.47 billion transactions in October, up 5.8% from the previous month, with transaction value rising 7.4% to ₹31.53 lakh crore. Separately, NPCI has deferred the planned introduction of merchant discount rate charges on select UPI payments, originally set for October 15, until after Diwali, and a new date has not been announced.

stories.Headline: iQIYI Revives 90-Year-Old Lost Film with NadouPro, Shortlisted for the AI Unit at the Golden Rooster Awards
stories.Summary:
Chinese streaming platform iQIYI has used its NadouPro AI platform to recreate "Visiting Shanghai after Sixty Years," a short film from 1938 that has been lost for nearly 90 years. Because no physical prints, reels or scripts survived, an eight-person team built the film from scratch in just two months at the iQIYI-XMU Joint Laboratory of Film Restoration. The team relied only on production still photos, posters and newspaper clippings as guides. The project has been shortlisted for the "2026 Future Images AI Unit" at the 39th Golden Rooster Awards, one of China's most prestigious film honors.

The film, one of China's earliest science-fiction works, used comedy to imagine life sixty years into the future. Recreating it required solving two difficult problems in generative video: keeping characters looking the same from shot to shot and controlling the camera precisely. NadouPro addressed the first by locking in permanent digital assets for each character's face, proportions and costumes before shooting. The team used the platform's 3D Director Studio to control positioning, composition and movement. The 1938 sequences follow the look of early black-and-white cinema, while the 1998 scenes use a documentary style with natural light and handheld camera work.

Enji YANG, the film's director, said NadouPro helped the team move from random image generation toward shots with clear directorial intent. He said the team still followed traditional methods, including script analysis, character design and storyboarding, before deciding how AI would realize the audiovisual design. Aigong ZHANG, the film's chief planner and director of the joint laboratory, said the project shows how AI can fit into a professional filmmaking workflow. Zidong JIANG, iQIYI's director of AI restoration technology, said the platform let the team move beyond the conventional restoration mindset and reconstruct the film creatively from historical materials.

The project builds on iQIYI's AI restoration work, which began in 2017 and includes its proprietary ZoomAI tools for scratch repair, super-resolution, noise reduction and frame interpolation. Through its joint lab with Xiamen University, the company has already returned several 4K classics to screens. The article presents the reconstruction as an extension of that work into recreating lost films rather than only repairing surviving ones. No further release dates or screening plans for the restored film are given in the article.

stories.Headline: 3 deliberate moves for businesses to maintain trust in AI decisions
stories.Summary:
Gartner's 2026 CEO and Senior Business Executive Survey found that 76% of leaders expect AI to be the technology most likely to disrupt their industry within three years. The same survey found that 59% of AI pilots never reach production, mostly because of problems inside organizations rather than the technology itself. Incorta, a company that provides a governed data and AI platform, has published guidance on how businesses can keep trust in their AI systems. Its advice centers on three deliberate steps that address why so many pilots stall and why AI outputs can be unreliable. The article appeared on November 6, 2026, and was produced by Incorta and distributed by Stacker.

Gartner notes that AI only pays off when the organization around it changes as well, which means redesigning processes, clarifying who makes which decisions, and aligning incentives. Without those changes, AI simply speeds up and amplifies whatever inputs already exist, whether they are good or bad. The article also says that AI can only give trusted answers when a business can say who has access to its data, how fresh that data is, where it came from, and what agents may do with it. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organizations will drop 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A separate IBM study from 2025 reportedly found that only 16% of AI programs have scaled across companies.

Incorta's first recommendation is to centralize AI models, tooling, and infrastructure so that spending is controlled and visible, letting a chief financial officer see the full cost in one place. Its second is to govern data so that teams can build what they need without creating security risks. The article cites IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, which found that one in five organizations had a breach tied to shadow AI, adding an average of $670,000 to breach costs. Of organizations that suffered an AI-related breach, 97% lacked AI access controls. Incorta's third recommendation is to build systems flexible enough to swap AI models, using adaptable interfaces and portable data so that businesses do not have to rebuild when better models arrive.

The article argues that once these foundations are in place, a business can rely on its AI responses and draw on a competitive edge that others cannot easily copy. Because competitors can access the same public models, the company's own governed data becomes the differentiator, including years of customer conversations, support tickets, contracts, and product and financial records. Incorta says that clear data governance, visible spending, and defined lines of ownership together let businesses trust the AI outcomes they generate. The piece is presented as sponsored content and was reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

stories.Headline: With an eye on America, China is beefing up its AI-controlled labs
stories.Summary:
China is expanding its AI-controlled laboratories in a bid to speed up scientific discovery and strengthen its industrial base, with the government playing a central role. In Shenzhen, a drug-discovery firm called XtalPi runs an autonomous facility where an AI model proposes hypotheses, directs robots to test them and records results to guide the next experiment, operating around the clock with few humans involved. China's prime minister, Li Qiang, praised such innovation during a visit early this year as the key to winning the future. The article frames this as part of a wider race with America to build and apply AI technologies in science.

China's new five-year plan, announced in March, called for faster exploration of AI-driven ways of doing science as part of a push to seize the commanding heights in the industrial application of AI. The state is building what it calls an AI-for-science stack that links specialised datasets, models and computing power needed to run these self-driving labs. In April the Chinese Academy of Sciences launched ScienceOne, also called Panshi or "Bedrock," a chatbot-like platform available to hundreds of Chinese universities and laboratories, with models trained on academic reports and non-text data. The article notes that China's scientific models still tend to lag behind America's, though a researcher at the University of Hong Kong praised the platform's bundle of datasets, agents and computing power. On the hardware side, XtalPi used its autonomous lab last year to help discover a molecule for treating a form of stomach cancer, generating millions of candidates and narrowing them to hundreds for robotic testing on lab-grown tissue.

The article attributes the stack-building partly to the government's leading role, noting that governments often hold the large datasets and can provide advanced computing power. Officials, according to the article, say these efforts will reduce dependence on Western technology and give China an edge in the AI race. Kyle Chan of the Brookings Institution, an American think-tank, said Chinese policymakers and American AI labs see eye to eye on this area. The article also contrasts the two countries: American automated-lab startups received about $1bn in venture capital last year and tend toward ambitious, speculative research, while Chinese firms are usually less ambitious and prefer work that can quickly generate profit. XtalPi, which serves 17 of the world's 20 largest pharmaceutical companies, is one example of this factory-like approach.

The article describes the context as a commercial and industrial one, noting that about half of all drugs licensed globally last year, by value, came from China, according to Goldman Sachs, up from 21% in 2024. In March Eli Lilly secured rights to develop and sell potential drugs from Insilico Medicine, a Hong Kong-listed firm using automated labs, in a deal worth up to $2.75bn. China also publishes four times as many materials-science papers as America, according to Nature, and in April researchers at City University of Hong Kong showed an automated lab could design and test molecules for solar cells. XtalPi and JinkoSolar say they are building a facility that will test 1,000 solar-cell prototypes a day, compared with one or two per researcher daily. Some Chinese AI leaders, including Zhou Bowen of Shanghai AI Lab, believe mastering science through such labs could help move toward artificial general intelligence, though the article presents this as a view held by some experts rather than settled fact.

stories.Headline: AI sharpens cat-and-mouse hacking battle as companies strengthen defences
stories.Summary:
Companies around the world are facing a wave of cyber threats that executives say artificial intelligence is accelerating and making more sophisticated, according to a Reuters report dated November 5, 2026. The incidents include hacked supermarket fridges, a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance in which hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of crypto, and an emergency over flaws in widely used web software. A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks, raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures and forced retailers to discard millions of dollars' worth of spoiled food. The surge is straining IT departments, whose staff are working overnight to patch vulnerabilities.

Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, roughly triple the figure from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list. Some firms are responding by turning to AI-powered security tools and increasing investment in them. German web hosting company Ionos said it changed its practices after a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring and AI-assisted patching around the clock. Ahold Delhaize, which operates Stop & Shop and Giant Food in the United States, was hit by two hacks in the past month, the first of which cost more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales and prompted a profit warning. McKinsey projects the global market for outside-vendor cybersecurity products and services will grow from $223 billion in 2025 to $346 billion by 2029.

Executives quoted by Reuters described the situation in stark terms. Booking.com's chief security officer, Marnie Wilking, said the contest resembles a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with hundreds of her company's engineers now building AI-powered defences. Ionos's chief technology officer, Markus Noga, said events of this magnitude now happen weekly or even every couple of days, and that a nine-to-five team is no longer enough. Ahold Delhaize's finance chief, Jolanda Poots-Bijl, said the company is adjusting to a new reality, noting that smaller firms are especially exposed while AI also helps firms detect and restore systems faster. Kraft Heinz's chief executive, Steve Cahillane, said the threat is real and growing.

The refrigerator attacks followed research published in August by cybersecurity firm Claroty, which outlined weaknesses in refrigeration controllers. After a first wave of attacks hit stores in France on October 11, Claroty researchers used widely available AI tools to reproduce the flaws and take control of a test device, which its field chief technology officer, Sean Tufts, said took them six dollars and 28 minutes. Separately, the October 21 disclosure of two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language prompted governments and companies from Tokyo to Helsinki to take websites offline as a precaution. Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit those PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours. Both sides are using AI, and the race is continuing, as Holcim's chief financial officer, Steffen Kindler, put it.

The partners describe these steps as a way to support Hong Kong's development as an international financial centre and AI innovation hub.

Nowa Zhu, Co-founder and CEO of Longbridge, said that agentic AI could change how people interact with financial information but that realising this requires trust, accountability and close collaboration across the financial ecosystem. Zhu added that Longbridge sees Hong Kong as an important market for shaping how AI is adopted responsibly.

Longbridge describes itself as a group that operates licensed financial businesses across several jurisdictions and holds 22 financial regulatory licences or qualifications, and it was founded in 2019. The announcement comes as AI systems move beyond providing insights toward supporting complex financial decisions, which raises questions about transparency and accountability, according to the release. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the Trump administration's push for AI infrastructure, has substantial personal investments in the AI industry, according to a November 2026 investigation by ProPublica that was republished by the North Dakota Monitor. The reporting found that Burgum's 2026 financial disclosure shows much of his wealth sits in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, and that between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those holdings are in AI companies, based on an analysis by the public lands group Save Our Parks. The articles say that in the year before he joined the administration, while he was North Dakota's governor, he realized between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, and in 2025 he sold AI stocks and equity that produced between $2.5 million and $15.1 million. Under his Senate confirmation ethics agreement, he resigned from positions at Arthur but kept his financial interests there.

The administration has also offered federally managed public lands for data centers, which the articles say could be built on as much as 91.3 million acres, an area comparable to Montana, according to a U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier in the year. Public opposition to data centers has grown, and the articles note that local and state processes have slowed projects in ways federal property may not allow. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects across six Western states, and the articles say the rent charged for data centers on public land, described by an Interior spokesperson as an annual fair-market-value rent, may be low enough that the public's economic benefit is unclear until projects are permitted. A federal land law from 1976 that predates data centers is being used to permit them, according to the reporting. The Boulder City, Nevada, project was paused by an Interior appeals board and sent back for further review after the BLM approved a change in plans in June without studying its environmental implications.

The Interior Department says Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations and that claims his decisions are driven by personal investments are false and unsupported. The department added that his work requires engaging industry leaders and international partners. Ethics experts quoted in the articles said his investments appear to be legal under a criminal statute with a high burden of proof, but Cynthia Brown of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington said non-criminal ethics rules bar officials from acting in ways that create the appearance of a conflict, and Richard Painter, a former Bush administration ethics lawyer, said Burgum should stay away from decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. Democratic senators wrote to Burgum in October demanding he stop efforts to use public lands for data centers and disclose his role. The articles also report that Steve Pearce, the BLM director, and Michael Boren, a Forest Service overseer, hold AI investments of their own, and that hundreds of Trump appointees have financial ties to major AI-linked companies, though the articles do not say what action, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: Yealink Brings Global Industry Leaders Together to Shape the Future of AI-Powered Workplaces
stories.Summary:
Yealink hosted its Workplace Forward Summit at BMW Welt in Munich, drawing 400 industry leaders, technology experts, enterprise customers and channel partners from the global collaboration ecosystem. Representatives from Microsoft and Qualcomm, industry group AVIXA, Frost & Sullivan analysts and leading system integrators took part in the event. Under the theme "Innovate for Trust," the company showcased its One-Stop Solution, which brings AI-powered tools for many workplace scenarios together with a unified experience for design, management and service. The summit was held in the company's 25th anniversary year, and the press release is dated November 5, 2026.

Yealink said it expects AI agents to transform the full room lifecycle, from design and deployment through daily use and ongoing maintenance. The company aims to use AI at each stage so that workplace environments are simpler to build, operate and maintain as spaces grow more complex. Speakers covered how workplace priorities are moving away from occupancy and toward effectiveness. Roopam Jain of Frost & Sullivan said room video devices were growing around 15% in the first half of the year. She named intelligent spaces, scalable simplicity and trust as three pillars shaping future workplaces.

Sessions addressed platforms, hardware and silicon, with Microsoft discussing its New System of Work and Qualcomm describing how on-device AI is changing cameras. Discussions on trust covered security, AI adoption and industry collaboration. Prof. Dr. Dennis-Kenji Kipker outlined four layers of enterprise AI security, while AVIXA stressed transparency, human control and measurable value. Yealink's One-Stop Solution is built on One Coverage, which spans workplace scenarios, and One Experience, which unifies design, management and service. Live demonstrations covered meeting rooms, Pro AV, SIP phones, headsets and public-area voice solutions.

Yealink describes itself as a global leader in video conferencing, voice and collaboration solutions, serving customers in more than 140 countries. The company reported a revenue compound annual growth rate of over 19% across the past five years, which it says is four times faster than the market average. The press release notes that Yealink ranks among the world's top three video conferencing providers and leads the global SIP phone market, citing Frost & Sullivan. The articles do not describe any further events following the summit.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq 100 eyes $1.8 trillion loss as Democratic win sparks AI delay fears
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, November 5, 2026, the Nasdaq 100 index was set to lose about $1.8 trillion in stock value as investors feared that the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections could slow the expansion of AI infrastructure. The drop followed a milder reaction the previous session, when the index, packed with major technology companies, had risen on hopes that an end to election uncertainty would lift overall sentiment. Semiconductor and neocloud shares, which had driven much of the recent gains, fell sharply for a second straight day on concern that data center projects worth billions of dollars could face delays. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index dropped 8.4%, its lowest level in more than six months, with heavyweights Nvidia and Broadcom leading the losses. The Nasdaq 100 was last down 4.5%, and the Nasdaq Composite was on track to confirm a correction, a 10% decline from its recent peak.

The selloff reflects a worry that political gridlock and tougher scrutiny of data center development could slow one of Wall Street's most important growth engines. UBS analysts estimated that around 30% of expected US data center capacity additions in 2028 could be at risk from potential construction pauses. CoreWeave, seen as a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending, slumped 12%, and five-year credit default spreads widened to a record high, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data. Nebius fell 15.2%, while data center operators Applied Digital, Cipher Digital and IREN each tumbled more than 14%. The weakness also reached utilities and equipment suppliers tied to the buildout, with GE Vernova down about 6% and Constellation Energy off 3%.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said Wall Street badly needs a positive AI story and predicted roughly two years of little progress amid divided government and angry politics. Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline Investment Management, said the market was moving from the promise of AI to the price of AI, while acknowledging the technology will be transformative over the long run. Microsoft fell 2% after Bloomberg News reported that it was tightening oversight of some data center projects from Nebius, IREN and Nscale. Separately, Qualcomm plunged 12% after quarterly smartphone-chip sales missed Wall Street estimates. Amazon.com fell 2.5% and Alphabet 1.4% as hyperscalers, which had held up the day before, also declined.

stories.Headline: Authorities tighten restrictions on data centres amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
Governments across several countries have tightened restrictions on data centres, citing concerns about electricity demand, water use and environmental harm tied to the AI boom, according to a Reuters report published on November 5, 2026. In the United States, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order that requires companies building AI data centres to meet environmental and transparency safeguards and to secure local community approval. The order also removes all data centres from the state's Fast Track permit program and bars state offices from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers. Texas Governor Greg Abbott paused approvals of new projects through the state's grid interconnection process, and developers must now disclose more about power demand, water use, tax incentives and ownership.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year construction moratorium on data centres using 50 megawatts or more of power, making New York the first U.S. state to enact a full moratorium. During that freeze, the state's Department of Environmental Conservation will not issue new discretionary permits while officials develop standards to assess environmental impact. In Maine, Governor Janet Mills vetoed bipartisan legislation that would have enacted an 18-month moratorium on new data centres using more than 20 megawatts. Mills said she supported a moratorium in principle but objected that the bill lacked an exception for a specific project in the Town of Jay. Residents of Monterey Park, California, voted in June 2026 to permanently ban data centres, the first U.S. city to do so at the ballot box.

Outside the United States, Amsterdam imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centre developments in 2019 and in April 2025 barred new facilities or expansions until at least 2030. Ireland's grid operator effectively blocked new connections around Dublin from 2021 until the freeze ended in December 2025, and new connections must now bring their own on-site power generation. Denmark adopted legislation, effective October 2026, that gives new data centres the lowest priority for grid connections, placing households, healthcare, industry, transport and renewable projects ahead of them. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government will create an "Office of AI" to set standards, including rules for large data centres on location, power and water use, with legislation due early next year. Portugal's Environment Minister Maria da Graca Carvalho said new rules are coming that would require data centres to run on renewable energy and use cooling systems that do not compete with household and business water supplies, even as the country promotes large projects such as the 1.2-gigawatt Start Campus in Sines.

stories.Headline: Kansas Board of Education set to vote on artificial intelligence policy, discuss elementary recess policies
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education is preparing to vote on a new policy covering artificial intelligence and student technology use, according to a report from KSNT. The board will meet Monday and Tuesday, November 9 and 10, 2026, in its November session. The vote concerns instructional technology policy for school districts and nonpublic accredited schools across the state. The board will also take up guidance on elementary recess during that same meeting.

The draft policy, which Kansas Education Commissioner Jake Steel will present, covers several areas of student technology use. Among the topics listed are the purpose and intended use of technology in elementary and secondary settings, student technology access, digital citizenship and student well-being, and artificial intelligence. It also addresses privacy and security, along with expectations for technology use and the consequences of violations. Board members will receive and discuss the recess guidance, but the recess policy itself is expected to come up for a vote at the December meeting.

The announcement came from the Kansas State Department of Education, which issued a press release about the meeting. Commissioner Steel is responsible for presenting the draft to the board. The report does not include any direct statements from the commissioner or board members about their positions on the proposals. It also notes that the board's decision on the technology policy will follow the discussion scheduled for the coming meeting.

The schedule suggests the state is moving on two fronts at once, with technology rules voted on in November and recess rules expected to follow in December. The articles do not say what the board will do if it fails to approve either measure at these sessions. They also do not indicate how the policies would take effect in local classrooms once adopted. Readers who want to follow the outcome can watch for the board's decisions after the November meeting and the December recess vote.
