The reporting centers on the firms themselves and on the analysts who cover them, with the article describing their outlook in general terms. It presents the banks' revised forecasts as a sign of caution rather than a verdict on any single company. The piece does not offer detailed quotations from company executives in the portion available here. Responsibility for the financial results rests with the individual firms, while the margin forecasts come from the investment banks that publish them.

The broader context is the effort to build a domestic alternative to Nvidia's chips under export restrictions imposed by the United States. The article does not give specific figures for the profits or the forecast cuts beyond the fact of the revisions. It also does not describe what the firms plan to do next to address memory costs or supply shortages. Whether the profitability trend continues will depend on how those supply pressures develop in the coming quarters.

Articles.Title: China’s AI chipmakers report first profits, but will the trend continue?

stories.Headline: Which movie most accurately depicts our AI-disrupted future? A new nationwide poll may surprise you
stories.Summary:
A Deseret News and University of Utah Hinckley Institute of Politics poll asked respondents which movie would most accurately depict life with AI, and "I, Robot" came out on top in both the Utah and national samples. "The Terminator" took second place in both, while the third-place film differed, with Utahns choosing "2001: A Space Odyssey" and the rest of the country choosing "War Games." The Utah survey was conducted Oct. 13-20 among 875 registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 3%, and the national survey was conducted Oct. 13-19 among 2,050 registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 2%. Morning Consult conducted the polling. A plurality of respondents, 24% of Utahns and 34% nationally, selected "none of the above."

The poll offered films such as "Big Hero 6," "Her," "Avengers: Age of Ultron," "M3GAN," and "Ex Machina" as alternatives. University of Utah film and media arts professor Kenneth Collins reviewed the results and said the choices reflect a broader pattern in popular culture, which has mostly imagined dystopian or apocalyptic outcomes from AI. He argued that the high share choosing "none of the above" suggests many people have not seen their future in these films and that stories offering a hopeful picture of AI remain largely untold. He pointed to the XPRIZE Foundation's Future Vision contest, which awarded $2.6 million to the winner for an optimistic, abundant future for humanity.

Separately, the article reports that ChatGPT, Grok and Claude each named "Her," the 2013 film about a lonely letter writer who falls in love with an AI operating system, as the most accurate depiction. The chatbots said the film better captures the everyday feel of living with AI than the catastrophic plots of the other options, though ChatGPT also noted that some films predict the technology well while others predict human behavior better. Claude said the film was accurate about the texture of daily life rather than its plot. The article does not describe any formal policy changes or regulatory actions tied to the poll.

Articles.Title: Which movie most accurately depicts our AI-disrupted future? A new nationwide poll may surprise you

stories.Headline: Genspark: How AI Agent Workspace Hit a US$2.6bn Valuation
stories.Summary:
Genspark, a Palo Alto start-up, reached a US$2.6bn valuation in June 2026, according to Reuters, after a further US$100m raise lifted its Series B to US$485m. The company began in 2023 as an AI search engine, but it pivoted in April 2025 to a Super Agent that plans and carries out tasks such as building slides, spreadsheets, documents and code. It announced a US$200m annual run-rate in March 2026, eleven months after relaunching as an agent company, when it had first reached US$10m. Its newest product, Genspark Claw, is an always-on AI agent with its own cloud computer for each user, reachable through WhatsApp, Slack or Teams.

The workspace draws on a mixture of agents built on more than 30 models, 150 tools and 20 premium datasets, and the company has added products including AI Slides, AI Sheets, AI Docs and AI Developer. Growth has been fast, with Genspark for Business passing 1,000 organisations by early 2026 and more than 6,000 within six months. The company became a launch partner for Microsoft Agent 365 in November 2025, bringing its agents into Teams and Microsoft 365, and added plugins for PowerPoint, Excel and Word in April 2026. Claw connects to about 20 apps, from Google Workspace to Salesforce, and was launched in March 2026.

The company is led by co-founder and CEO Eric Jing, a former Baidu executive, who founded Genspark with Kay Zhu in 2023. Eric Jing has said that Genspark has built an all-in-one AI Workspace where agents autonomously plan and execute to deliver finished outcomes. Co-founder and COO Wen Sang has said that the company sees a fundamental shift in how everyone will interact with work. Investors include Emergence Capital, which led a US$275m Series B at a US$1.25bn valuation in November 2025, along with LG Technology Ventures, SBI Investment, UpHonest Capital and Pavilion Capital. Genspark names OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft among its technology partners, and its models from those partners sit within its orchestration system.

Articles.Title: Genspark: How AI Agent Workspace Hit a US$2.6bn Valuation

stories.Headline: Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times reported on November 6, 2026, that Tesla plans to end production of its Cybertruck, as chief executive Elon Musk shifts the company's focus toward robotics and artificial intelligence. The report appeared under the headline "Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI." The article itself is largely a subscription page, and the body text visible in the extract does not give further details on timing, production volumes, or the reasoning behind the decision. Nothing in the material indicates how many vehicles have been built or sold, or what will happen to existing owners.

The available text does not specify any figures, dates, or formal requirements beyond the report's publication date. It also does not say whether the decision has been confirmed by Tesla through an official statement, whether it affects other models, or how it will affect the company's finances. The surrounding material is almost entirely promotional content about subscription plans, which means the reporting that would normally explain the decision is not visible in the extract. Readers would need the full article to learn more.

Because the extract contains so little reporting, the most accurate account of the story is limited to the headline claim and its publication details. The report links the planned end of the Cybertruck to a broader change in Musk's priorities, but the text does not explain that link in any detail. Any further context about the company's plans for robotics or AI, or about how those plans relate to the vehicle, is absent from the material provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI

stories.Headline: Immigration Seekers Face Risks Using AI for Legal Advice
stories.Summary:
Documented, a New York City immigration news outlet, published an article on November 6, 2026 warning that AI tools often give incomplete immigration legal advice. The piece draws on a report from the startup Vals AI, which tested the most popular AI models on immigration scenarios and checked their answers against rubrics written by immigration law experts. The article's author, Dara, is a journalist and senior fellow at the American Immigration Council who has covered immigration policy for years. The story points to the growing reach of AI in everyday searches, where a 2026 Pew Research study found that 42% of Americans use AI chatbots to look for information.

According to the Vals AI report, even the best-performing model, a costly version of Anthropic's Claude, gave incomplete answers in most situations, and other models did worse. The report concluded that AI tools should not be relied on to independently advise clients on their specific situation. The article gives two main reasons: AI models are limited by their training data, which may predate recent policy changes, and they cannot tell which details matter, so they may miss facts that change a case. When asked about 2025 and 2026 policy changes, even models that could search the web provided less than a third of the information experts sought. The weakest category was temporary or fragile status, including Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, which are the cases where people face the highest risk of losing status.

The article notes that the report's findings are the author's reading of the Vals AI study and of surveys, not the statements of a government agency or company spokesperson on the matter. A 2025 survey by Rev found that 43% of Americans were comfortable asking AI for help clarifying legal terms, but only 6% would rely on it for an immigration case. The author also cites a 2021 University of Denver study showing that few immigrants with immigration-related problems used the internet as a resource, and many of those who did went straight to agency websites. The article says that only a quarter of closed immigration court cases as of August 2026 had legal representation, which leaves many people with few options beyond online sources. The author's advice is to seek out real immigration lawyers when possible and to rely on trusted expert sources such as free legal clinics and reliable news outlets.

Articles.Title: Immigration Seekers Face Risks Using AI for Legal Advice

stories.Headline: Oman’s Phaze Ventures gathers $40m toward $75m AI fund platform
stories.Summary:
Oman's Phaze Ventures, a Muscat-based venture firm, has gathered $40 million toward a planned $75 million AI fund platform, according to a Private Equity International report published on November 6, 2026. The firm is in the market with its second fund, Fund II, and the article says it is backed by Oman's sovereign wealth fund. The report describes the raise as coming as Gulf venture capital matures. The article gives no further detail on the fund's structure or closing timeline. Phaze Ventures has already made 10 AI investments, according to the report, spanning the healthcare and finance sectors.

The $40 million figure represents capital gathered so far, against a $75 million target for the platform. The article does not say how the remaining $35 million is expected to be raised, nor over what period. It also does not name the investors beyond the sovereign wealth fund backing. The article is written by Luna Zhu and attributes the fundraising details to the firm's activity in the market rather than to a named executive. No direct statement from the firm's leadership is included in the text available.

The report does not offer comment on the firm's strategy beyond describing its investments and fundraising. Readers seeking the firm's own account of its plans would need to look to statements the firm itself has issued. The development sits within a broader picture of Gulf venture capital growing more established, a trend the article cites as the setting for the raise. The source does not describe any next steps beyond the continuing fundraising, and it does not indicate when a final close might be announced. Further reporting may clarify the fund's final size and investor base.

Articles.Title: Oman’s Phaze Ventures gathers $40m toward $75m AI fund platform

stories.Headline: Dartmouth’s president has evaded Trump so far. Will she outlast AI?
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth College president Sian Leah Beilock has become one of the most prominent academic voices in favor of artificial intelligence, even as other women newly appointed to Ivy League presidencies have left their posts under pressure from the Trump administration. The Boston Globe profile, published in November 2026, describes Beilock as the last woman standing among that group. Her public push includes an essay in The Atlantic in September titled "Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth" and a welcome message to incoming students. Beilock has used her position to advocate for AI on campus at a time when many colleges are debating whether to restrict it.

Under her direction, Dartmouth gave students access to the Claude chatbot through a partnership with Anthropic. In October the college held a three-day conference celebrating Dartmouth as the birthplace of AI, which it says it helped name in 1956. The event included a conversation with a former chief technology officer of OpenAI who is a Dartmouth alumnus. The article notes that the conference was held the day after provost Santiago Schnell resigned, and its theme asked what must remain human. Beilock has also said faculty and students must learn to think alongside AI and have hard conversations about learning in a world where it plays a major role.

The resignation of Schnell, her second-in-command, came after he used AI to write and publish articles, including an opinion piece in The Washington Post and a statement to the student newspaper. A faculty committee Beilock convened reviewed his work and chat logs and found he had violated several Dartmouth policies, especially on academic honesty. Beilock said in a letter that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment they expect from students. She has also said the episode prompted useful conversations about what creation means and how technology can help people think better rather than replace their thinking.

Beilock arrived at Dartmouth in 2023 with a five-point plan covering student mental health, civil discourse, career counseling, carbon neutrality, and innovation. Earlier, she kept her position and kept Dartmouth out of conflict with Trump by meeting quietly with his staff, adopting a policy of institutional neutrality, and declining to sign a protest letter over federal research cuts. Critics on campus argue the school's deal with Anthropic came after the company settled a copyright lawsuit over pirated books, and that open discussion arrived too late. Supporters, including engineering professor Eugene Santos, say universities should explore new technology, and the article does not report further decisions on the college's AI policy.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth’s president has evaded Trump so far. Will she outlast AI?

stories.Headline: Is Your AI Ready to Support a Critical CX Moment?
stories.Summary:
This is a sponsored feature from CX Today, not a news event, so the story is about guidance for customer service operations rather than something that happened on a particular date. Content Guru's Harris (the article's quoted expert, identified only by surname) argues that AI-supported customer service is most tested when outages, extreme weather, or public safety incidents cause demand to spike. The article describes these as the moments when automation faces its hardest test, because organizations must absorb sudden volume increases while making sure customers with urgent problems still reach the right help quickly. It also notes that a critical moment is not always about volume, since emergency services and utilities may receive contacts tied to safety risks or vulnerable customers at any time.

The article sets out what resilience requires. Harris says the service should stay consistent whether it handles one contact or 10,000, with extra compute and tokens added as demand rises but the customer experience unchanged. Organizations should automate high-volume, low-intensity enquiries and free human agents for urgent or emotional cases, and AI must be able to recognize urgency early and route the conversation. Harris says that where even a 0.1% chance of a wrong automated outcome is unacceptable, firms should use a deterministic pathway or capture basic information and pass it to a human. The piece also recommends proactive messaging, such as an SMS alert about an outage, to stop avoidable contacts, and it stresses that CRM and customer data systems must stay available and carry context across channels.

On testing, Harris says organizations should check AI at scale before rollout, generating thousands of use cases that range from satisfied customers to very negative experiences, combined with load tests and scenario simulations of infrastructure failures. Failing to handle urgent requests, giving unsafe guidance, or failing to transfer a customer should count as a failure of the implementation. Harris also advises avoiding vendor lock-in, so that a single model or vendor failure does not disable the service during an incident. Harris's closing point, quoted in the article, is that organizations must plan for the worst even though they hope it won't happen. The article does not describe any specific incident, regulatory change, or deadline.

Articles.Title: Is Your AI Ready to Support a Critical CX Moment?

stories.Headline: The MedTech AI revolution starts with getting the foundations right
stories.Summary:
The Veeva MedTech Summit in Amsterdam, where Oliver Johnson of Med-Tech Insights reported on the event, was the setting for discussions about artificial intelligence in the medical technology industry. The main point was that organisations need sound foundations before AI can deliver results. Speakers argued that reliable data, consistent processes, appropriate governance and capable people matter as much as the technology itself. The article is an opinion-style feature rather than a breaking news report, and it draws on several presentations and interviews given at the event.

Becki Brasher, Regulatory Affairs Director at Medtronic, described a four-year journey in which the company first harmonised processes, improved data consistency, consolidated systems and set up governance structures before adopting AI. She said the company had to earn the right to use AI rather than starting with the technology. The article notes that introducing AI into fragmented environments can produce outputs that are hard to trust, validate or scale. It also stresses that employees need knowledge and oversight to use new tools in their daily work.

The closing keynote, featuring Erik Orzechowski and Benjamin Rochette, focused on how companies can move quickly on AI without weakening quality, safety and regulatory standards. The speakers argued that governance should be built into technology development from the start, with closer collaboration between IT, Quality and Regulatory teams. They also said oversight should be proportionate, so that an AI tool handling low-risk administrative work needs less control than one affecting patient safety. Brasher, for her part, said human judgement should stay in place until trust in AI accuracy is established.

The article places these views in the context of a broader warning that a convincing AI answer is not necessarily a correct one. Speakers compared using AI without understanding the underlying subject to using a calculator without knowing the mathematics, and raised concern about future professionals losing the expertise needed to challenge AI outputs. Suggested next steps include starting with controlled pilot projects, measuring value through time savings, shorter cycle times, less rework, quality and adoption, and keeping governance adaptable as the technology and regulations change. The author says interviews from the summit will be published in the coming weeks.

Articles.Title: The MedTech AI revolution starts with getting the foundations right

stories.Headline: AI in homebuilding: Using AI and ERP systems to make better decisions faster
stories.Summary:
The article is a HousingWire interview, published November 6, 2026, in which Zebulon Lowe speaks with Bob Swainhart, Vice President of Enterprise Solutions at Constellation HomeBuilder Systems, about using AI and ERP systems to help builders make better decisions. The core premise is that homebuilders often already hold the operational data they need, and the difficulty lies in putting that data to use. Swainhart explains that reliable data helps leadership teams respond faster and more accurately to shifts in the market, with examples including tracking home closings and mortgage performance. The interview also looks ahead to what Swainhart describes as the next phase of AI in homebuilding, which centers on intelligent workflows. These workflows are meant to automate routine tasks, improve productivity in the field, and keep important business information connected across the systems that builders depend on.

The article frames these changes as a shift from collecting information to acting on it. The emphasis falls on turning operational records into business intelligence that management can use in real time, rather than on any specific product release or mandated requirement. The piece does not list figures, dollar amounts, percentages, or deadlines, so no such numbers are reported here. It also does not describe any regulatory or contractual obligation tied to these systems. What the article does provide is a picture of where Swainhart sees the industry heading, with automation and connected data as the practical goals.

Responsibility for the views expressed rests with Swainhart, who speaks as an executive of Constellation HomeBuilder Systems, the company whose work he discusses. The article presents his comments as his own perspective in an interview format and does not attribute any independent verification of his claims. Readers should therefore treat the statements about the benefits of AI and ERP systems as the position of the interviewee and his employer. The article itself is a feature piece in HousingWire's business technology coverage, and it sits alongside other recent items on mortgage technology and automation. The article does not describe any next steps, follow-up events, or future publications beyond the continued expansion of these tools that Swainhart outlines.

Articles.Title: AI in homebuilding: Using AI and ERP systems to make better decisions faster

stories.Headline: AI spending is on the rise, but are companies measuring the right returns?
stories.Summary:
Business leaders are expected to invest an average of $173 million in AI over the next 12 months, according to KPMG's latest US AI Quarterly Pulse Survey, and that rising spending is raising questions about how companies measure what they get back. KPMG argues that productivity gains, the easiest AI benefit to quantify, have dominated the conversation, and that relying on them alone risks missing value in customer relationships, innovation speed, decision-making quality, and new revenue sources. Stanford University's 2026 AI Index reports that 88% of surveyed organizations used AI in at least one business function in 2025. Some of AI's most significant effects may be less immediate or harder to pin down, so they may not appear in short-term financial results.

KPMG suggests treating AI investments as a portfolio rather than a single category, separating use cases that aim for near-term operational returns from those that aim to unlock growth or reshape operating models. The firm offers five questions to test AI value: what business problem the investment is meant to change, what performance looked like beforehand, whether success is about cost, revenue, quality, speed, or customer experience, when a meaningful return should be expected, and whether the project is creating enough value to scale, change, or stop. Matching the metric to the use case means a customer-facing system might be judged on retention or sales, an internal tool on time saved, and a product-development system on speed to market. The article presents this as a way to see more accurately whether each investment is achieving its intended outcome.

The article also points to the people using the technology as a major factor in results. A joint study by KPMG and The University of Texas at Austin analyzed more than 1.4 million workplace AI interactions from 2,597 employees over eight months, finding that the strongest users framed problems carefully, challenged outputs, refined responses, and applied their own judgment. KPMG's Q3 2026 AI Pulse Survey found that 65% of leaders expect AI agents to drive the integration of AI collaboration skills into workflows, and that the share developing role-specific guidelines for working with AI agents rose from 21% to 55% year over year. Shears, who leads KPMG's aIQ program, says it combines AI tools with training and governance, including an aIQ Academy. The article is sponsored branded content, and KPMG's Rahsaan Shears is the source for the company's views throughout.

Articles.Title: AI spending is on the rise, but are companies measuring the right returns?

stories.Headline: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
stories.Summary:
Arjun Panickssery, writing a LessWrong shortform post on December 30, 2023 (the page is dated November 6, 2026), said he struggles to believe that autonomous AI research and development is as ingenious as it is often described. He reported monitoring several side projects in which an AI model, which he called Astra, was used on tasks such as building a new Scrabble engine, a bot for Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, and formalizing proofs for an AI philosophy contest. In each case, he said, the model's judgment was poor in basic ways, and he gave examples of the model missing the most important papers in a literature review, running experiments with too little training data to be informative, and pursuing trivial directions in a long research wiki. He also judged an Apart hackathon, where eight submitted papers were often similar to each other and methodologically incomplete in a way that overlooked the most straightforward analysis. He described one exception, hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops, where he improved a Scrabble benchmark roughly tenfold, but only after supplying key ideas himself.

The post's comment thread adds a related picture, and it leans on named evaluations to support it. One commenter, Julian Bradshaw, argued that AI systems perform well when a human points them in the right direction, and that this need for human guidance is still necessary. He cited P-Zero's TasteVal, which reported a breakpoint around December 2025 after which Opus 5.5 reached about 2.30 times human expert compute efficiency, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.15 to 4.37, though only 1.14 times on normalized task score. By contrast, Epoch AI's InnovationEval found that Fable 5 could not reach 5 percent of human real-world innovation gains on an AI R&D task, despite claiming more than 40 percent performance. A third Epoch study, "Can AI automate Epoch?", found that Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra reached only about 65 percent of human Epoch employee performance.

Bradshaw suggested the gap partly reflects task design, since TasteVal specified research problems tractable to known methods while the Epoch tasks required novel ideas or were open-ended. The commenters also disagreed about model quality and about the wider context. Anthony DiGiovanni said that Opus 5.5 was significantly better at clear writing than Astra 6, while Roman Kornev argued that the real change is the amount of steering applied to tasks relevant to AI safety, and pointed to OpenAI and Anthropic research on covert underperformance and persona vectors. The articles do not say how the comment thread concluded, and they do not indicate any further steps or planned follow-up by the author.

Articles.Title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious

stories.Headline: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process
stories.Summary:
Cedar Rapids lawyer Tim Semelroth has been warning colleagues and the public that artificial intelligence is creating real problems in the legal system, and he has been doing so through more than 30 presentations around the country since he first wrote about lawyers' practical uses of AI three years ago. He describes AI as "Average Intelligence" because of widely reported "hallucinations," fabricated material that has appeared in legal briefs and other papers. Some 2,000 such filings have been reported, and judges have sanctioned lawyers who submitted them. Because AI draws on internet material that includes misinformation and poor legal opinions, it cannot reliably tell that content apart from legitimate cases.

The costs fall on the courts and on the people who must respond. Lawyers must review AI-generated filings, judges must rule on them, and both spend time and money doing so. Semelroth warns that if judges face very long, AI-written briefs, the system could slow badly. He says lawyers have an ethical duty to understand the technology and check its output, since clients, witnesses and staff are already using it, sometimes to prepare for legal matters.

He advises that nothing AI produces should leave an office without a human reviewing it, and he distinguishes free AI tools from the subscription versions lawyers use, which carry safety protocols that are still not fail-safe. For the public, he says AI is a poor source of legal advice because chats carry no privacy guarantee, citing a New York case in which a judge allowed prosecutors to see a defendant's chat history. The Iowa Supreme Court has also acted. Its first AI-related ruling upheld the 2023 conviction of Max Amyda, 37, of Woodbury County, for third-degree sexual abuse, after he argued that video evidence was a "deepfake."

The court found his claim rested on conjecture and that the video's distinctive characteristics, including the victim's identification of her body, items in her room and Amyda's hand, supported its admission. In July, Chief Justice Susan Christensen signed an order adopting a new chapter of the Iowa Court Rules on judicial use of AI tools. Those rules take effect Jan. 1 and create a Judicial Branch Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Governance Committee, on which Semelroth served as part of the earlier working group and University of Iowa professor Megan Graham now sits, to approve tools and set their permitted uses. Semelroth also says AI can be a useful thinking partner when used with proper human oversight.

Articles.Title: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process - The Gazette

stories.Headline: Potential Sciences, an AI startup building large-scale chemical data sets, secured backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, as part of an eight-figure raise (Joel Khalili/Wired)
stories.Summary:
Potential Sciences, a British startup that uses artificial intelligence to speed up drug design, launched on November 5, 2026, and announced seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars. The company is backed by SovAI, the UK government's AI venture capital fund, and by Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or the company's valuation. The startup plans to build large chemical datasets by simulating interactions between atoms, small molecules, amino acids and proteins using basic physics.

The company's aim is to train AI models that can predict how drug candidates will behave in the human body, so that unpromising molecules can be ruled out before reaching the lab. Its founder and CEO, Hatem Helal, argues that this approach would lower the cost of experimentation and could make it economical to develop treatments for rare diseases. He describes the goal as more bespoke medicines tailored to individual biology. The article notes that a large share of AI drug discovery work relies on a single public database, the Protein Data Bank, which Helal says is too small to train sufficiently advanced models. Potential Sciences is therefore relying on synthetic data generated through simulation.

Helal said the company wants molecules that will not work in the clinic to fail quickly, and he described the broader aim as improving predictions of how molecules interact with human biology. Academic experts quoted in the article were cautiously positive. Peter Wolynes of Rice University said the approach would likely be an improvement but described current protein engineering as far behind where it needs to be. Alan Fersht of the University of Cambridge said he was optimistic that accurate interaction calculations would eventually revolutionize drug development. Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, joined the startup's board and said its physics-based approach and access to computing resources set it apart.

The article places the company within a crowded field that includes Basecamp Research, Isomorphic Labs and CuspAI, and it says SovAI was established earlier this year with roughly $800 million and access to the UK's national AI supercomputer. Wolynes also cautioned that designing a drug is far less of a bottleneck than the testing needed to establish safety and effectiveness, so treatments will still take a long time to reach patients. The article also raises the risk that the same tools could be used to design dangerous chemicals, and Helal acknowledged that concern. The company has not yet decided how it will earn revenue or whether it will make its models freely available.

Articles.Title: Potential Sciences, an AI startup building large-scale chemical data sets, secured backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, as part of an eight-figure raise (Joel Khalili/Wired)

stories.Headline: Equinix opens SG6, its sixth Singapore data center, with liquid cooling for AI workloads
stories.Summary:
Equinix, the digital infrastructure company based in Redwood City, California, announced on November 6, 2026 that it has opened SG6, its sixth data center in Singapore. The facility is designed for artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and other data-intensive workloads, and it adds to Equinix's global network of more than 280 data centers. The company says the site gives customers the infrastructure they need to connect, innovate and scale as AI-driven demand grows. SG6 is located in a市场 the company describes as one of the most strategically connected in Asia-Pacific.

The facility is among the first built under Singapore's Data Centre Call for Application framework. It uses advanced cooling, including proprietary systems and liquid cooling, to support power-hungry GPU equipment. Equinix says SG6 is designed to reach a Power Usage Effectiveness of 1.20 and is targeting Green Mark Platinum certification. The building also includes rooftop and facade solar panels, rainwater harvesting and lower-carbon construction materials. The company links the project to its sustainability goals of net zero emissions by 2040 and 100 percent renewable energy coverage globally by 2030.

Adaire Fox-Martin, Equinix's chief executive and president, said the company has invested in Singapore for nearly 25 years and called the city one of its most important markets worldwide. Cyrus Adaggra, the company's president for Asia-Pacific, said the region is at the forefront of digital transformation and that SG6 will help customers expand across the area. Equinix has said its Singapore data centers have had 100 percent renewable energy coverage since 2020. The company also described the initial investment of about $290 million, which provides 8 megawatts of capacity and roughly 1,550 cabinets in the first phase.

Equinix entered Singapore in 2002 and has grown from one facility to six, and it says its Singapore sites connect to more than 17 subsea cable systems. The company also plans to open a Co-Innovation Facility at SG6 in 2027, in partnership with the National University of Singapore, to research cooling, energy storage and related technologies. Upon full build-out, the SG6 site is expected to offer up to 20 megawatts of IT capacity. The articles do not say more about the timing of that build-out.

Articles.Title: Equinix Opens SG6 in Singapore, Expanding AI-Ready Capacity in One of Asia-Pacific's Most Connected Markets

stories.Headline: Kos Biotechnology Partners Announces Investment in Fathom Therapeutics to Advance Novel, AI-Driven Drug Discovery Platform
stories.Summary:
Kos Biotechnology Partners, a global life sciences investment firm based in New York and Athens, Greece, announced on November 6, 2026 that it has invested in Fathom Therapeutics. The investment was made through Kos BioVentures, the firm's first life sciences fund, as part of Fathom's Series A financing. Sutter Hill Ventures led the oversubscribed $55 million round, which also drew other leading investors. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire.

Fathom Therapeutics is a drug design company that applies quantum chemistry, physics-based molecular simulation, and artificial intelligence to find new small molecule medicines. Its proprietary Microcosmos platform combines these methods to predict how proteins move and how they interact with drug molecules at atomic resolution. The company says this approach could help reach biological targets that have been considered difficult or impossible to drug. The financing is intended to help Fathom scale the platform, advance its internal pipeline, and expand its partnerships.

Fathom's chief executive is Dr. Huafeng Xu, a pioneer in computational drug design, and the company was co-founded by Yujie Wu, its chief technology officer, and Jesús Izaguirre, its chief computational scientist. Dr. Simos Simeonidis and Alex Tzoukas, the co-founders and managing partners of Kos, praised the company's expertise in quantum chemistry and AI and said the firm believes the technology could change how medicines are discovered. Xu welcomed the Kos team to the investor group and said the company looks forward to working with them. The release says the team includes scientists behind the Anton supercomputer and widely used computational methods for predicting protein-drug interactions.

The release places the investment within Kos's broader strategy of backing therapeutic technologies, differentiated drug discovery platforms, and globally competitive biopharmaceutical companies. Kos says it manages $125 million in assets and invests across all stages of development in therapeutic breakthroughs, biodefense, and tech-enabled pharma services. The announcement does not disclose the size of Kos's own stake or the valuation of Fathom. It also does not describe specific clinical milestones or timelines for the company's drug candidates.

Articles.Title: Kos Biotechnology Partners Announces Investment in Fathom Therapeutics to Advance Novel, AI-Driven Drug Discovery Platform

stories.Headline: Educators face pushback over classroom AI use as grades drop
stories.Summary:
Educators in Central Florida are facing growing pushback over the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms as grades drop. The pushback comes as tech companies adjust their tools for educational settings. Google is allowing schools to disable its AI features while keeping standard search working. The option was introduced amid concerns about how artificial intelligence affects student performance. A study by researchers at the University of California, Irvine, found that students who used AI for writing and research scored 20% lower in science than students who did not.

School districts across the region are setting different rules for AI in instruction. Orange County Public Schools requires students to get a teacher's approval before using AI on any assignment. Seminole County has taken the opposite approach by authorizing specific AI platforms for student use. Its approved tools include Google's Gemini and Microsoft Copilot Chat. The varying rules show how local districts are still working out where AI fits in the classroom.

The article does not say whether either district plans to change its policy. The article is based on reporting by James Tutten of WFTV.com, published November 6, 2026. It does not identify a single official or company that is directly responsible for the classroom changes, and it does not give direct statements from district leaders about their reasons. The story describes the policy choices but leaves open how schools will weigh the test results against the tools' benefits. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Educators face pushback over classroom AI use as grades drop - WFTV

stories.Headline: Producing Viral Video Assets Using Rap Duo AI On Tight Deadlines
stories.Summary:
Rap Duo AI is a tool that turns two separate portrait photos into a synchronized rap performance, a product promotion rather than a news event. The article is a sponsored-style feature published on MyNewsGh.com on 5 November 2026, and it does not describe any incident, announcement, or policy change with a named actor. It presents the service as a way for creators to avoid the cost and scheduling problems of shooting two-person videos. Because the piece carries no breaking news, the required summary of an event cannot be fully drawn from it.

The article argues that short-form video platforms reward collaborative formats such as duets, comedic roasts and rhythmic music challenges. It says that arranging physical two-person shoots is costly and slow, especially when collaborators live in different time zones, and that separately recorded audio often sounds mismatched. The service, described as accepting two front-facing selfies, is presented as a way to generate 12-second vertical clips in minutes. The article gives pricing examples of twenty-nine dollars for five songs and ninety-nine dollars for thirty-five songs, along with a claim of roughly one dollar per track on monthly tiers. It also states that failed renders are not charged and that exported video carries no watermark.

The article does not name a journalist or any official, and no one is quoted. Its content reads as a product pitch, so the claims about performance, lip-sync accuracy and pricing come from the publication's own description rather than independent verification. The article notes real limits, saying that stylized lighting, extreme profile angles or covered faces degrade lip-sync accuracy and that long-form content still requires a separate editor. It does not report any further developments or next steps beyond the service's own offerings.

stories.Headline: Asian shares sink out of fear of a sudden slowdown in investment in artificial intelligence - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday, led by South Korea, Taiwan and Japan, after technology shares slumped on Wall Street and investors grew uneasy about future spending on artificial intelligence. The Seoul Kospi index dropped 8.52% in the first moments of trading, its lowest level since February, which triggered a 20-minute trading suspension under South Korea's automatic halt mechanism. Taiwan's Taiex fell 8.85% at the opening, and Japan's Nikkei 225 lost more than 6% and briefly fell below 60,000 points. The selloff followed a 5.52% drop in the Nasdaq on Thursday, its worst session since April 2025.

Investors reacted to the possibility that Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections could bring tighter limits on building data centers and expanding the infrastructure needed for AI. Semiconductor makers were hit hardest, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix falling more than 10% and 13% respectively before recovering part of their losses. South Korea's finance minister, Lee Hyoung-il, called an emergency meeting of top economic officials, and the authorities agreed to temporarily loosen rules on leveraged investing by small investors to contain forced sales. In Wall Street, the Nasdaq closed at 24,315 points, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,353.73 points, and the Dow Jones dropped 3.44%. Nvidia slid 9.3% and AMD plunged 17.3%.

Taiwanese companies central to the AI supply chain, including TSMC, Foxconn, MediaTek and Delta Electronics, were among the most affected, given the island's role in advanced chip manufacturing and data center equipment. In Japan, chip equipment makers, data center-linked firms and SoftBank, a major international AI investor, led the losses. Indian markets bucked the trend, with the Nifty 50 and Sensex rising during the session, which Reuters links to foreign capital inflows, a recent fall in oil prices and limited exposure to AI-related investment. Analysts consulted by Reuters warned that the Asian reaction may overstate the consequences, since slower projects do not necessarily mean canceled data center investment or disappearing demand for AI components.

Articles.Title: Asian shares sink out of fear of a sudden slowdown in investment in artificial intelligence - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Chemours Launches New Cooling Fluids to Tackle AI Data Center Heat Surge
stories.Summary:
Chemours, the chemical company, has launched a new line of two-phase liquid cooling fluids called Faizeon for data centers running artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. The announcement was made in early November 2026, with ChemAnalyst reporting on November 5 and CSRwire on November 3. The portfolio targets the rising heat generated by more powerful processors and denser server racks, which the articles say conventional cooling systems struggle to handle. The fluids are dielectric, meaning they do not conduct electricity, and they work through phase change, absorbing heat as they turn from liquid into vapor.

The line includes five products. Faizeon 100 and 110 are low-pressure fluids for direct-to-chip cooling, with 110 having an intermediate boiling point and zero ozone depletion potential. Faizeon 200 is aimed at medium-pressure systems and high-density AI and computing processors, while Faizeon 220 is the company's highest-performance direct-to-chip fluid for demanding GPU environments. Faizeon 500, formerly marketed as Opteon 2P50, is designed for full-server immersion cooling and may support waste heat recovery. According to the company, the fluids can lower cooling-related energy use and nearly eliminate cooling-related water use, depending on system design, and they are engineered for recovery, reprocessing and reuse.

Chemours cited independent third-party testing showing that a two-phase direct-to-chip system using Faizeon 200 kept a graphics processing unit up to 19 degrees Celsius cooler than a single-phase, water-based system while using a lower coolant flow rate. Denise Dignam, the company's president and chief executive, said that AI growth is putting pressure on data center infrastructure and that cooling has become a critical constraint. She said the company is drawing on more than 90 years of thermal management expertise to help operators handle higher heat loads. Chemours also said it is working with several partners, including the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory, NTT DATA, 2CRSi, DataVolt, Munters, Accelsius and ZutaCore, to advance adoption.

ChemAnalyst notes that the launch strengthens Chemours' position in specialty cooling fluids and could support demand for fluorinated heat-transfer fluids and related intermediates. The outlet adds that large-scale demand will depend on data center deployment, system compatibility, regulatory acceptance and lifecycle economics. It also says no immediate broad price increase for affected commodities is expected, since the launch alone does not create significant new feedstock consumption or supply constraints. The articles do not describe specific commercial orders or timelines for wider rollout beyond these partnerships and the stated market opportunity.

Articles.Title: Chemours Launches New Cooling Fluids to Tackle AI Data Center Heat Surge - ChemAnalyst

stories.Headline: CRR Hires 2 Inspectors for Cyber, CER and AI Rules [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
The Commission for Railway Regulation (CRR) is hiring one senior inspector (Grade I) and one inspector (Grade II) for a new cyber security, critical infrastructure and artificial intelligence (CCIAI) division, according to a notice TechCentral.ie published on 5 November 2026. Both posts are permanent, full-time and based in Blackrock, County Dublin. The senior role covers the rail and cableway sectors within the CRR's statutory remit and carries a stated salary of €87,510 to €101,776 a year. The notice names the NIS2 Directive, the Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Regulations and the Artificial Intelligence Act as the frameworks the division will work under. The notice does not name a candidate, a manager or a spokesperson, and it contains no on-record quotation.

The pairing of a railway regulator with AI and cyber remits reflects how EU law assigns enforcement to national bodies that already know the industry. NIS2 and the CER rules both cover transport, and a rail or cableway operator may face cyber, resilience and AI obligations at once. The notice does not explain the design choice, so the view that a combined division avoids three separate inspection regimes is our analysis. Inspectors in this field must also weigh security against safety, since older operational technology often cannot be patched on demand. The CER rules add a resilience question about whether essential services keep running whatever the cause, including dependencies on a single provider.

The AI Act's safety-component rules may reach predictive maintenance and automated monitoring tools already used in transport. Two points deserve plain disclosure. The TechCentral.ie page carrying the notice is labelled as sponsored content, so readers should treat it as an advertisement for the roles. The dates also conflict: the senior listing's application deadline is given as 12 noon, Irish time, on Friday 17 July 2026, which predates the publication date, and the advert we read shows a later closing date and a higher top-of-scale salary. The material we verified does not show whether the competition was reopened, the terms updated or an older listing republished.

Applicants should check the CRR's own application page for the current closing date and pay scale. Two posts will not move the wider labour market, but they show Irish regulators competing for scarce people who combine technical depth with legal literacy against private employers in Dublin. Greater inspection capacity is likely to raise compliance spending for operators and create work for assurance and advisory firms, though we have no data on the number of applications received. The CRR's next steps beyond the posted vacancies are not stated in the notice.

Articles.Title: CRR Hires 2 Inspectors for Cyber, CER and AI Rules [2026] - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: Who pays when AI takes from creators? Europe rethinks copyright rules
stories.Summary:
Europe is reconsidering whether its two-decade-old rules on enforcing intellectual property can cope with artificial intelligence, as disputes over creative work multiply. The European Parliament's Legal Affairs Committee has continued discussing changes to the Intellectual Property Rights Enforcement Directive, which was adopted in 2004 and sets common procedures for enforcing copyright, patents and trademarks. A European Commission study found that enforcement varies unevenly across EU countries, including in how courts assess injunctions and in the costs faced by smaller rights holders. The debate has been driven by examples such as a book used as AI training material, a song feeding a music generator, and a news article turned into a chatbot answer.

MEP Axel Voss, who reported back from a September meeting of the EU Intellectual Property Office Observatory, said generative AI, copyright licensing and fair compensation are growing concerns. He told the committee that a balance is needed between protecting creativity and cultural values and allowing technological innovation, and he pointed to the need for transparency and proper licensing. Another MEP, René Repasi, presented arguments attributed to Leire Pajín, saying that public interest should be weighed, including effects on public health, critical infrastructure and emergency response, and he favoured case-by-case assessment. The Commission's representative, Denis Dambois, said the problems may stem more from differences in national enforcement than from the directive itself. He argued that these differences call for closer dialogue with member states, judicial cooperation and sharing of best practice rather than rapid legislation, and he warned against separate criteria for different intellectual property rights.

Courts are also weighing in on AI and copyright. A day before the committee meeting, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar at the EU Court of Justice advised that AI chatbots retrieving and reusing news articles to generate answers could, under certain conditions, infringe publishers' rights, in a case brought by Hungarian publisher Like Company against Google over its Gemini tool. In France, the Paris Court of Appeal rejected Meta's challenges and required it to negotiate in good faith with French media organisations over payment for their content. Culture Action Europe has warned that the EU's voluntary AI Code of Practice does not by itself guarantee compliance with copyright law, which could leave artists reliant on costly litigation. In Germany, a case brought by the collecting society GEMA found that the AI music generator Suno had infringed six protected compositions.

The Commission is considering broader changes to digital copyright policy, and a consultation that closed on 3 November sought evidence on AI training, online piracy of live events, performers' remuneration and copyright in scientific research. A June 2026 EUIPO study estimated that monitored websites offering infringing content, goods or services generated €382 million in advertising revenue worldwide in 2025, including €28.5 million within 18 monitored EU countries. The EU already has relevant instruments, including the 2019 Copyright Directive, which sets rights for publishers and rules for certain content-sharing platforms, the Digital Services Act, which requires intermediaries to offer reporting mechanisms for illegal content, and the AI Act, which imposes copyright-compliance and transparency duties on providers of general-purpose AI models. The article does not say what specific legislative changes will follow from the consultation or the committee's discussions.

Articles.Title: Who pays when AI takes from creators? Europe rethinks copyright rules - EU Perspectives

stories.Headline: Ahrefs adds prompt theme analysis to Brand Radar, comparing your own and competitors' visibility in AI search
stories.Summary:
Ahrefs Pte. Ltd. announced on November 6, 2026, that it has added a prompt category analysis feature to Brand Radar, its tool for tracking how brands are mentioned and cited in AI search. The feature sorts the questions users put to AI tools such as ChatGPT and Google's AI Overviews into topic categories. The company says the change lets users compare their own brand's visibility with that of competitors in each subject area, rather than only looking at overall mentions.

Each prompt can carry up to three topic categories, and the first one is treated as the main category. The categorization uses the same taxonomy as Ahrefs' Keyword Explorer, so users can start theme-level analysis without classifying prompts by hand. In the "By category" view of the Prompts report, users can see the share of prompts falling into each category next to brand mention rates, expand categories into subcategories, and search by category name. By default, counts use only the main category, but turning off the "Main category only" setting includes all assigned categories.

The release describes the feature as a way for marketers to see where their brand is strong and where competitors lead, and to decide which content or information areas to prioritize. The category column and filters are also available in the Topics, Cited pages, and Cited domains reports, which show which pages and domains AI tools cite for a given theme. Ahrefs describes itself as an all-in-one marketing toolkit built on its own large-scale web crawler, and says it serves users in more than 180 countries. The release does not say whether the feature is available to all plans or give any pricing or rollout timeline, so the details of next steps remain unclear.

Articles.Title: Ahrefs adds prompt theme analysis to Brand Radar, comparing your own and competitors' visibility in AI search

stories.Headline: Employees at Microsoft, long known for its stability, are grappling with its decision to offer buyouts to 60,000 people as its spending priorities shift to AI (Emmy Martin/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its work force, in the largest such offer in the company's history. The announcement came last week, and employees rushed to an internal site within an hour to see whether they had been included, so many that colleagues joked the site had buckled under the traffic. It was the company's second buyout this year. The offer landed on a staff already on edge about artificial intelligence.

The buyouts follow a clear shift in where the company is putting its money. Two days after the announcement, Microsoft reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year. Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, yet it is plainly directing its resources toward AI.

Employees describe a workplace that has changed sharply. For years, Microsoft was known for strong benefits and stability, even though its pay often trailed rivals such as Google and Meta. As recently as September, Forbes ranked it the world's best employer for the third straight year. Six Microsoft employees who spoke anonymously said the buyout offer hit workers already strained by pressure to use AI, stagnant pay, and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure.

Some workers have started to organize in response. Before the buyout offer, current and former employees circulated an open letter accusing the company of pursuing AI with a speed-at-all-costs approach. The letter asked Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how AI is built and used, and to stop tying AI use to rewards or reprimands. The article does not say how the company has responded to the letter, and it leaves open what the coming months will bring for those who remain.

Articles.Title: Employees at Microsoft, long known for its stability, are grappling with its decision to offer buyouts to 60,000 people as its spending priorities shift to AI (Emmy Martin/New York Times)

stories.Headline: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions?
stories.Summary:
Voters in the United States delivered large gains to the Democrats in this week's midterm elections, and a rising backlash against data centres played an unexpectedly important role. Candidates campaigning for local limits on data centres won across ten states, and according to exit polls, about 56% of voters said AI data centres were a crucial or major factor in their vote. The result reflects a growing tension between America's push to lead in artificial intelligence and the reluctance of local communities to host the infrastructure that supports it. The Trump administration has made data centre expansion a core pillar of its technology and economic strategy, and in July 2025 the president signed an executive order to speed their development. In June alone, US$4.4 billion was spent on building data centres, a fivefold increase from November 2022, when ChatGPT was first released.

About 75% of data centres under construction sit in Republican-led states, yet opposition grew there as well. Pew Research found American sentiment hardening against data centres between January and August this year, with most Americans believing they do more harm than good. Residents cited energy costs, environmental pressures and noise, and in areas near US data centres, wholesale electricity prices rose by as much as 267% over the past five years. Many people also questioned what they would gain from AI if they were being asked to cover those costs. Candidates from both parties shifted toward stronger regulation as the opposition spread, though Democrats moved faster to campaign for tighter oversight.

Democrat-led states including New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon have introduced local bans or are debating statewide ones. Gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, all major growth areas for data centres, were won by candidates calling for pauses on new projects. The article notes that data centre stocks in the US fell as the Democratic sweep became apparent, and that Democrat-led states account for around 45% of planned US capacity. Tighter rules could bring project delays and higher costs, and investment might move to jurisdictions with more accommodating regulation.

With the 2028 presidential election approaching, the authors expect data centres and AI to become key political battlegrounds. In Australia, the market is much smaller than in the US but growing quickly, and local opposition is rising as well. A A$1.2 billion data centre project on Sydney's north shore was scrapped in September after strong community objections, and residents in West Footscray in Melbourne used bins and cars to block power line construction for a data centre. The Australian government is developing mandatory national standards for large data centres covering energy and water use, siting and community engagement, though how strict they will be and how they will fit with state and territory rules remains unclear.

Articles.Title: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions? - The Conversation

stories.Headline: NIST Tests AI Tool to Map Building Interiors for First Responders
stories.Summary:
NIST's Communications Technology Laboratory, through its PSCR Innovation Lab, is testing an automated tool called INSIGHT that turns building scans into structured data to help first responders plan for indoor emergencies. The article, published November 6, 2026 by HPCwire, explains that outdoor disasters give responders satellite imagery, GIS, GPS, and drone data, but indoor incidents do not offer those tools. Existing building records are usually flat two-dimensional blueprints that may be outdated and often leave out standpipes, shutoffs, alarm panels, and AEDs. The pipeline is designed to produce that missing information more quickly and at lower cost than manual documentation. The article says the stakes are high because responders currently must make risky decisions with incomplete information.

NFPA 1660 and NFPA 950, safety standards published by the National Fire Protection Association, call for detailed, interoperable pre-incident data, but departments have no practical way to produce it at scale. INSIGHT addresses this by generating scene graphs from scans, with a human reviewer correcting the automated output rather than labeling everything from scratch. The article states that the results can be delivered to responders within seconds over existing broadband infrastructure. It also describes a query-time role filter that lets dispatch, incident command, and discipline-specific teams each see the view most relevant to them.

PSCR describes the tool as following the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which calls for explainable and accountable automation in high-risk settings. Independent detection paths within the pipeline check one another, and any disagreement between them is flagged for a person to review. Building codes are used to identify implausible results. The article attributes a key finding to a 2025 cross-dataset analysis that used PSCR-funded Point Cloud City data, which showed that existing 3D methods performed at near zero on small safety fixtures such as exit signs, AEDs, and alarm panels.

INSIGHT is built to address that measured gap. The article says the current work covers only the pre-incident planning phase, and PSCR plans later phases that add live tracking and command applications. The pipeline is built on a public dataset and open-source tools, and its outputs follow ISO 19164, IndoorGML, and IFC naming conventions, with source code and dataset documentation to be published. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NIST Tests AI Tool to Map Building Interiors for First Responders

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines, a small AI startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released a new model called Inkling 2 Small. According to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, the model is set to challenge Chinese models, which have led the open-weight field for several years. The company said it will make the model's weights available next week, after the model was initially offered as proprietary. The model has 594 billion parameters, accepts image inputs and produces only text. Thinking Machines said it is stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops.

Artificial Analysis gave it a score of 31 on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Gemini 3.8 Flash, while Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 score 60 and 59. Reviewers said it improved 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding over its predecessor. Artificial Analysis said the model's planned weight release would make it the highest-scoring open-weight model developed outside China based on current rankings. The firm also described Inkling 2 Small as notably slow per task and very verbose, and called its pricing somewhat expensive at $0.30 per million input tokens against a class median of $0.24.

It also reported that the hallucination rate on its AA-Omniscience test fell from 61% to 27%. The staggered release follows a pattern in which AI companies test models with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers for a few weeks before publishing weights, given heightened security concerns. French lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model the same way, and it matches OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra in coding, which is rare for Western open models. The article notes that Chinese models from DeepSeek and Moonshot have rivaled far more expensive closed models since DeepSeek's R1 appeared in January 2025.

Articles.Title: Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

stories.Headline: AI Tutors in Corporate Training: Design Determines Results
stories.Summary:
Randomized trials published in 2026 suggest that AI tutors help corporate and technical training only when they are built to teach rather than to finish tasks for the learner. A study in Nature Human Behaviour, published on October 26, 2026, found that management consultants at Boston Consulting Group who had access to ChatGPT, along with training on its use, scored 18 to 49 percentage points higher than untreated peers on data science tasks outside their skill sets. That advantage disappeared once the tool was removed, and the study's authors wrote that demonstrated technical capability did not show that knowledge had been acquired. Researchers at Boston University describe such general-purpose assistants as exoskeletons that extend what a worker can do without teaching the worker to do it.

The findings point to a different standard for learning tools. Evaluations should measure unassisted skill retention rather than course completion or task output, and designers should require attempts before explanations. In a preregistered Boston University field experiment with 86 Online MBA students, a structured tutor grounded in course materials produced 6.6 more points out of 55 than ability-matched peers and 2.6 more points on the instructor's final exam out of 100. Voice and text delivery produced the same learning, although voice cost 2.8 times as much to deliver. A Chinese cluster-randomized trial of 2,574 power utility employees found that an adaptive platform produced small knowledge gains that held at a follow-up about six weeks later, though the authors noted that the delivery medium and instructor contact changed too, so adaptivity alone cannot be credited.

The reports tie these lessons to Mexico, where surveyed firm adoption of AI rose from 24.3% in September 2025 to 48.5% in June 2026, reaching 69.9% among firms with more than 1,000 workers, according to MBN. The same report cites Mexico's National Human Resources Survey 2026, which found that 82% of employees have received no training in general-purpose AI tools. The MBN reporting also says that 65% of Mexican workers report difficulty obtaining certifications, against 48% globally, and that lack of time is the main barrier to skill development. Training providers such as UVM for Business, part of Laureate Mexico, have responded with short-format platforms like Menthera that aim to tie training to business outcomes rather than hours logged.

The articles also warn that adding a tutor does not guarantee gains. An October 2026 randomized trial of 2,379 undergraduates at a large US public university found that access to a course-integrated AI tutor lowered final grades by 0.37 standard deviations and reduced learning management system participation by 0.90 standard deviations, with greater losses among first-generation students. The authors suggested the tutor displaced existing engagement without improving performance. The articles frame this as a warning for companies that add tutors to existing programs without redesigning how employees learn.

Articles.Title: AI Tutors in Corporate Training: Design Determines Results

stories.Headline: CoreWeave vs. Nebius: Which Is the Better AI Neocloud Stock to Own for the Next 3 Years?
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, a Motley Fool analysis by Marc Guberti argued that Nebius is the better pick than CoreWeave for investors with a three-year horizon. Both companies, which rent out AI computing capacity as so-called neoclouds, fell sharply that day, with Nebius down about 15% to $120.37 and CoreWeave down about 10% to $43.66 at the close. A separate Yahoo Finance report by David Moadel said AI data center stocks were hit by a wider selloff after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterms. The same report tied pressure on IREN, another neocloud, to word that Microsoft spent less on capital projects than planned.

The Motley Fool piece rests on balance sheet strength and pricing. CoreWeave has a current ratio of 0.46, meaning it has fewer current assets than current liabilities, so it will need to raise money or refinance debt soon. Its bonds briefly traded at a 15% yield in secondary markets, which would raise its costs if it had to refinance at that rate. Nebius has a current ratio of 4.03, and it covers 50% to 60% of its capital spending with customer prepayments. Nebius also said it moved from about $12 million per megawatt to deals above $20 million, and short-term deals at $40 million to $50 million per megawatt.

On growth, CoreWeave still leads in size, with $2.6 billion in second-quarter revenue against $582.3 million for Nebius. CoreWeave ended that quarter with a $104.2 billion backlog and added $25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter. Its sales rose 112% from a year earlier, while Nebius grew 454%. For year-end annual recurring revenue, CoreWeave projects $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, while Nebius had pointed to up to $9 billion before its contracts improved, which shrinks CoreWeave's revenue lead from nearly five times to about two times. The article notes Nebius already has a higher market cap than CoreWeave, at $38.47 billion versus $26.71 billion.

Guberti, the Fool author, argues that CoreWeave has tied up most of its capacity in long-term contracts and so cannot easily benefit from rising prices, while Nebius has open capacity and short-term deals it can reprice within months. The Yahoo report said The Information found Microsoft spent $5 billion less than planned on capital projects, though it is unclear how much came from delays at IREN's Childress campus in Texas. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said last week that capital spending was $45.2 billion because some third-party capacity expected in the first quarter was delayed. Yahoo also said Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Greg Abbott, wants an immediate moratorium on data centers in Texas.

IREN's stock traded near $19.70, down 9%, while Nebius was around $125.88, down 11%, and CoreWeave near $44.89, down 7%, in intraday trading. IREN delivered the first of four 50-megawatt deployments for Microsoft in August and aims to have $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue running by December 31. Its multiyear Microsoft contract calls for $9.7 billion in GPU server leasing at Childress. IREN is due to report first-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the market close on November 5, with analysts expecting sales to fall 9% to $221.7 million and an adjusted loss of $0.67 per share.

Articles.Title: AI Cloud Crash Puts CoreWeave and Nebius on Sale. Their Next Reports Decide What Happens Next

stories.Headline: Chip Stocks Cheaper Than S&P 500 as AI Premium Vanishes - Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXQ)
stories.Summary:
Chip stocks have fallen to a valuation below the broader market, a shift that analysts say marks the end of the premium investors paid for artificial intelligence exposure during the recent boom. According to a note shared on Friday by Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, the PHLX Semiconductor Index, tracked by the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (SOXQ), trades at 13.7 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, while the S&P 500 trades at 17.7 times. That leaves chipmakers at a 22% discount to the market, compared with a 15% premium during the AI cycle. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

The index peaked at 14,634.72 on June 22 and closed Thursday at 9,011.14, a decline of 38% over 136 days, while the S&P 500 lost 2% over the same period. Bank of America tracked four earlier semiconductor downturns, in 2011, 2015 to 2016, 2018 and 2022, in which chip stocks fell between 23% and 46% and the S&P 500 fell between 12% and 25%, so the current gap is unusual. Chips rebounded on Friday, with the index rising 4.9% and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) gaining 4.3%, but the index remained 35% below its peak. The article also reports that 28 of the 30 stocks in the iShares Semiconductor ETF now trade at least 20% below record highs.

The analysis ties the selloff to spending by cloud providers, which Bank of America says run about $300 billion a quarter, or $1.2 trillion annualized. Consensus expects $1.55 trillion in 2027, but if spending holds at the current pace, 2027 would come in about $355 billion, or 23%, below expectations. Arya said a 20% cut in 2027 capital spending would reduce sales for AI chipmakers by more than 20% and earnings by 35% to 40% or more. He added that today's discount already reflects considerable skepticism about the cycle. The article notes that in past cycles the index bottomed near 12 times forward earnings, which would imply at most another 12% of downside, but Arya expects earnings cuts to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and says investors will likely need to see them before confidence returns.

Arya's note is the source of the valuation and spending figures, and the article does not name anyone else responsible for the sector's decline. In his baseline case, with a bottom in the first quarter of 2027, he favors Lam Research, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and Texas Instruments. If the downturn extends into mid-2027, he expects Cadence Design Systems and Synopsys to hold up better, while in a sharp recovery high-beta names such as Micron and Advanced Micro Devices would lead. Over the past month Lam Research and Micron each fell more than 30%, while Texas Instruments slipped less than 5%. The article concludes that whether the market has fallen far enough depends on how much hyperscalers actually spend in 2027.

Articles.Title: Chip Stocks Cheaper Than S&P 500 as AI Premium Vanishes - Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXQ)

stories.Headline: Semiconductor Costs, AI Governance Reshape Tech Investment
stories.Summary:
Intel's shares fell more than 20 percent after its third-quarter 2026 earnings showed projected cash burn and weaker forward guidance, which it linked to cyclical softness in the PC market and heavy foundry spending. The sell-off signals liquidity and capital spending strain across the chip supply chain. The articles say this affects corporate IT planning, data center investment and hardware purchasing in Mexico. Some of the coverage points to the Guadalajara Design Center, which focuses on cost-effective enterprise AI architectures and hardware validation, as a sign of closer North American integration.

Marvell Technology has agreed to acquire optical components maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at US$115 billion. The combination would join semiconductor, networking and photonics capabilities as demand for high-speed connectivity reshapes AI data center infrastructure. The articles say the deal would let Marvell compete more directly with Broadcom while widening its technologies for linking increasingly complex AI systems. Separately, Anthropic reported US$17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue as it prepares for a potential initial public offering. Its amended registration statement also disclosed US$895.4 billion in future purchase commitments and lease agreements.

Mexico's road modernization faces the challenge of keeping existing bridges and highways safe and operating, not only building new ones. Growing freight traffic, aging assets and greater exposure to climate events have led some managers to consider digital twins, which monitor critical bridges, flag anomalies and anticipate maintenance. The article raises the open question of how managers can confirm these systems catch real problems without producing false alarms or delays that compromise safety. Mexico's AI investment, meanwhile, is reaching a stage where adoption costs cannot be separated from governance costs. Companies are expanding AI into customer service, financial decisions, recruitment, software development and operations, yet many still lack structures to determine who is accountable when these systems fail.

Articles.Title: Semiconductor Costs, AI Governance Reshape Tech Investment

stories.Headline: Fleetworthy launches RADAR, new AI fleet management technology
stories.Summary:
Fleetworthy has launched RADAR, a new AI-powered feature built into its fleet management platform, announced at its roadshow in Nashville, Tennessee, on Nov. 4, 2026. The technology is embedded directly in the company's existing software rather than sold as a separate chatbot or analytics product. It initially launches within the Toll Management product, where it helps customers monitor toll activity, spot spending trends and receive recommendations without manually reviewing reports. Customers can ask questions such as why a particular charge appeared or how a transponder is performing.
