The framework is designed to refine candidates toward target relative density, directional Young's moduli, and thermal conductivities using a surrogate model. Its geometry generators render smooth mesh representations that can be exported directly for additive manufacturing, avoiding an extra voxel-to-mesh step. The article says the generated designs closely matched the requested properties in both in-distribution and controlled out-of-distribution tests. The trained models are also integrated into an agentic interface that supports iterative language-based design and three-dimensional visualization.

The eight classes span four procedural generators: ordered and disordered truss and plate lattices, ordered bicontinuous and shell triply periodic minimal-surface structures, and disordered bicontinuous and shell spinodoid structures. The authors describe the work as addressing gaps in unifying these classes under one conditional design framework and in translating natural-language requests into structured conditions. They say the framework builds on earlier work such as Txt2Microstruct-Net and TrussGPT, which handled voxel-based and truss-only language-guided design. The article reports fabricated examples with a length of 40 millimeters, and it says the authors plan to continue developing the framework, though specific next steps are not detailed in the excerpt available.

Articles.Title: Language-guided inverse design of multiclass metamaterials using generative artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Systematic Review Analyzes Artificial Intelligence for Water Quality Monitoring
stories.Summary:
A systematic literature review of artificial intelligence in water quality monitoring has synthesized findings from 91 primary research studies published between 2020 and 2026. The review, which applied the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses framework, examined how machine learning models detect contamination events, model complex nonlinear environmental relationships, and support predictive decisions across aquatic environments. The authors searched five academic databases, namely IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. Review and survey articles were excluded so that secondary literature was not pooled with primary work, leaving 91 studies that met predefined criteria. The article was published on November 6, 2026, in Artificial Intelligence Review.

The authors built a structured taxonomy describing the strengths, limitations, interpretability, and reported applicability of different AI model families. They did not report a pooled performance comparison or run a meta-analysis, because the studies differed widely in target variables, datasets, preprocessing, and validation protocols. The review identified several obstacles to current use, including heterogeneous and inconsistent data, overfitting, computational complexity, sensor calibration problems, limited generalization, and the lack of standardized benchmark datasets. The authors note that conventional assessment, based on manual sampling and laboratory analysis, is labour-intensive, costly, and slow, and is unsuited to continuous real-time monitoring of large water bodies. The review also points to emerging directions such as Explainable AI, Federated Learning, Edge AI, Graph Neural Networks, Digital Twins, Foundation Models, and multimodal environmental intelligence.

The paper is authored by N. Rani, P. Mittal, A. K. Panigrahy, A. S. Rao, and Y. K. Sharma. The authors frame their work as a reference for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, and they state that they place their findings within the methodological limits of existing studies. They present the taxonomy as a guide for building future monitoring systems that support sustainable management of freshwater resources under pressures from urbanization, industrialization, climate change, and other human activity. The articles do not describe any regulatory requirement or policy change arising from the review. They also do not report any follow-up studies or next steps beyond the research directions the authors outline.

Articles.Title: Systematic Review Analyzes Artificial Intelligence for Water Quality Monitoring

stories.Headline: CPI | Japan Steps Up Pressure on US Tech Giants Over Security and AI
stories.Summary:
Japan is seeking earlier access to information about software security vulnerabilities from major US technology and artificial intelligence companies, as its government responds to a rise in cyberattacks. The initiative, reported by MLex, is aimed at strengthening cybersecurity cooperation with foreign technology providers whose products are widely used across Japan's economy. Officials are reportedly preparing an emergency cybersecurity package that could be discussed at a ministerial meeting as soon as Friday, November 6, according to Reuters citing Nikkei. The proposed measures would focus on receiving advance notice of significant software weaknesses, giving public agencies and operators of essential services more time to protect their systems before technical details become public.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi directed officials in late October to develop stronger cybersecurity protections after attacks increased, according to Nikkei as reported by MLex. The urgency follows a series of October disruptions involving government and corporate websites across several countries. Reuters reported that the disclosure of serious security flaws affecting the PHP programming language led to millions of attempted intrusions, and some website administrators restricted access or took systems offline temporarily. Japan has also announced plans to set up a team that will use artificial intelligence to simulate cyberattacks and find weaknesses in computer systems, Reuters reported. The effort would add automated testing to the country's work on identifying security threats.

The government has also approached major US AI developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, about obtaining broader access to their advanced AI models, according to Nikkei as cited by Reuters. Those talks followed cyberattacks suspected of involving AI-assisted techniques. Early disclosure of vulnerabilities would let Japanese authorities coordinate protections before attackers exploit newly found flaws, though the articles note this raises questions about how companies handle sensitive security information and decide which governments or organizations get access before public release. The cybersecurity push comes as Japan also examines the influence of major technology companies over digital markets, including their business practices and their use of data in artificial intelligence, according to MLex's separate reporting on that scrutiny.

Articles.Title: CPI | Japan Steps Up Pressure on US Tech Giants Over Security and AI

stories.Headline: From Ticketing To Vocals, The ‘Mind-Blowing’ Ways Concerts Are Using AI
stories.Summary:
Billboard reported on November 5, 2026 that artificial intelligence is being used across the live concert business, from ticket sales to sound mixing. The article, written by Ariel King, centers on Nine Inch Nails, whose front of house engineer, Jamie Pollock, used L-Acoustics' Source Intelligence on the band's Peel It Back Tour for the first time this year. That technology applies nongenerative machine learning to pick out an artist's voice in real time and send it to the crowd without the background noise a microphone might pick up onstage. Pollock kept the experiment quiet during the whole run, yet fans noticed the clearer vocals. The article also notes that the technology has since been used by Bruno Mars, Rüfüs Du Sol and Harry Styles on the road.

The article says the tools cover several areas of the industry. In marketing, companies such as Laylo and HIVE send text and email campaigns for artists and venues, and Laylo's user-generated-content agent finds fan videos and asks fans for permission to use them in ads. Ticketmaster has added AI chatbots, including ChatGPT and Claude, so fans can ask about tour plans and view seats before buying through its own site. SeatGeek launched a product in October called TourIQ, which uses data the company already collects to recommend a price for every seat in a venue. At the Hollywood Bowl, the team installed 26 L-Acoustics speakers, and the Los Angeles Philharmonic used the new system for the first time on June 20.

Several executives describe these tools in their own words. Saumil Mehta, global president of Ticketmaster, says the company applies AI and machine learning at every layer of its ticketing platform to identify bots and help fans get tickets. Patrick Hannigan, HIVE's co-founder and chief technology officer, says some of the company's clients now have AI draft all of their emails, text messages and Meta ad campaigns. L-Acoustics CEO Laurent Vaissié says the company's technology helps engineers get a cleaner signal from noisy stages and calls the results "pretty mind-blowing." Fred Vogler, the Hollywood Bowl's principal sound designer, says the new system gives audiences clarity and low distortion that they had not heard outdoors before.

The article also points to a downside. Scalpers are using more bots than ever, and singer RAYE wrote on Instagram in October that her London Royal Albert Hall show had received 1.8 million presale sign-ups, including "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations." The article notes that ticketing platforms expect situations like this to become more common and are preparing for them. Suno, an AI company, hired former Ticketmaster executive Michael Chua in October to lead its new Suno Live Experiences division. The article does not say what further changes are planned beyond these tools.

Articles.Title: From Ticketing To Vocals, The ‘Mind-Blowing’ Ways Concerts Are Using AI

stories.Headline: New AI tool speeds up food science research and development
stories.Summary:
A food scientist at Penn State University has been using artificial intelligence to make food engineering research easier to access and apply, according to a Brownfield Ag News report published November 5, 2026. The report, written by Nicole Heslip, centers on a tool called AgentXtract, which mines scientific research data. Xu Zhou, who works in the Department of Food Science, is the researcher behind the work. The tool is described as an AI system that can answer questions in plain language, so users do not need to read large numbers of papers or work through complex equations.

Zhou told Brownfield that people can simply ask questions in natural language and receive explanations grounded in scientific research. The system is compared to Penn State Extension's Tilva app, which gives science-based answers to agricultural questions. Zhou also said the tool can help keep institutional knowledge from being lost when experienced workers retire. He noted that much hands-on expertise sits with human experts, and that losing them would mean losing that expertise. The article does not describe any specific rules, mandates or funding requirements tied to the tool.

Zhou is the person quoted as responsible for the project, and he said the work could speed up early-stage research and development in the food industry. He added that it could also support gains in food safety, quality and waste reduction. The report does not say whether AgentXtract is commercially available, how widely it is in use, or what its accuracy has been tested against. It also does not describe any next steps or timeline for the research. The coverage is a short feature rather than a breaking news story.

Articles.Title: New AI tool speeds up food science research and development

stories.Headline: BMO Turns to Agentic AI to Resolve Card Issues
stories.Summary:
BMO, the Toronto-based bank, has begun using an artificial intelligence agent called AI Agent Assist to help its staff resolve credit card transaction issues for clients. The tool was announced on Friday, November 6, 2026, and it is built for internal use by employees at BMO's Virtual Connect contact centre. It uses agentic AI to reduce the time workers spend moving between systems while they handle client calls about their credit card transactions. The bank described the launch as a way to speed up service for a large volume of such calls.

The bank said its Virtual Connect centre receives more than 500,000 calls each year from Canadian clients about credit card transactions, and each call currently takes an average of 12 to 14 minutes to resolve. With AI Agent Assist, BMO hopes to cut the time spent on client inquiries by 20% to 30% and to process about 40% of eligible credit refund requests automatically. For qualifying inquiries, clients could receive their credit as soon as the same day. The tool delivers AI-enabled transaction matching, policy retrieval and case preparation directly to employees for review, which the bank said should reduce the need to place customers on hold.

Holly Jackson, who leads Virtual Connect, said clients calling about a credit card transaction want clarity and a quick resolution. She said the tool gives employees the information and guidance they need so they can spend more time helping the client and less time switching between systems. BMO also said the tool was designed around a human-in-the-loop principle, meaning people remain central to key decisions. The bank's own description frames the system as support for its workers rather than a replacement for them.

The launch comes as PYMNTS Intelligence research shows finance departments adopting generative AI quickly while remaining cautious about letting AI act on its own. Generative AI use for cash flow management rose from 16% in 2025 to 80% in 2026, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence and JPMorgan collaboration, while agentic AI use dipped slightly from 6% to 5%. PYMNTS wrote last month that AI is becoming common in systems that analyze cash and recommend actions, while autonomous execution remains rare. The articles do not say how the tool will perform once it is fully in use.

Articles.Title: BMO Turns to Agentic AI to Resolve Card Issues

stories.Headline: Visa Finds AI Models Fail 43% of Shopping Test Runs
stories.Summary:
Visa reported on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that 22 artificial intelligence models from 12 labs failed a large share of realistic shopping tests. Across the test runs, 57.2% passed and 42.8% failed, according to a press release from the company. The results came from Visa's new industry benchmark for AI shopping, called the Visa Agentic Commerce Benchmark. The article describes the findings as the first round of testing.

The benchmark checks whether an AI model can identify a consumer's needs from a conversation, gather enough information to justify a purchase, and decline to buy when nothing meets the customer's requirements. For the first round, Visa had the models attempt challenges that included buying a television, a laptop or a personal care appliance. Among the best-performing models, 82.2% of runs passed, while among the worst-performing models, 28.9% passed. The five models with the highest average cost per run passed 67.1% of runs, compared with 50.2% for the five least expensive models.

Visa stated that 54% of the failed runs still ended with the AI making a purchase. In those cases, the purchase either did not meet the customer's stated requirements or the AI had not uncovered all of those requirements. Rubail Birwadker, global head of growth at Visa, said in the release that AI agents could power the next era of commerce but that trust is key to making it work. He described the benchmark as another way Visa is working to raise standards across the industry.

The release also said the test can be used by consumers. The article places the findings alongside a PYMNTS Intelligence report that found nearly 132 million U.S. adults have bought a product with AI's help. That report indicates AI has gained a role in product discovery, while consumers still control the purchase decision. The article does not say what further rounds of testing or changes to the benchmark are planned.

Articles.Title: Visa Finds AI Models Fail 43% of Shopping Test Runs

stories.Headline: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey has filed a consumer protection lawsuit against Snap, the maker of Snapchat, according to a November 6, 2026 report from MLex. The suit alleges that Snap deceived West Virginia parents and children about how safe its platform was, even though the company knew it exposed young users to sexual exploitation, harmful content and compulsive-use design. It also claims Snap rushed the launch of its "My AI" chatbot to children without adequate safety testing. The complaint further says the company misled families about what the chatbot does with private conversations and location data.

The articles provided do not describe specific penalties, damages sought, or a court schedule, so those details are not available from this material. The reporting indicates the case rests on claims that Snap made misleading statements to families about its safety practices and its chatbot. A complaint document is referenced in the report, but its contents beyond the summary are not reproduced in the text provided. Snap's response to the allegations is not included in the articles.

The lawsuit is brought by the state attorney general, who is the official named as the party pursuing the claims against the company. The report frames the action as a consumer protection case centered on children's safety and the handling of their data. Beyond the filing itself, the articles do not say what further steps are planned or when any ruling might come. More to follow.

Articles.Title: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot

stories.Headline: Review Separates Artificial Intelligence From Robotic Execution In Total Knee Arthroplasty
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a narrative review and evidence map in the journal Arthroplasty, concluding that direct clinical evidence showing artificial intelligence gives patients benefit beyond conventional robotic assistance in total knee replacement remains limited. The team searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, along with citation searches, for peer-reviewed English-language studies published between January 2015 and January 2025, with the final search run on April 15, 2026. The authors note that robotic systems and artificial intelligence are often lumped together under the label AI-assisted robotic surgery, even though they serve different roles. A single reviewer handled screening, a limitation the authors say was partly offset by review and approval from all co-authors. They deliberately avoided pooling results across studies because the interventions were too varied.

The review separates physical surgical execution from algorithmic prediction, tracing the development of platforms such as Mako, ROSA, CORI, and NAVIO alongside optical navigation systems. These tools were introduced to improve the accuracy of bone cuts, component placement, and limb alignment, and the evidence for that technical precision is considered mature. Artificial intelligence, by contrast, operates mainly in adjacent tasks such as radiographic interpretation, implant sizing, patient selection, dissatisfaction forecasting, risk stratification, and postoperative monitoring. In studies predicting postoperative patient dissatisfaction, models reached moderate accuracy, with area-under-the-curve values between 0.70 and 0.82. Those studies were mostly retrospective and single-institution, with sample sizes from several hundred to a few thousand patients, and only a minority included external validation.

Intraoperative artificial intelligence was described as earlier in its development, with direct knee-specific comparative studies scarce. The authors say the central problem is what they call the alignment-to-function gap, meaning that accurate implant alignment does not automatically produce better pain relief, function, or implant survival. Patient dissatisfaction can stem from soft-tissue imbalance, pain sensitization, unrealistic expectations, psychological factors, comorbidities, or rehabilitation difficulties, which robotic cutting tools cannot address. The review also finds that evidence for postoperative artificial intelligence monitoring is largely indirect or drawn from small pilot studies, and that economic data specific to knee replacement are scarce, with only one study providing direct knee-specific cost and length-of-stay figures.

The authors raise concern that expensive robotic platforms tend to concentrate in well-funded academic centers, which bears on equity of access. The article does not say what regulatory or clinical changes, if any, will follow from the review. To address these gaps, the authors recommend that future studies drop the umbrella term AI-assisted robotic surgery and specify when computational components operate, how much autonomy the surgeon retains, and which comparators are used. They call for multicenter trials that test robotic precision against conventional surgery, test artificial intelligence decision tools against non-AI robotic platforms or standard templating, and validate across diverse patient groups.

Articles.Title: Review Separates Artificial Intelligence From Robotic Execution In Total Knee Arthroplasty

stories.Headline: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Depression Detection Performance Drops In Large Studies
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence models built to detect depression perform far worse in large populations than in small benchmark tests, according to a narrative review published in Discover Mental Health. Small case-control studies with 30 to 200 participants often report accuracies between 93 and 100 percent under internal validation. In studies covering several hundred to nearly 15,000 people, language, speech, and clinical-record models reached only about 0.69 to 0.78, and neuroimaging models reached 54 to 61 percent. The review, by Younas and colleagues, covered text, speech, facial behavior, electroencephalography, and multimodal approaches. It drew on papers published from January 2015 through August 2026.

The authors found that many studies share methodological weaknesses. Most models are trained against self-report scales such as the PHQ-8 rather than diagnostic interviews. External validation on independent datasets is rare, and widely used public benchmarks show demographic and interviewer-prompt biases. No study so far has shown that using AI detection improves patient outcomes. Each technology also carries its own limits, with large language models performing inconsistently depending on the prompt, and electroencephalography results failing to hold up at scale.

The authors conclude that AI currently has plausible value for scalable pre-screening, continuous monitoring, and triage, but not as an autonomous diagnostic replacement. They say genuine clinical readiness will require larger, demographically diverse datasets, interview-based reference standards, rigorous external and prospective validation, and transparent reporting. They also call for fairness auditing and privacy-preserving designs under clinician supervision. The review's authors are listed as Younas, Paripati, Niharika, Panda, Mwita, Alghzawi, Sahu, Modi, and Aminpoor. The review was reported on November 6, 2026, and the article does not describe any follow-up steps beyond the recommendations the authors set out.

Articles.Title: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Depression Detection Performance Drops In Large Studies

stories.Headline: BuzzFeed Stock in Free Fall as Pivot to AI Blows Up in Its Face
stories.Summary:
BuzzFeed's stock fell sharply on November 5, 2026, dropping from a high of $2.09 earlier that year to $0.57 in a single morning, a 38 percent decline. The fall followed the company's third-quarter earnings report, which showed earnings per share of negative $0.22, 13 cents worse than analysts had expected. Back in March, the company had warned there was "substantial doubt" about its ability to continue operating, after reporting a net loss of $57.3 million for 2025. The stock had already drawn some enthusiasm in May, when a family affiliate of TV personality Byron Allen bought a majority stake in the company.

Allen's affiliate pushed the company toward free-streaming video, audio and user-generated content, and Jonah Peretti received the title of "president of BuzzFeed AI." Allen said the company was chasing YouTube and aimed to become a free video streaming service powered by AI. BuzzFeed has since laid off 33 percent of its remaining staff, roughly two months after Allen took over. The article notes that the company's AI push began in 2023 after the launch of ChatGPT, when it published quizzes and AI-generated travel guides that drew criticism.

The article places much of the blame on Peretti, who has long championed AI and launched several apps built on the technology. It describes his decision to double down on AI content as the source of the company's troubles. In a May interview with The Verge, Peretti said AI was the thing he was most passionate about and claimed it would create a new medium for content. The article says no evidence of that new medium has yet appeared, and it frames the broader picture as one of continued losses and a shrinking business.

Articles.Title: BuzzFeed Stock in Free Fall as Pivot to AI Blows Up in Its Face

stories.Headline: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that the company could be ready for an initial public offering in 2027. He made the remarks at the WSJ Tech conference, and the same day the company said it had formed a strategic partnership with JPMorganChase to supply the bank with artificial intelligence services. The details come from a Wall Street Journal report that PYMNTS cited. Brockman's comments were made as the company faces questions about its financing.

Under the partnership, OpenAI will give the bank access to cybersecurity-focused models through its Daybreak program. According to OpenAI's website, Daybreak gives approved individuals and organizations access to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, along with security solutions, partners and support for protecting systems. After the event, Brockman posted on X that the two companies will explore how advanced AI can help the bank's engineers, security teams, employees and customers. He wrote that he was especially excited about working together on cybersecurity to protect the financial system. Brockman also said the company wants to go public when the timing is right for it.

Brockman's remarks followed a Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI had secured about $11 billion in commitments for its current funding round, less than half of its initial $30 billion target. The report said the company plans to raise more money from family offices and high-net-worth individuals over the coming weeks to reach $20 billion. OpenAI had described this round as an "opportunistic" bridge before a potential IPO, according to a report from October 22. In June, the company said it had submitted a confidential S-1 registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission. At that time it said it had not decided on timing and that it may be a while, because some plans are likely easier as a private company.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO

stories.Headline: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool
stories.Summary:
Economist Mackensie Alston, Ph.D., visited Swarthmore College last week to deliver the annual Frank C. Pierson lecture, titled "Constructing the Criminal: Race and the Perception of AI-Generated Suspects." Alston is an assistant professor in the Department of Finance at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and a faculty affiliate for the Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities at the University of Notre Dame. The lecture was hosted by the college's economics department and honors Frank Pierson '34, a former department chair whose work on anti-discrimination in labor economics aligns with Alston's field. Her latest research uses AI-generated images, differing only by race, to examine bias among police candidates and to improve hiring practices.

Alston said her interest in economics began with Dan Ariely's 2008 book "Predictably Irrational," which challenges the idea that people always act rationally. She described wanting to document behavior that existing theory could not explain, and she designs experiments to test such phenomena. The articles note that economists use lab, online, and field experiments, as well as observational data, and Alston said she prefers defining economics as the study of decision-making. Conclusive research, she argued, lets policymakers test ideas before wide adoption and compare predictions with real-world outcomes. Her work applies this approach to the factors behind police decisions to use potentially lethal force.

Alston drew on Gary Becker's 1968 rational criminal model, which weighs the probability and severity of punishment against the payoff from crime. She and her partner, Dr. Emily Owens, were motivated by research showing Black people face mistreatment by police in many ways. The articles report that improved anti-bias training has shown positive effects, but its impact can fade and depends on ongoing supervisor support. Alston's approach instead targets bias in new officers before they are hired. She has so far conducted two studies using AI images created with Midjourney and Gemini Proshop, and her results have not yet been published because further studies are planned.

During the question period, Alston said she is weighing ways to address social desirability bias, including asking participants how others might describe the images. When asked whether the AI origin of the images affected responses, she said about 70 percent of participants thought the images resembled AI, with 30 percent disagreeing. In an interview with The Phoenix, she stressed interdisciplinary work, noting that economists, sociologists, and psychologists each contribute distinct insight. She suggested that such cooperation can help the academic community move toward solutions.

Articles.Title: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America
stories.Summary:
Turkey has recovered 100 looted historical artifacts from the United States, a milestone the Voice of Emirates reported on November 6, 2026. The operation was carried out by Turkish authorities, who used artificial intelligence and digital analysis to locate the pieces and check their historical origins. The article describes the recovery as the latest step in an ongoing effort to bring back objects that were illegally taken out of the country. Officials were said to have used image analysis and data comparison to match the artifacts' technical features and trace how they moved between owners.

The article says the artifacts had ended up in private collections or foreign institutions after being smuggled abroad. Returning them is presented as part of a wider effort to protect historical heritage and preserve cultural identity. The technology helped with both finding the objects and gathering evidence of where they came from, which the article says strengthens the case for their return. It also notes that the work depended on documenting each piece in enough detail to prove its origin.

The article credits Turkish authorities with leading the recovery but does not name specific officials or quote any statements from them. It does not identify the American holders of the artifacts, the institutions involved, or the individuals suspected of smuggling them. The piece frames the success as an example of how modern technology is becoming a valuable tool against the illicit trade in cultural property. It stresses that the recovery reflects the importance of international cooperation in protecting human heritage.

The article calls for continued legal and technical efforts to pursue those responsible for smuggling historical objects. It also says that returning such artifacts to their countries of origin is essential. The report does not describe any further steps, charges, or timelines for the remaining cases. Readers should look to later coverage for details on the legal process and the artifacts' eventual return.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America

stories.Headline: When doctors and AI medical opinions diverge, humans must question the difference, according to experts
stories.Summary:
Researchers writing in npj Digital Medicine say that when a doctor and an AI tool reach different conclusions about a patient, the gap should be made visible and examined rather than settled by default. The paper, titled "Realizing the value of the divergence event in clinical human-AI interaction," was published in November 2026 and led by Charles E. Binkley of Hackensack Meridian Health. The authors argue that clinicians are told to act as the "human in the loop" but are rarely given a method for doing so. They also say that making AI output easier to explain has not reliably improved clinical decisions and can create false confidence in wrong answers.

The authors propose treating these disagreements as "divergence events," because the human and the machine draw on different kinds of knowledge. A physician brings a bedside sense of the patient and insights from family conversations, while an AI model draws on electronic health records and patterns from thousands or millions of past cases. Their proposed structure asks the clinician to form an independent judgment first, then review the AI output, and then revisit the evidence and their own reasoning if the two differ. One example given is using an AI system as a second, separate reader of breast cancer screening images, with an explicit step to identify exactly where the two readings part ways. The authors say this sequence may reduce liability concerns and help guard against a decline in clinical reasoning skills.

The paper was written by a team that included Florence X. Doo and experts from the University of Maryland School of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, New York Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center, and Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. The authors state that how the field handles these moments will determine whether AI becomes a real partner in safer decisions. They call for making human-AI interactions visible to clinicians in real time and to the field over time. A separate commentary from Science 2.0 on a different topic, deepfake AI doctors in supplement advertising, is unrelated to the paper's findings and is not reflected here.

Articles.Title: When doctors and AI medical opinions diverge, humans must question the difference, according to experts

stories.Headline: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate
stories.Summary:
The University of Montana has established the Human-Centered AI Career Certificate, the first of its kind in the state, and it is being offered this year. Lee Banville, director of the School of Journalism, and Michael Cassens, an associate professor of game design and interactive media, created the nine-credit certificate together and teach its three courses, all of which are taught online. Banville said the goal is to help students understand that artificial intelligence will affect people's lives and careers, not to promote or discourage its use. He stressed that the program is not a sales pitch for the technology.

Cassens said the certificate would strengthen students' resumes and give them foundational knowledge for a changing technological landscape. He said students would be required to use AI tools for assignments, including ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Meta and UM's own model, Chat MT, to see how each works. A typical exercise would be entering the same prompt into several models to compare their responses. Cassens said he accepts AI use as long as students can reasonably defend their choice and explain it openly.

The first course, Creatively Exploring AI, is already taught by Cassens and covers AI's history, hallucinations, biases, terminology, ethics and effects on various disciplines. The second course, Calling Bullshit in the Age of AI, is a journalism class taught by Banville that focuses on critical thinking and recognizing when AI is wrong, and it will be renamed next semester. The third, Human-Centered Leadership in AI, is a new class that Cassens will offer in the spring, adapted from a leadership course he previously taught. Cassens said the curriculum is meant to be adaptable as the technology changes and that the program is grounded in human concerns.

Student reactions are mixed: Grace Smith, a 23-year-old graduate student in game design, said the courses promote discussion rather than either side of the debate, while Kylie Heit, a 23-year-old senior cello performance major from Helena, said the program normalizes AI and that its "Human-Centered" title is misleading. Banville acknowledged that many people fear AI and that real questions about it deserve attention, but he noted that a free one-day, one-credit AI course the School of Journalism offered last spring drew only about 15 students, far fewer than he expected. He hopes the certificate will attract more interest and that students will engage with the topic regardless of local debates over data centers. He told students that the tools are already here and will change their lives, and that his aim is for them to be prepared to decide how, when and whether to use them.

Articles.Title: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate

stories.Headline: Sysco Counts on AI Routing and Bidding for $500 Million in Savings
stories.Summary:
Sysco, the largest food service distributor in the United States, is using artificial intelligence to cut what it costs to move and buy goods, according to a November 6, 2026 report from PYMNTS. The company runs 333 distribution centers in 10 countries that serve about 670,000 customer locations. Its U.S. trucks drive more than 4.5 million miles a week. Sysco's routing software is live in pilot regions and has raised the number of cases delivered per mile by 2% to 4%.

Sysco introduced a $500 million AI efficiency program in a September 9 press release. The program has four workstreams covering supply chain productivity, automation across merchandising and procurement, indirect spend management, and customer experience with back-office simplification. The company expects $100 million in net cost savings this fiscal year and at least $500 million by the close of fiscal 2029. Sysco plans to roll the routing software out to every U.S. broadline operating location this fiscal year, with a second phase starting at the end of the year. Each 1% gain in cases per mile is worth about $3 million across the company.

Sysco CEO and Chair of the Board Kevin Hourican discussed the routing results and the program on the fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings call on November 3. He said the company's first AI-run supplier bid finished about 30% above its savings target, with a person supervising. Sysco Chief Financial Officer Brandon Sewell said the reverse-auction tools cover more than $1 billion of annual indirect spend. Hourican also said that AI360, the company's in-house sales tool, helped raise Sysco brand mix in local accounts by 44 basis points, and that sales consultants still make the final decisions.

The article places Sysco within a wider trend. A PYMNTS Intelligence report from July found that wholesale enterprises use AI for 35 of 75 tracked business tasks, compared with 20 in retail and 22 in construction. The same research found that 85% of wholesale executives said future AI spending will prioritize margins and profitability. Sysco rival US Foods reported a 2% gain in cases delivered per mile from its own routing software, according to a PYMNTS report from October 28.

Articles.Title: Sysco Counts on AI Routing and Bidding for $500 Million in Savings

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity
stories.Summary:
Washington, DC, has become a focal point for a growing backlash, as several American museums have faced a wave of rejection for exhibitions built on artificial intelligence. Visitors have voiced clear reservations about displaying works that rely on digital technology instead of human creativity. The reporting describes the response as a widening debate over the limits of technology in art and culture. Questions have arisen about whether algorithm-made works hold real artistic value and whether they can express human experience, emotion, and ideas. These concerns come as AI tools spread quickly and can produce images that mimic the styles of well-known artists.

Many museum visitors argue that art is not defined only by its final form but also by the creative process and the personal effort behind it. They stress that human experience matters, and they question whether works made almost entirely by AI are authentic enough for major cultural institutions. Supporters of the technology see these experiments differently, describing them as a natural extension of artistic evolution that can open new horizons and offer fresh ways to present ideas. The debate reaches beyond museums to artists, critics, and cultural bodies. It also touches on intellectual property rights, the sources of images and data used to train these systems, and who bears responsibility for works produced with algorithmic help.

Museums now face the challenge of balancing technological progress with maintaining public trust. According to the reporting, they must clarify the tools used in producing exhibited works and how much a human artist was involved. Some creators also worry that the rapid output of modern software, which can produce large volumes of work quickly and cheaply, may shrink opportunities for traditional artists. The article notes that the American museum debate shows technological development does not automatically earn public acceptance. It suggests the relationship between art and AI still needs clear guidelines that protect creators' rights and preserve the authenticity of the artistic experience without stifling innovation.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity

stories.Headline: Top 100 AI Venture Capitalists 2026: K2 Global and Ozi Amanat
stories.Summary:
K2 Global and its founder, Ozi Amanat, have both been named to the 2026 Strebulaev–Jackson AI Venture Rankings, according to a press release issued through GlobeNewswire on November 5, 2026. The rankings, published by Stanford Graduate School of Business Professor Ilya Strebulaev and researcher Blake Jackson, identify leading venture capital firms and individual investors based on their investments in U.S.-based artificial intelligence companies. Amanat is listed alongside investors including Peter Thiel, Reid Hoffman, Vinod Khosla, Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen. K2 Global was also named among the Top 100 AI venture capital firms worldwide, and the press release says it is the only Singapore-headquartered firm on that list and one of just five firms based outside the United States.

The rankings evaluate investment value creation using valuations, dilution, net profit and investment attribution, and they cover qualifying investments in U.S.-based AI companies through August 31, 2026. The release describes K2 Global as a relatively small, independent venture capital firm that invests across artificial intelligence, robotics, neuroscience, defense technology and other frontier sectors. Its portfolio is said to include SpaceX, Neuralink and Shield AI. The announcement does not say how the rankings were weighted beyond those factors or how many investments qualified for each firm.

Amanat, in the release, described the recognition as meaningful, saying it came after years of finding exceptional founders and backing them as they build companies. He said the honor was alongside investors he had long admired and acknowledged that the work had not always been easy. He also thanked the founders and investors who had supported the firm and said the best was yet to come. The release itself was prepared by the company and its distribution through a press-release service, and the publishing outlet notes that its editorial teams were not involved in creating the post. The source of the rankings is a Substack article by Strebulaev and Jackson, which the release links to.

Articles.Title: Top 100 AI Venture Capitalists 2026: K2 Global and Ozi Amanat

stories.Headline: Putnam Career & Technical Center students explore the future of AI
stories.Summary:
The Putnam Career and Technical Center in Putnam County, West Virginia, hosted a student-led cybersecurity conference on Thursday, November 5, 2026, themed "AI: The New Digital Frontier." Marshall University professor Dr. Josh Brunty gave the keynote presentation at the event. Education and technology professionals helped students navigate an AI-driven world and gave them a sense of what their future could look like. The sessions also covered how students can protect themselves in that environment. The conference was organized as a way for students to explore how artificial intelligence is shaping their lives and careers.

Jeff Pitchford, the cybersecurity instructor at the center, said the event gave students a chance to speak one-on-one with industry leaders who work in the middle of the field. He stressed that networking is an important skill and called the day a strong opportunity to build those connections. Pitchford also said the presenters talked with students about how AI will affect the workforce. He told the station that AI is not going to take all the jobs, which he described as a stressful concern for many young people. Instead, he said, AI can take aggregated data and make work easier and faster, and it can help workers spot problems they might otherwise miss.

Presenters came from several institutions, including professors from Marshall University, West Virginia State, Glenville State and BridgeValley. The article describes the conference as a way for students to see how these schools and companies think about AI and security. It does not report any formal changes, requirements or policies that resulted from the event. The article is a local news report published by WOWK 13 News and does not describe any follow-up events. It also does not indicate whether the conference will be repeated next year.

Articles.Title: Putnam Career & Technical Center students explore the future of AI

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer explains why no AI stock seems safe from the market carnage
stories.Summary:
CNBC host Jim Cramer said on Thursday that uncertainty over the future of the data center build-out has made artificial intelligence stocks increasingly difficult to value, and that this has driven steep selling over the previous two sessions. The sell-off spread across the AI trade, reaching chipmakers as well as companies that supply power and electrical equipment for data centers. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell 3% on Wednesday and another 10% on Thursday, while GE Vernova and Sandisk dropped 7% and 22% respectively on Thursday. Cramer's comments were published on November 5, 2026.

Investors fear that regulatory hurdles and local opposition to new data centers could slow the build-out, which would undercut the growth forecasts that support chipmakers' valuations. Cramer used Nvidia as his main example, noting that the chipmaker trades at roughly 12 times next year's earnings with an expected growth rate of 70 percent, which makes it look cheap. He warned, however, that those projections assume demand stays strong for years, and that the stock would not be a bargain if the U.S. cannot permit new data centers as quickly as it does now. Cramer also questioned Micron's long-term take-or-pay contracts, which give some revenue visibility even if customers do not take delivery, and he wondered how firm those deals would be if a customer ran into financial trouble.

Cramer praised Advanced Micro Devices' latest earnings as among the best quarters he had seen, and he cited CEO Lisa Su's projection that the broader data center market could eventually reach $1 trillion. He said the stock, which he noted was at $188 in March and is now at $404, looks expensive by that measure, and he suggested this may be the real problem. Cramer framed the central question as whether regulatory hurdles will significantly slow data center construction or only delay it. He said that until the outlook becomes clearer, even strong earnings may not justify AI stock valuations. He also disclosed that Cramer's Charitable Trust, run by the CNBC Investing Club, owns shares of Nvidia and Micron.

Articles.Title: Jim Cramer explains why no AI stock seems safe from the market carnage

stories.Headline: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production
stories.Summary:
A study published in the Journal of Industrial Ecology by Liu and Tang in 2026 evaluated how artificial intelligence can be used in sustainable apparel design and production. The authors reviewed AI tools used for concept generation, sewing-pattern engineering, virtual prototyping, production planning, consumer evaluation, and circular information systems. They organized the review by lifecycle stage, sustainability problem, and how well each tool had been validated. The findings were reported on November 6, 2026, by Scienmag and bioengineer.org.

The research drew on four separate sets of data covering design, specialist appraisal, consumer response, and production metrics. These included 4,200 garment-design records and assessments of 350 designs by 28 specialists. A consumer experiment tracked 858 participants who completed the study out of 864 recruited, and 426 enterprise pattern records with measured cutting-waste rates were also analyzed. In the consumer experiment, participants appeared to show higher purchase intention for co-created and labeled products, but lower intention at the higher price premium. The authors noted that the precision of one statistical reconstruction was limited by rounding in the reported inputs.

The clearest direct evidence of material savings came from manufacturing pattern engineering. Using ridge regression across the observed enterprise, quarter, and product mix, the model achieved a test root mean square error of 0.049 and a mean absolute error of 0.038, compared with a baseline root mean square error of 0.096 when predicting cutting-waste rates. To organize the results, the authors proposed an integration framework built on three pillars: data and technical integration, circular design performance, and validation and governance. It also uses four evaluation dimensions: digital plausibility, design feasibility, market viability, and verified sustainability performance. The authors themselves stated that direct sustainability verification remains limited to production-stage cutting waste and that broader lifecycle outcomes would need separate validation.

Articles.Title: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production

stories.Headline: Building On Progress In China–USA Talks On AI – Analysis
stories.Summary:
On 24 September 2026, US President Donald J. Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a summit in Washington, DC, where artificial intelligence was a major topic. Analysts writing for the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) describe the meeting as a break from earlier Xi–Biden summits, which had been held on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings. This time the summit was the main purpose of Xi's state visit, and Xi went to Washington even though a United Nations General Assembly session was under way in New York. The meeting followed a May 2026 summit in Beijing and produced a deadline of November 2026 for a follow-on technical dialogue, along with an agreed bilateral communication channel for reporting AI incidents, which some have called an "AI hotline."

The authors argue that the talks need trade and industry expertise to move from broad pledges to practical rules. Earlier summits were dominated by foreign ministry and state department officials, while the May and September 2026 meetings included trade officials and chief executives from major technology firms, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, OpenAI and Apple. The authors say those executives should move from the banquet table to the negotiating table. They also say both countries depend on something the other controls, namely US limits on Chinese access to advanced chips and computing power and Chinese limits on exports of critical minerals, and that this mutual dependence could give the dialogue a starting point. The article does not say whether the chip or mineral restrictions were discussed at the September summit, though both official summaries appear to have left them aside.

The authors identify several unresolved problems. The US summary uses the term "super intelligence," while China's official report continues to use "artificial intelligence," a difference they say could complicate how incidents are defined and how the hotline is framed. They also note that it is unclear which incidents would be reported, who would report them and how, since AI companies often detect anomalies first and the US has no single mandatory national reporting system for them, whereas China already operates a tiered system under its Cyberspace Administration. The authors say the coming dialogue will be a key test of whether both sides can agree on definitions of AI incidents, designated points of contact and reciprocal information sharing. They conclude that progress is more likely if technical and operational experts from trade and industry take part, since these groups drive AI development and its integration into the economy.

Articles.Title: Building On Progress In China–USA Talks On AI – Analysis

stories.Headline: AI and Misinformation Are Turning Migrants Into Targets
stories.Summary:
Misinformation about migrants is spreading quickly, and artificial intelligence is making it worse, the head of the UN Migration agency warned in Geneva on 2 November 2026. Speaking at the opening of the International Dialogue on Migration, IOM Director General Amy Pope said false narratives are turning public anxiety into suspicion and turning people into targets. She said economic uncertainty, conflict and climate pressures are testing governments and communities, and that public trust in migration management is under growing strain worldwide. Pope told the gathering that facts alone will not restore confidence, and that institutions must listen and act even when what they hear is uncomfortable.

The agency says false and misleading claims about migrants, spread through social media and generative AI, are deepening division and mistrust within communities. As trust erodes, governments face stronger public resistance and have less room to cooperate, while migrants face greater risks along their journeys. This is happening as development funding shrinks and international cooperation comes under pressure. The stakes are large, since more than 304 million people live outside their country of birth, including 168 million migrant workers. Money sent home by migrants reaches around one billion people, roughly one in eight people on the planet, paying for food, schooling and healthcare.

Pope set out three areas for action. First, countries along the same routes should plan together to expand regular pathways, strengthen protection, manage borders humanely and support dignified return. Second, communities hit by repeated floods and failing harvests need early investment so people can stay where possible and move safely when they must. Third, reliable data and the voices of affected people should guide decisions, with technology that protects personal information and guards against bias. Pope framed the message as one of trust built gradually, through agreements kept and people treated fairly.

The timing matters because of several upcoming milestones. In May, a record number of States and stakeholders reaffirmed their commitment to safe, orderly and regular migration at the International Migration Review Forum. The UN will review global progress on the Sustainable Development Goal target on well-managed migration in July 2027, followed by the SDG Summit in September 2027, where discussions on what follows the 2030 Agenda will begin. The IDM, marking 25 years, will feed its outcomes into the IOM Council in December, which will hold a high-level panel on strengthening political trust for migration governance.

Articles.Title: AI and Misinformation Are Turning Migrants Into Targets

stories.Headline: Outsmart Artificial Intelligence with CEDMO Game!
stories.Summary:
CEDMO, the Central European Digital Media Observatory, has released an educational game called CEDMO Game that invites players to test how well artificial intelligence models can spot disinformation. The game was developed at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies (KInIT) as part of CEDMO consortium activities and was published on the CEDMO website on 5 November 2026. Researchers Ján Čegiň, Tomáš Matejov, Jakub Šimko, and Ivan Srba contributed to its development. The announcement asks whether AI can reliably identify false information and how it reacts when the same information is phrased slightly differently.

The game works by giving the player a short text, which they already know to be true or false, alongside the verdict of an AI model designed to detect disinformation. The player must rewrite the text so that its meaning stays the same while the model changes its estimate of whether the text is disinformation. To start, a player needs only an email address, with no account or password required. Teachers can create a session, set a time limit, choose texts from a prepared library or add their own, and students join with a numeric code or QR code.

The game is available in Czech, Slovak, Polish, and English, although the AI model itself currently works only in English. The developers say the game is meant to show how sensitive AI systems are to linguistic nuance and how small wording changes can alter a verdict even when the content is unchanged. Tomáš Matejov said players can see within minutes how a few changed words can lead the model to a different evaluation of the same information. Ján Čegiň said that understanding these limits should help people use AI more responsibly and approach information with more critical judgment.

The announcement describes the game mainly as a tool for schools and educational activities, though anyone can use it. The article frames the game as a counterpoint to uncritical trust in AI outputs, noting that models are powerful but not infallible. It does not describe any further phases of the project or any plans beyond the current release. Interested users are directed to the CEDMO website to play the game.

Articles.Title: Outsmart Artificial Intelligence with CEDMO Game!

stories.Headline: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece rather than a news report, and it draws on a specific event: a 2026 pilot run by the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy with the AI health-tech company Doctronic. The pilot began in January 2026 and used an automated AI system to process renewals of refill or repeat medications for 190 chronic conditions, based on earlier prescriptions written by licensed physicians. The state office said the system would work within strict parameters and under physician oversight, and it was meant to ease the workload of doctors and widen patients' access to care. Within three months, in April 2026, the Utah Medical Licensing Board called for the immediate suspension of the pilot, which ended the first legally AI-led system to renew prescriptions for chronic non-controlled medications.

The board said the pilot compromised patient safety and put patients at risk. It also said that AI or other financial motives should not be allowed to override the duty to protect patients, and that this was what had happened in this case. The author, Bhabani Shankar Nayak, a professor of business management at London Metropolitan University, uses the episode to argue that AI companies are pressing governments worldwide to deploy AI in healthcare for profit. He argues that medical professionals and researchers are calling instead for a "human loop" covering every stage of an AI system's life, from problem formulation and data collection through model development, validation, and final decisions on how the tools are used. He also contends that the same principle applies in every sector, since people's welfare should not be sacrificed for productivity or profit.

The author's broader claim is that AI and its language models carry demographic, racial, gender, social, cultural, and class biases from the way problems are framed, data is collected, and models are built and tested. In his view, these biases can produce wrong diagnoses and wrong prescriptions, and uncritical commercial adoption threatens both human welfare and the scientific development of AI. He calls for transparent governance with sustained human oversight and accountability, so that people control the technology rather than being controlled by it. The article does not report any official response beyond the licensing board's statement, and it does not describe any further steps planned for the Utah pilot or for similar programs elsewhere.

Articles.Title: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd

stories.Headline: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
stories.Summary:
Amazon's Marketplace team has described a new system, built on Amazon SageMaker AI, for judging the quality of A+ Content, the rich media section on Amazon product detail pages. The article, published on the AWS Blogs site on November 5, 2026, explains that brands range from large companies with in-house design teams to small brands with limited resources, which produces uneven content. Selling partners that use high-quality A+ Content reportedly see sales rise by 8 to 20 percent compared with those that do not. Because A+ Content has few strict specifications for image ratio or word count, the article says content composition varies widely, and the authors argue that checking each asset separately misses how text, images, and video work together on the page.

The proposed approach renders the full product page as a single snapshot and asks a vision-language model to evaluate it holistically across four dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension receives a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a written rationale. These outputs feed a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on consensus labels from one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators, who rated 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories as high or low quality. The article reports that each annotator's agreement with the consensus, measured by Cohen's kappa, ranged from 0.845 to 0.915. The authors say the classifier, which is retrained on a CPU rather than fine-tuning the foundation model, reached 0.89 accuracy and a 0.90 F1 score on a 20 percent holdout set, compared with 0.80 accuracy and 0.84 F1 for a simple averaged baseline.

The article also adds optical character recognition to measure text density, character density, spacing, and overall readability, because the vision-language model is weaker on fine-grained readability issues. Combining these readability signals with the vision-language model's scores produced 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score on the same holdout set, and the authors use SHAP explanations to show which factors drove each decision so that selling partners receive actionable recommendations. The authors present the work as a model for scoring content at scale on Amazon SageMaker AI, covering data annotation, hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. The article excerpt provided does not say whether the system has been deployed to all sellers or what changes to Amazon's listing policies will follow, so no further rollout details can be confirmed from it.

Articles.Title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI

stories.Headline: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of forty-six environmental studies has mapped the energy, water, material and land demands of artificial intelligence, finding that the physical infrastructure behind machine learning draws heavily on electricity, water, minerals and land. The work was carried out by researcher Sibongiseni Hlabisa and published in the journal Carbon Neutral Systems. The authors searched Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar for studies published from 2015 to 2025, starting from about 3,130,000 records and narrowing them through successive screenings until forty-six sources met all inclusion criteria. The corpus combined twenty-two peer-reviewed articles and proceedings, seventeen technical and government reports, four preprints and three reference volumes.

The review's central finding is that artificial intelligence cannot be judged through carbon figures or narrow efficiency measures alone, because its footprint grows as computing workloads expand. Training a single large model such as PaLM-2 or GPT-3 is reported to consume between 1.3 and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of electricity. The International Energy Agency projects that data center electricity demand will rise from 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 under its base case, approaching 1,200 terawatt-hours by 2035, with the United States accounting for nearly half of global growth. Water is needed both to cool servers and to make chips, with evaporative cooling using roughly 7,000 to 12,000 liters per megawatt-hour and each silicon wafer requiring 1.8 to 2.5 cubic meters. Hyperscale data centers typically occupy 30 to 100 hectares, and the review notes that some regulators, including authorities in Ireland and Singapore, have already moved to limit or condition new facilities.

The authors argue that policymakers should move beyond voluntary corporate efficiency metrics toward binding regional limits on cumulative electricity, water withdrawal and land conversion tied to local ecological capacity. They point to practical measures such as capturing waste heat for district heating, recycling ultrapure water in chip plants, recovering metals from retired hardware, and shifting non-urgent computing to times and places with surplus wind or solar power. The review also warns that the benefits of computing are concentrated in the Global North while extraction and e-waste burdens fall on the Global South, and it acknowledges significant empirical gaps in the underlying evidence. The articles supplied do not say how these recommendations will be taken up by governments or industry, so the outcome remains open.

Articles.Title: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes
stories.Summary:
Researchers from The Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University published a systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Radiology finding that magnetic resonance imaging artificial intelligence models show moderate accuracy in identifying pain-related nerve phenotypes in patients with non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia. The team pooled eight eligible studies comprising 628 nerve-level observations. Using a bivariate random-effects model, they found a pooled sensitivity of 0.83, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.78 to 0.87, and a pooled specificity of 0.81, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.74 to 0.86. The summary area under the curve was 0.86, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.82 to 0.88. The authors describe these tools as potential adjunctive diagnostic instruments rather than replacements for clinical judgment.

Trigeminal neuralgia causes recurrent, brief, shock-like facial pain that is often triggered by light touch, eating, or speaking, and it can severely disrupt sleep and daily life. The authors used the term non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia to cover classical and idiopathic forms once structural causes such as tumors or multiple sclerosis plaques have been excluded. Distinguishing these forms matters because it shapes decisions about procedures such as microvascular decompression. Standard visual review of scans is limited, since vessel contact against the nerve also appears in people without symptoms. The review notes that the diagnostic criteria for classical disease require definite morphological changes, not contact alone.

Quantitative radiomic and machine-learning methods aim to detect subtle differences that the eye cannot reliably see. The reviewers searched the literature following the PRISMA 2020 statement and its diagnostic accuracy extension, and registered their protocol in PROSPERO under identifier CRD420261394456. The initial searches produced 164 citations, which became 103 unique publications after removing 61 duplicates. After screening, 38 full-text reports were assessed, and eight studies met all eligibility criteria. Six studies used 3.0-Tesla scanners, one used a 1.5-Tesla system, and one used both field strengths.

Model types ranged from logistic regression and support vector machines to neural networks and ensemble classifiers. The review found mild heterogeneity, with inconsistency values of 20.77 percent for sensitivity and 27.65 percent for specificity. Risk-of-bias assessments flagged concerns including small samples, limited external validation, and possible data leakage during feature selection. The authors caution that the evidence rests on only eight mostly single-center, retrospective studies without independent multicenter testing.

They also note that the analysis combined contralateral-nerve designs with healthy-control comparisons, two tasks they describe as biologically different. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed that radiomics-only models achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.84 and specificity of 0.84, while models combining radiomics with morphological variables reached 0.86 and 0.78. Excluding one influential study shifted the pooled sensitivity to 0.82 and specificity to 0.78. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes

stories.Headline: How Artificial Intelligence is reshaping accounting - KSNV
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing the accounting profession, and this was the focus of Intuit Connect in Las Vegas, where the company's event highlighted how the technology is reshaping the work. News 3 spoke with Matt Wilpers, a Peloton instructor and former accountant, to learn why human involvement still matters in an industry being transformed by automation. The article was published on November 5, 2026, and was posted by KSNV, a Las Vegas station. The piece is short and centers on that single conversation. The article does not describe any new law, rule, or specific requirement.

It frames the change as a shift in how accounting work gets done, with automated tools taking on tasks that people once handled by hand. Its main point is that the human role remains important even as those tools spread through the field. The article does not provide figures, dates for any policy, or detailed examples of which tasks are being automated. The article attributes its perspective mainly to Matt Wilpers, who is identified as a Peloton instructor and former accountant. According to the piece, Wilpers was asked why people matter more than ever in an AI-driven world, and the article presents his views as the reason human judgment still counts.

The article does not name anyone else as responsible for the trend, and it does not include any statement from Intuit beyond the event itself. The surrounding page carries unrelated local news, including changes to short-term rental rules in Clark County and a ballot measure outcome in Nevada, but none of those items is connected to the accounting story. The article does not say what comes next for the technology, the event, or the profession. Any further developments would have to come from later reporting, and the piece itself offers no timeline or follow-up plans.

Articles.Title: How Artificial Intelligence is reshaping accounting - KSNV

stories.Headline: Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push — SI6 to bring 80X more compute performance, Dojo 3 headed to space
stories.Summary:
Tesla has unveiled a revised AI accelerator roadmap, along with a new naming scheme that replaces "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in the chip labels. The disclosure, reported by Tom's Hardware and published on November 6, 2026, lays out the company's next chips and its plans for a new training accelerator. According to the article, Tesla now labels its chips SI4, SI5 and SI6 rather than AI4, AI5 and AI6, and the same branding is being applied to older parts. The article notes that Elon Musk had also confirmed SpaceXAI would be renamed SpaceXSI.

The roadmap projects that the 6th Generation inference accelerator, SI6, will deliver roughly 80 times the compute performance of the existing 4th Generation chip, SI4. The article's table lists estimated compute of 17,280 to 46,080 TOPS for SI6 and 72 TOPS for SI4, with SI6 built on TSMC 3nm or Samsung 2nm-class processes and using a multi-chiplet design with GDDR7 memory. The third-generation Dojo training accelerator, D3, is described as a chiplet-based design combining 2.5D and 3D packaging with stacked HBM, a clear departure from the wafer-scale, SRAM-centric Dojo D1. Tesla has not yet disclosed D3's compute performance, memory capacity, manufacturing process or development schedule, though it says D3 will be optimized for space, training and scaling.

The article attributes the roadmap to Tesla, which presented it in a recent company briefing, and cites Elon Musk as the figure behind the new naming. It reports that Musk canceled the wafer-level Dojo project in August 2025 and said in August 2026 that SpaceX and xAI would use Nvidia hardware exclusively in their terrestrial and extraterrestrial data centers. The article also points to a social media post noting that the renaming appears to echo a push by President Trump to replace "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence." The article does not say how the new naming will affect Tesla's product timelines or whether Tesla will pursue wafer-scale integration for D3, and it treats that question as unresolved.

Articles.Title: Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push — SI6 to bring 80X more compute performance, Dojo 3 headed to space

stories.Headline: The New York Times Doesn’t Understand AI’s Role in Suppressing Wages
stories.Summary:
A Gizmodo column published November 6, 2026, by Matt Novak argues that the New York Times missed the more important way artificial intelligence is affecting the American labor market. The Times article, written by Ben Casselman under the headline "A.I. Was Supposed to Come for Our Jobs. So Far, Evidence Is Mixed," asked whether AI has disrupted employment, and Novak says it never mentions wages. Novak notes that the piece was published on a Friday and came shortly after the midterm elections, which he says showed widespread public hostility toward AI and data centers. He also points to the Times's mention of Microsoft offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, while white-collar sectors such as accounting, legal services, and finance mostly added jobs in October.

Novak describes the broader labor numbers as mixed but not alarming. The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, more than expected, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent. He writes that wages rose just 3.1 percent over the past year according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, while the latest available annual inflation rate was 3.7 percent in September, which means real wages have fallen. He cites a Federal Reserve Bank of Boston study from September finding that workers who feared losing their jobs to AI were less likely to believe they could negotiate higher pay. He argues that low unemployment usually pushes wages up, and that AI has seemingly broken that pattern.

Novak attributes the argument largely to David Kelly, Chief Global Strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, who said on CNBC in September that workers feel threatened by AI and lack the confidence to ask for raises. Kelly is paraphrased as saying that the wage growth figure, measured year over year, was the lowest since May 2021. Novak also quotes CNBC host Leslie Picker agreeing that workers may feel they had better keep their heads down. Novak himself says the Times piece is "mostly fine" as a snapshot of public confusion, but he contends that it overlooks the possibility that AI is weakening bargaining power before any effect appears in unemployment figures. He lays out several scenarios, including a slow hollowing out of the middle class and a decade of lower living standards, while acknowledging that no one can yet know which will occur.

Articles.Title: The New York Times Doesn’t Understand AI’s Role in Suppressing Wages

stories.Headline: Copyright Suits Over AI Training Continue With Latest Surge Against Meta
stories.Summary:
Meta is facing a new wave of lawsuits accusing the company of using copyrighted works to train its artificial intelligence models without the authors' permission. The suits are the latest in a series of cases testing how intellectual property law applies to AI. Reporter Brendan Pierson wrote about the filings in a Law.com article published on November 6, 2026. The article's framing is that the litigation continues to build against the company. One of the plaintiffs' lawyers, Kyle Roche of Freedman Normand Friedland, explained his firm's approach.

He said the firm chose to sue on behalf of individual authors rather than bringing a class action. According to him, a class action can be difficult because it may be hard to prove that all members of the class were affected by the AI companies' conduct in the same way.
